The Institute of Ismaili Studies
The Institute of Ismaili Studies was established in 1977 with the object
of promoting scholarship and learning on Islam, in the historical as
well as contemporary contexts, and a better understanding of its
relationship with other societies and faiths.
The Institute’s programmes encourage a perspective which is not
conﬁned to the theological and religious heritage of Islam, but seeks to
explore the relationship of religious ideas to broader dimensions of
society and culture. The programmes thus encourage an interdisci-
plinary approach to the materials of Islamic history and thought.
Particular attention is also given to issues of modernity that arise as
Muslims seek to relate their heritage to the contemporary situation.
Within the Islamic tradition, the Institute’s programmes promote
research on those areas which have, to date, received relatively little
attention from scholars. These include the intellectual and literary
expressions of Shiʿism in general, and Ismailism in particular.
In the context of Islamic societies, the Institute’s programmes are
informed by the full range and diversity of cultures in which Islam is
practised today, from the Middle East, South and Central Asia, and
Africa to the industrialised societies of the West, thus taking into
consideration the variety of contexts that shape the ideals, beliefs and
practices of the faith.
These objectives are realised through concrete programmes and
activities organised and implemented by various departments of the
Institute. The Institute also collaborates periodically, on a programme-
speciﬁc basis, with other institutions of learning in the United
Kingdom and abroad.
The Institute’s academic publications fall into a number of
interrelated categories:
v

1.
Occasional papers or essays addressing broad themes of the
relationship between religion and society, with special reference
to Islam.
2.
Works exploring speciﬁc aspects of Islamic faith and culture, or
the contributions of individual Muslim thinkers or writers.
3.
Editions or translations of signiﬁcant primary or secondary texts.
4.
Translations of poetic or literary texts that illustrate the rich
heritage of spiritual, devotional and symbolic expressions in
Muslim history.
5.
Works on Ismaili history and thought, and the relationship of the
Ismailis to other traditions, communities and schools of thought
in Islam.
6.
Proceedings of conferences and seminars sponsored by the
Institute.
7.
Bibliographical works and catalogues that document manuscripts,
printed texts and other source materials.
This book falls into category two listed above.
In facilitating these and other publications, the Institute’s sole aim is to
encourage original research and analysis of relevant issues. While
every effort is made to ensure that the publications are of a high
academic standard, there is naturally bound to be a diversity of views,
ideas and interpretations. As such, the opinions expressed in these
publications must be understood as belonging to their authors alone.
Words of Power
vi

Shiʿi Heritage Series
Shiʿi Muslims, with their rich intellectual and cultural heritage, have
contributed signiﬁcantly to the fecundity and diversity of the Islamic
traditions throughout the centuries, enabling Islam to evolve and
ﬂourish both as a major religion and also as a civilisation. In spite of
this, Shiʿi Islam has received little scholarly attention in the West,
either in medieval or modern times. It is only in recent decades that
academic interest has focused increasingly on Shiʿi Islam within the
wider study of Islam.
The principal objective of the Shiʿi Heritage Series, launched by The
Institute of Ismaili Studies, is to enhance general knowledge of Shiʿi
Islam and promote a better understanding of its history, doctrines and
practices in
their historical
and contemporary manifestations.
Addressing all Shiʿi communities, the series also aims to engage in
discussions on theoretical and methodological issues, while inspiring
further research in the ﬁeld.
Works published in this series include monographs, collective
volumes, editions and translations of primary texts, and bibliographi-
cal projects, bringing together some of the most signiﬁcant themes in
the study of Shiʿi Islam through an interdisciplinary approach, and
making them accessible to a wide readership.

Note on Transliteration and Conventions
The transliteration of Arabic and Persian in this book follows the rules
of the Encyclopaedia of Islam, with some modiﬁcations: j instead of dj,
ch instead of č, q instead of k. . Turkish transliteration conforms to
modern Turkish orthography.
Unless otherwise indicated, the translation of all Qurʾānic verses
follows that of A. J. Arberry, The Koran Interpreted, occasionally with
some modiﬁcations required by the context.
Qurʾānic verse references are given in the text. References of h. adīths
and biblical citations are summarised, in alphabetical order, in
Inventories I and II. The footnotes in the main text specify the entry
number in the relevant Inventory.
Unless otherwise indicated, all citations in Parts One to Three are
from the manuscript British Library Oc.Or.5957 of the Jāwidān-nāma-
yi kabīr, the magnum opus of Fad.l Allāh Astarābādī, known also, with
reference to its incipit, as the Jāwidān-nāma-yi shish ibtidāʾ.
The original Persian text of the long citations from the Jāwidān-
nāma and the works of Fad.l Allāh’s followers is included at the end of
the book. In order to facilitate the location of the original text of any
particular citation, the Persian text of citations is arranged according
to the numbers of the corresponding folios.

Preface and Acknowledgements
When, in the mid-1990s, I came to Paris with a small book of ʿImād al-
Dīn Nasīmī’s poetry in my pocket, I could not have known that it
would take me on a long and surprising journey.1 In fact, I nearly
forgot this book for the next few years, overtaken by work on another
project. However, when the time came to choose the topic for my
Master’s dissertation, Nasīmī’s poetry suddenly came back to my
mind, singing its strange distiches. These verses from the 9th/15th
century had an almost post-modernist ring to them, with their
resonant lines reverberating the same phoneme or syllable several
times, then suddenly ﬂowing into beautiful, powerful words and
rhymes. I knew next to nothing about Nasīmī, except that he was a
courageous man who died ﬂayed alive. I knew still less about his
intellectual and spiritual background. The short introduction to his
book of poetry mentioned a group called H. urūfīs and a certain Fad.l
Allāh from Astarābād, their leader, whose teachings would have much
1 Nasīmī (d. 820/1417–1418), the famous poet and legendary ﬁgure, especially in
the Turkic world was, during a certain period, one of the closest followers of Fad.l Allāh
Astarābādī, the founder of the H. urūfī movement. For the general information about
Nasīmī, see F. Babinger, ‘Nesīmī’, EI2, vol. 8, p. 8, and A. Gölpınarlı, ‘Nesīmī’, Islâm
Ansiklopedisi (İstanbul, 1960), vol. 9, pp. 206–207. A more detailed account on his life
and works can be found in ʿA. Mirfetrous, Zindagī, ashʿār wa ʿaqāʾid-i Nasīmī, shāʿir
wa mutafakkir-i h. urūfī ([Stockholm?], 1992); Kathleen R. F. Burrill, The Quatrains of
Nesimi, Fourteenth-Century Turkic Huruﬁ(The Hague and Paris, 1972) and B. S.
Amoretti, ‘Caratteristiche huruﬁte del divano persiano di Nesimi’, Studi Iranici 17
(1977), pp. 267–285. For Nasīmī’s inﬂuence in the Arab world, see H. T. Norris,
‘Aspects of the Inﬂuence of Nesimi’s HuruﬁVerse, and his Martyrdom, in the Arab
East between the 16th and 18th Centuries’, in G. Veinstein, ed., Syncrétismes et hérésies
dans l’Orient seldjoukide et ottoman (XIVe–XVIIIe siècle) (Paris, 2005), pp. 163–182,
and on Nasīmī as a ﬁgure of H. allājian legend, see L. Massignon, La Passion de Husayn
ibn Mansûr Hallâj (Paris, 1975), vol. 2, pp. 261–268.
xiii

inﬂuenced Nasīmī. But who were the H. urūfīs and what kind of
teachings found expression in Nasīmī’s poetry?
When I mentioned these questions in a conversation with
Mohammad Ali Amir-Moezzi, my supervisor at that time, I did not
seriously consider them as a possible topic for academic work. After
all, Nasīmī was a famous poet and I was sure that his own works and
anything related to them had been thoroughly researched long ago. I
only expected some references from my erudite professor. I was
surprised to hear that most of the H. urūfī texts had not yet been
published, and that the primary sources of H. urūfī thought, the works
of Fad.l Allāh Astarābādī himself, were still little known. This is how I
found myself studying the few published H. urūfī works for my Master’s
dissertation, then embarking on the work on Fad.l Allāh’s magnum
opus, the Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr, the ‘Great Book of Eternity’, for my
Ph.D.2
I will not dwell here on the particular features of the Jāwidān-nāma
as a text; they are described further below in the Introduction. It
should be mentioned, however, that the Jāwidān-nāma does not
contain any systematic presentation of the doctrine. It is essentially a
huge corpus of fragments. The main purpose of the present book is to
produce a comprehensive presentation of the central doctrinal lines of
the Jāwidān-nāma, such as they appear from the analytical study of the
relevant fragments.
The Introduction begins with a general outline of Fad.l Allāh’s
spiritual career and of H. urūfī history after his death. It also contains a
discussion of the signiﬁcance of Fad.l Allāh’s ideas in the context of
intense transformation that the Eastern Islamic world underwent in
the period between the Mongol invasion and the consolidation of the
Ottoman, S.afawid and Mughal empires. A separate section of the
Introduction summarises the history of academic research on the
H. urūﬁs. It is followed by some methodological remarks directly
related to the assessment of the existing research, its achievements,
its shortcomings and the place of the present book therein.
Methodological observations are continued in the last section of the
2 O. Mir-Kasimov, ‘Etude de textes h.urūfī anciens: l’oeuvre fondatrice de
Fad.lallāh Astarābādī’ (Paris, 2007).
Words of Power
xiv

Introduction, with a particular focus on the structural particularities of
the Jāwidān-nāma.
The next three parts of the book (Chapters 1 to 13) deal with
aspects of Fad.l Allāh’s doctrine such as it can be restored from the
body of fragments. Part One (Chapters 1 to 6) brings together
cosmogonical and cosmological doctrines of the Jāwidān-nāma.
These doctrines are centred on the speciﬁc conception of the
ontological divine Word. The creation and temporal evolution of the
universe are described as a kind of metaphysical linguistics, with its
semantics (Chapter 1), morphology (Chapter 2) and syntax (Chapters
3, 5 and 6). Within this presentation, the Human Being, Time and
Universe appear as differentiated equivalents of the original Word,
essentially identical to each other because they are produced in
accordance with the same primary model. The Excursus (Chapter 4)
focuses more particularly on knowledge and love, two pivotal
elements of the Jāwidān-nāma’s anthropology. Part Two (Chapters
7 to 11) is devoted to the Jāwidān-nāma’s prophetology, that is, the
progressive revelation (tanzīl) of the original divine Word through
prophetic missions and its return to the origin (taʾwīl) at the end of
time. The central themes of this part are the relationship between
divine and human languages, and the theory of taʾwīl, which is the
core doctrine of the whole work. Related to the latter is the theory of
the ‘motherly’ (ummī) knowledge, and the ‘motherly’ prophets and
saints, which seems to be an original development (Chapter 10),
interestingly combining mainstream Sunni prophetology and escha-
tology with Shiʿi ideas concerning the role of the Imāms and their
saintly investiture, the walāya. Part Three (Chapters 12 and 13) deal
respectively with the ways of individual and collective salvation,
including the Jāwidān-nāma’s eschatological views. The Conclusion
contains a preliminary examination, based on the contents of the
Jāwidān-nāma, especially concerning the place of Fad.l Allāh’s eclectic
thought in the landscape of Muslim intellectual and spiritual currents,
and a reﬂection, also based on the textual evidence of Jāwidān-nāma,
on the possible messianic project of Fad.l Allāh, his approach to the
reuniﬁcation of the Muslim community, and reactualisation of the
universal message of Islam addressed to mankind as a whole, in
particular to Jews and Christians. This last purpose can arguably be
discerned behind Fad.l Allāh’s extensive use of canonical biblical texts
Preface and Acknowledgements
xv

and apocrypha, which constitutes one of the most intriguing features
of the Jāwidān-nāma.

Introduction
Fad.l Allāh Astarābādī and his Followers
Fad.l Allāh Astarābādī (740–796/1339–1394), the founder of a doctrine
and movement which came to be known as H. urūﬁyya (‘letterism’,
from Arabic h. arf, pl. h. urūf, ‘letters’), was arguably one of the most
inﬂuential messianic leaders to emerge in Iran, during a critical period
between the disintegration of the Mongol Ilkhanate and the rise of the
S.afawid dynasty. Fad.l Allāh’s eclectic doctrinal views, which bear a
strong mark of esoteric Shīʿism and also draw on several other currents
of Islamic thought, such as S.ūﬁsm (especially that of Ibn al-ʿArabī and
some of his followers), theology, Qurʾānic exegesis and philosophy,
will be analysed in the following chapters and the Conclusion. In this
ﬁrst section of the Introduction, I will summarise some points essential
for the understanding of the genesis and orientation of Fad.l Allāh’s
thought in the context of post-Mongol Iran, and discuss a number of
other topics, such as sources available for the study of H. urūfī history
and thought, the nature of inspiration, either claimed by Fad.l Allāh
himself or ascribed to him by his followers, the social and political
activity this inspiration entailed, and the scope of the expansion and
inﬂuence of Fad.l Allāh’s ideas.
The name H. urūﬁyya is generally used in external sources for the
followers of Fad.l Allāh. However, at least in his major work, the
Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr (the ‘Great Book of Eternity’),1 Fad.l Allāh
does not seem to apply any speciﬁc name to his doctrine. Indirectly, it
could be characterised as the doctrine of taʾwīl, both in the narrower
sense of Qurʾānic exegesis and the broader sense of a method of
1 For the sake of brevity, I refer to this work as Jāwidān-nāma throughout this
book. The ‘short’ version of the Jāwidān-nāma will be mentioned further below.

ontological hermeneutics.2 This hermeneutics, which perceives the
universe as the ontological writing of God and a transcription of His
existence-giving Word, mediates the passage from the external forms
of objects and beings so perceived to the invisible Word that produced
them all. When applied to the forms of human writing – that is, to
words and letters, especially those of the prophetic books – this
method seeks an absolute and ﬁnal exegesis of all revealed texts by
bringing them back to their origin in the divine Word. The focus on
letters as basic elements of the taʾwīl may explain why Fad.l Allāh and
his followers were referred to in external sources as ‘letterists’,
H. urūﬁyya.3 The terms and expressions found in the Jāwidān-nāma
and in the works of Fad.l Allāh’s followers as possible self-designation
include ‘dervishes’ (darwīshān), ‘monotheists’ (muwah. h. idūn), ‘people
of the truth’ (ahl-i h. aqq) and ‘people of the [divine] bounty’ (ahl-i
fad.l), as well as Qurʾānic expressions such as ‘possessor of the
knowledge of the Book’ (man ʿindahu ʿilm al-kitāb) and ‘the midmost
community’ (umma wasat.).4 This absence of a speciﬁc self-
designation could suggest that, contrary to the opinion of some
external sources, Fad.l Allāh and his followers did not regard
themselves as separated from the rest of the Muslim community or
deviating from the basic tenets of Islam.
There are several reasons which make the name ‘H. urūfī’ confusing
when referring to Fad.l Allāh and his followers. Firstly, h. urūﬁyya might
be understood as a reference to the general trend of ‘science of letters’
(ʿilm al-h. urūf) in medieval Islamic thought.5 Secondly, and most
2 The expression s.āh. ib-i taʾwīl (Master of taʾwīl) occurs in the Jāwidān-nāma and
was applied to Fad.l Allāh by his disciples. For the meaning of this expression in the
Shiʿi context, see the Glossary: ‘Return to the Origin’.
3 One of the earliest external sources referring to the followers of Fad.l Allāh as
H. urūﬁyya is probably by Ibn H. ajar al-ʿAsqalānī (d. 852/1448): ‘He [Fad.l Allāh]
founded a group known as H. urūﬁyya’ (ibtadaʿa al-nih. la allatī ʿurifat bi-l-H. urūﬁyya).

Fad.l Allāh and some of his followers were proliﬁc writers, and their

The preservation of H. urūfī literature was initially organised by Fad.l
Allāh’s disciples who ﬂed their persecutors in Iran and settled among
the Ottoman dervish brotherhoods, especially among the inﬂuential
Bektāshīs. Within the Bektāshī order of dervishes, the H. urūfī literature
and teachings were transmitted and developed in the works of
Ottoman authors until the dissolution of the Bektāshī order by the
decree of Sultan Mahmud II in 1826.8 The manuscripts of H. urūfī
works that attracted the attention of Western scholars and triggered
academic research in this ﬁeld, which will be summarised below, also
came initially from the Bektāshīs. Today, a wealth of H. urūfī
manuscripts, including doctrinal and historical works, Fad.l Allāh’s
biographies and poetry, mostly in Persian and Turkish, is extant and
available in the manuscript collections of several libraries across the
world.9
The historical evolution of H. urūfī literature and its main
components, such as doctrinal works, didactical and mystical poetry,
historical, biographical and polemical writings, and dream diaries, is
still little studied. A rough distinction could be made among the
following categories: (1) Foundational works of Fad.l Allāh Astarābādī,
of which the most important is the Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr. Other
works attributed to Fad.l Allāh are: the Jāwidān-nāma-yi s.aghīr, a short

Introduction

The wealth of available works, combined with its broad diffusion
and lasting inﬂuence, makes H. urūﬁsm one the most documented
messianic movements of post-Mongol Iran. The early H. urūfī texts
contain highly elaborated doctrines encompassing, as we will see
further in this book, most of the central topics of medieval Islamic
religious thought. From the point of view of its scholarly level,
erudition and scope, Fad.l Allāh’s work arguably represents one of the
earliest and most complete intellectual realisations of what can be
called ‘post-Mongol mystical and messianic current’. It provides,
therefore, substantial information on the intellectual background of
the transformations that took place in Muslim societies during the
period preceding the rise of the Islamic empires of the late medieval
and modern eras.
The information about Fad.l Allāh and his followers found in the
known external sources is fragmented and incomplete. Standard
historiographical and bio-bibliographical works contain generally only
short notes concerning Fad.l Allāh and some of his outstanding
followers, in particular the poet ʿImād al-Dīn Nasīmī, as well as some
signiﬁcant events associated with the H. urūﬁs, such as the attack on the
Tīmūrid prince Shāhrukh Mīrzā in Herat in 830/1427.14 In addition,
later sources often only reproduce, with slight modiﬁcations, notes
from the earlier sources, which decreases even more the amount of
useful information.15 This seems to be in line with the general
character of the Muslim historiographical tradition, which registers in
any detail only such groups and movements that were able to survive
over a signiﬁcant period of time.16 In our actual state of knowledge,
which is by no means conclusive, external sources seem useful not so
much for the study of H. urūfī history and doctrines as such, but for the
textes h.urūfī anciens’, Persian text in Appendix I, pp. 495–731, French translation in
the main text).
14 Shāhrukh Mīrzā (d. 850/1447), was the fourth son of Tīmūr, the founder of the
Tīmūrid dynasty, and the most powerful among his successors. I will return to the
attack on Shāhrukh in the following pages.
15 For more detailed information concerning the accounts found in external
sources, as well as a selection of citations, see S.. Kiyā, Wāzha-nāma, and Y. Āzhand,
H. urūﬁyya.
16 Cf. J. van Ess, Der Eine und das Andere: Beobachtungen an islamischen
häresiographischen Texten (Berlin and New York, 2011), vol. 2, p. 1355.

Similar to the situation with external sources, the academic study of
H. urūfī literature is still in its infancy.19 In addition, if the external
sources reﬂect the reception of H. urūfī movement by the Sunni
majority, the H. urūfī writings themselves convey an idealised image
of the founder and of early H. urūfī history, and should therefore be
approached critically. However, in combination with external sources
and in the light of available information on the contemporary historical
and intellectual context, they allow us to reconstruct, to some extent,
the main stages of the formation and evolution of this group. On the
other hand, the ‘subjective’ point of view on the emergence of the
movement and its subsequent historical development, as reﬂected in
the works of H. urūfī authors, is of central interest for our under-
standing of the origins and formation of the charismatic and
messianic tendency, which permeated the discourse of religious
authority in Islamic world in the 8th/14th and 9th/15th centuries. In
what follows, I will focus on the evidence relevant to the issues such as
the formation of Fad.l Allāh’s charismatic personality, the nature of his

The detailed accounts on the biography of Fad.l Allāh can be found
in works such as the Khwāb-nāmas (Books of Dreams) of his two
direct disciples, Sayyid Ish.āq Astarābādī and ʿAlī Nafajī.20 Fad.l Allāh
was born in 740/1339–1340 in Astarābād (Gurgān), an Iranian city
south-east of the Caspian Sea. He lost his father in childhood, and in
his early years received some training in Islamic jurisprudence (ﬁqh)
from the friends and colleagues of his father. One day, he
accidentally heard a wandering dervish who recited a verse of the
well-known mystic and poet Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī (d. 672/1273). This
piece of poetry deeply moved young Fad.l Allāh and eventually
determined his spiritual vocation. Fad.l Allāh abandoned his home
and his practice at the court of law for the life of a wandering
dervish, which he led for the next 20 years.21 From the Khwāb-
nāmas, it can be concluded that the spiritual career of Fad.l Allāh was
marked by a series of dreams or visions.22 Among these, two seem
particularly important. The ﬁrst took place apparently in Khwarezm.
20 Sayyid Ish.āq Astarābādī, ms. Islanbul, Millet Kütüphanesi, Ali Emiri Farsça
1042; ʿAlī Nafajī, ms. Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Vat. Pers. 17; the latter has been
studied by H. Ritter, ‘Studien zur Geschichte der islamischen Frömmigkeit – II, Die
Anfänge der H. urūfīsekte’, Oriens 7/1 (1954), pp. 1–54. As we will see further below,
dream interpretation was one of the central activities of Fad.l Allāh. It is immediately
related to taʾwīl, the method of universal ontological hermeneutics, which constitutes
a core concept of his doctrine. This probably explains the existence of several H. urūfī
works entitled ‘Dream Diary’ or ‘Book of Dreams’.

S. Bashir, Fazlallah Astarabadi and the Huruﬁs (Oxford, 2005).
22 As a source of supernatural knowledge, dreams played an important role in the

From the same Khwāb-nāmas we also learn that, after this event, Fad.l

hama payghambarānast). Other people acquire their knowledge
(iʿtiqād) of the eminence of Muh.ammad’s degrees through blind
imitation and explanations provided by someone else (bi-taqlīd
wa bayān-i dīgarān), but he received this knowledge through
[direct] inspiration and contemplation (kashf wa ʿiyān).’33
In the year 775[/1374] . . . the knowledge of the ontological
hermeneutics of the disjointed letters of the Qurʾān (ʿilm-i taʾwīl-i
muqat.t.aʿāt-i Qurʾān), as well as the secrets of the religious law
(asrār-i dīn-i sharīʿa), such as prayer and fasting, were disclosed
(kashf) to him.34
It is interesting to consider the descriptions of Fad.l Allāh’s successive
inspirations in relation to the theory of taʾwīl, such as it emerges from
the fragments of the Jāwidān-nāma. It seems that, in the Jāwidān-
nāma, Fad.l Allāh distinguishes two major consecutive stages of taʾwīl.
The ﬁrst, exempliﬁed by the Qurʾānic story of Joseph and his aptitude
for interpreting dreams, is the taʾwīl of compound units, such as dream
images or compound lexical units.35 The second and ultimate stage of
taʾwīl exempliﬁed, in particular, by the biblical story of the broken
tablets of Moses, operates with simple units, either as phonemes,
regarded as direct expression of the most fundamental metaphysical
truths, or as letters, which are their visible loci of manifestation
(maz.har, pl. maz.āhir).36 Signiﬁcantly, while the citations concerning
the ﬁrst mystical experience underline the interpretation of visible
images, they also allude to the spontaneous understanding of sounds,
such as the singing of birds, on which the second experience (simple
sounds and letters) is focused. The descriptions of the two revelatory
events experienced by Fad.l Allāh seem thus to correspond to the two
stages of taʾwīl outlined in Fad.l Allāh’s theoretical work. From this
point of view, these two events appear as milestones in a progressive
initiation in the knowledge of the taʾwīl.
The passages related to Fad.l Allāh’s second mystical experience
mention also the high prophetic status it would have conferred upon

Fad.l Allāh. He is the ‘Master of Time’, a title with clear messianic
connotation.37 He is the ‘King of all the prophets’, possessing
knowledge of the innermost meaning of religious law directly from
the source of prophetic revelation. This statement seems further
corroborated by the evidence from the works of other H. urūfī authors,
who mention Fad.l Allāh and his works with extreme reverence, hardly
falling short of deiﬁcation.38 The idea that Fad.l Allāh actually claimed
a prophetic status and that of the eschatological Saviour has been taken
over and further developed in some external accounts on the H. urūﬁs,
in particular in those that aimed at establishing a case of ‘heresy’
against them.39 It is not unusual, therefore, that Fad.l Allāh’s position
in regard to his own mission is presented in modern academic
literature in the light of these external and often hostile sources.
But did Fad.l Allāh really claim a privileged status for himself? A
thorough answer to this question is impossible without an analysis of
all of his extant works. Nonetheless, it is interesting that the fragments
of the dream diary ascribed to Fad.l Allāh, and sometimes referred to
by the title of Nawm-nāma, do not contain any explicit description of
his revelatory experiences similar to those cited above. Neither does his
major doctrinal work, the Jāwidān-nāma. In fact, this latter work

contains no personal information whatsoever.40 This, of course, does
not mean that Fad.l Allāh did not at all claim some form of religious
authority following his spiritual enlightenment. Some fragments of the
dream diary seem to conﬁrm that he did indeed entertain an extremely
lofty idea of his mission. In these fragments, he compares himself to
the prophets, Shiʿi Imāms and legendary kings of pre-Islamic Iran, and
claims to have been initiated in the supreme knowledge available to
mankind, that of the extreme limit of prophecy and the primordial
Covenant. In a dream, he sees himself wearing the garments of the
eschatological Saviour. But in other visions he seems to be anguished
by the foreknowledge of his imminent death.41 The fact that he was
conscious of being charged with a particular historic mission is also
indirectly conﬁrmed by what we know about his political activity,
which was continued by his followers. However, the actual object of his
claim could be more modest than presented by his followers and later
polemical literature. The theoretical works of Fad.l Allāh, and in
particular the Jāwidān-nāma’s prophetology and eschatology, do not
indicate any explicit expectation of a new prophet after Muh.ammad. It
cannot be unambiguously concluded from this work that mankind has
entered the very last period before the end of time, when the Saviour
would appear physically. What is thoroughly developed in the
Jāwidān-nāma is the doctrine of taʾwīl, which becomes the dominant
feature of its prophetology beginning with Jesus, and the only form of
sacred knowledge after Muh.ammad.42 Fad.l Allāh probably regarded
himself as depository of the full knowledge of taʾwīl, a s.āh. ib-i taʾwīl,

and an inaugurator of the progressive revelation of this knowledge to

explicitly formulated by Fad.l Allāh himself, it seems to be implied in
his own works and in the writings of his followers.
Whatever the exact claim of Fad.l Allāh, it apparently could not
remain conﬁned to the purely intellectual sphere, and required his
active political and social involvement. I have already mentioned the
contacts that Fad.l Allāh established with local ruling dynasties
following his ‘dream of the star’. These efforts were pursued and
probably intensiﬁed after his ﬁnal enlightenment. Both H. urūfī and
external sources contain indications of his ideas on an alliance with
such regional powers as Tīmūr (d. 807/1404) and Toqtamish Khān
(d. 807/1404–1405 or 808/1405–1406).43
It might be that some of these indications do not correspond to
historical reality. But the very fact of their mention in the sources
points to an important tendency that can be observed also in several
other messianic movements of that time. Fad.l Allāh was not only a
religious thinker, he also attempted to establish his interpretation of
Islam, based upon an implicit claim of direct inspiration, as a source of
legitimisation for a political power that would, in exchange, adopt his
doctrine as its ideological basis and make possible the realisation of his
messianic programme. Fad.l Allāh can therefore be seen as one of the
ﬁrst harbingers of the mystical and messianic pattern of religious
authority that, although not fully implemented by the Tīmūrid rulers,
led to the consolidation of the concept of charismatic messianic
kingship that played an important role in the emergence of the S.afawid
dynasty in Iran, and also affected the construction of the Mughal and
probably Ottoman Empires.44

Introduction

The question of religious authority explains also the vigorous and
aggressive reaction of the Sunni ‘orthodoxy’ against Fad.l Allāh and his
doctrine. From what we know from both anti-H. urūfī polemical
writings and H. urūfī apologetics, it can be concluded that the charges
against Fad.l Allāh were grounded largely on political, not doctrinal,
reasons. The details of Fad.l Allāh’s complex thought were usually
ignored or misinterpreted by the ‘orthodox’ doctors, eager to establish
a case of ‘heresy’ against him.45 As we will see in the following parts of
the present study, Fad.l Allāh’s doctrinal writings do not contain any
explicit position that would dramatically contradict the fundamental
principles of the Sunni worldview or religious law. If it was not for his
political activity challenging the existing jurisprudential establishment,
which legitimised the authority of the ʿulamāʾ, Fad.l Allāh’s thought
would most probably have been considered as just another form of
mysticism and peacefully integrated into the Sunni ‘orthodoxy’. The
rejection and persecution of Fad.l Allāh and his followers was clearly
caused not just by theological controversies; they reﬂect a conﬂict
between two competing paradigms of religious authority.46
Fad.l Allāh was sentenced to death by the religious scholars and
jurists of his time, and executed by Mīrānshāh (d. 810/1408), one of
religious authority, one of the versions of which was offered by the H. urūfīs. The
interest of the Tīmūrid Mīrzā Iskandar b. ʿUmar-Shaykh (d. 818/1415) in the ideas of
contemporary mystics and theologians could point in this direction. On this topic, see
İ. E. Binbaş, ‘Timurid Experimentation with Eschatological Absolutism: Mīrzā
Iskandar, Shāh Niʿmatullāh Walī, and Sayyid Sharīf Jurjānī in 815/1412’, in Mir-
Kasimov, ed., Unity in Diversity, pp. 277–303. On charismatic kingship and its
relationship with millenarian motives in Iran and Mughal India, see A. Azfar Moin,
The Millennial Sovereign: Sacred Kingship and Sainthood in Islam (New York, 2012).
On the role of millenarianism in the activity of the Ottoman Sultan Sulaymān the
Magniﬁcent (1520–1566) see C. Fleischer, ‘The Lawgiver as Messiah: the Making of
the Imperial Image in the Reign of Süleyman’, in G. Veinstein, ed., Soliman le
Magniﬁque et son temps (Paris, 1992), pp. 159–177.
45 Cf. Mir-Kasimov, ‘Takfīr and Messianism’.
46 For a discussion of paradigms or ‘patterns’ of religious authority and their
interaction through the history of Islam, see Mir-Kasimov, ‘Introduction: Conﬂicting

It seems that for roughly half a century after the death of the
founder, the H. urūfīs continued to look for an alliance with a political
force. However, even if they succeeded in some cases to gain both
positive popular opinion and the favours of a ruler, all their attempts
eventually failed because of the vigorous resistance of the ʿulamāʾ, and
were followed by massive persecutions and massacres of the H. urūfīs.51
In 830/1427, a H. urūfī named Ah.mad Lur attacked Shāhrukh Mīrzā
(d. 850/1447), the principal successor of Tīmūr, at a mosque in
Herat.52 This attack was probably motivated by the H. urūfī hatred for
the Tīmūrids, and to seek revenge for the execution of Fad.l Allāh. It is
also possible that the attack was part of a larger plan of support for the
Karakoyunlu clan in their struggle against the Tīmūrids.53 However,
even if such a plan existed, it was ruined by the failure of Ah.mad Lur’s

In 835/1432–1433 a H. urūfī group revolted in Is.fahān, killing two
sons of Shāhrukh’s minister Amīr ʿAbd al-S.amad and probably the
minister himself. The revolt was crushed and its leader, a man named

the leadership of a certain Mawlanā Yūsuf, together with a daughter

who eventually obtained Jahānshāh’s agreement to execute the
‘heretics’. According to some sources, in 845/1441–1442, about 500
H. urūfīs were killed and their corpses burnt in Tabrīz.55 This event
probably marks the end of the H. urūfī attempts to establish an alliance
with the Karakoyunlu princes and the end of their direct political
activity in Iran.
After the second half of the 9th/15th century, the H. urūfīs became
more visible in the Ottoman Empire and in the following century,
Ottoman Turkish replaced Persian as the principal language of H. urūfī
writings. Their doctrinal inﬂuence in the Ottoman Empire was such
that, as J. K. Birge puts it: ‘The truth appears to be that many, if not all,
of the dervish orders of Turkey became to a greater or lesser extent
inﬂuenced by H. urūﬁsm.’56 In the Ottoman Empire, as in Iran,
H. urūﬁsm became part of the mystical and messianic ferment that
participated in the construction of a new sovereign paradigm of
religious and political authority.57 One of the most important H. urūfī

As was the case in Iran, in the Ottoman Empire the H. urūfīs
attempted to establish an alliance with local rulers. The sources
mention H. urūfī activity during the reigns of the Sultans Muh.ammad
Fātih. (1444–1446),59 Bāyazīd (1481–1512) and Sulaymān the Magniﬁ-

and ruthlessly crushed by the religious establishment. As a result, the
H. urūfīs seem to have abandoned the idea of direct political action and
gradually joined the ofﬁcially recognised dervish orders, in particular
the Bektāshīs. When Sultan Mah.mūd II (r. 1808–1839) dismantled the
Bektāshī order, the H. urūfīs, according to E. G. Browne, ‘took refuge
amongst the Naqshbandī, Qādirī, Rufāʾī and Saʿdī orders of
les Melāmī-Hamzevī dans l’empire Ottoman’, in Mir-Kasimov, ed., Unity in Diversity,
pp. 307–327. One of the most signiﬁcant Ottoman mystical and messianic movements
contemporary to the H. urūfīs was that of Badr al-Dīn Samāwnā (d. 819/1416), and his

There was apparently a strong H. urūfī presence in the Balkans,
where the H. urūfīs arrived most probably with the Bektāshīs
participating in the Ottoman campaigns.63 However, as previously
noted, in the current state of our knowledge, it is difﬁcult to determine
the relationship of these groups with the original H. urūfī doctrine of
Fad.l Allāh.
In modern Turkey, H. urūfī works continue to be published, after
their transliteration from Arabic to the Latin characters of the modern
Turkish script.64 The work on the H. urūfī written heritage is also
presently ongoing in Turkish academic circles.65 The artistic heritage
of the H. urūﬁsm, in particular poetry, has become an integral part of
general Turkish culture.66 Such outstanding poets as the already

mentioned ʿImād al-Dīn Nasīmī, who was among the most intimate

particular, of the Azeri and Ottoman Turkish. It is also interesting that
in modern Turkish ﬁction, Fad.l Allāh and the H. urūfī cabbalistic
doctrines reappear, for example, in the work of Orhan Pamuk.67
Notwithstanding their political failure, the H. urūfīs arguably
represent one of the most inﬂuential ideological and intellectual
contributions to the formation and consolidation of the mystical-
messianic pattern of religious authority in the period contemporary
with or preceding the rise of the great Muslim empires of the
Ottomans, S.afawids and Mughals. The attempts of messianic leaders
such as Fad.l Allāh or Muh.ammad Nūrbakhsh (d. 869/1464) to use this
pattern directly as the source of legitimisation of an existing political
power – which could result in a kind of symbiotic coexistence of a
political power legitimised by a messianic doctrine, and a messianic
doctrine given the status of ofﬁcial creed by a political power – were
not successful. This direct line of action gave, at the best, such
ephemeral hybrid political formations as the Sarbadār or Mushaʿshaʿ
semi-independent states. But gradually, as the political establishment
began to understand and use the potential of mystical-messianic
pattern, this pattern evolved, in conjunction with other factors,
towards a model of charismatic kingship which concentrated religious
and political authority in the hands of a single person. As we have
mentioned in the preceding pages, the model of charismatic kingship
apparently began to re-emerge in Iran during Tīmūrid rule, and was
fully implemented by the S.afawids. In addition, it is quite possible that
the evolution of the S.afawids prior to their transformation into a ruling
dynasty, from a Suﬁorder without any messianic overtones into a
radical messianic movement, was directly inﬂuenced by H. urūfī
messianic doctrines circulating in the Bektāshī and Qizilbash milieus.
Similarly, although the H. urūfī attempts to establish a direct relation-
ship with the Ottoman sultans apparently failed, they arguably
manuscripts of Fad.l Allāh’s Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr are circular ﬁgures such as that
which appears on the cover of this book.
67 For the H. urūfī motifs in his Kara Kitap (The Black Book) see Bashir, Fazlallah,
pp. 123–127.

exercised a lasting inﬂuence within the framework of institutionalised
mysticism cultivated by the Ottomans, which was essential for the
construction and legitimisation of the sultans and a powerful
instrument for the control of heterogeneous populations of the
empire.68 Similarly, the Nuqt.awīs (from Arabic nuqt.a, ‘point, dot’), an
offshoot of the H. urūfīs founded by a follower of Fad.l Allāh named
Mah.mūd Pasīkhānī Gīlānī, probably provided some doctrinal basis for
the millenarian religious experiments of the Mughal emperor Akbar
(d. 1605).69 It can be expected that further progress in studies on the
intellectual history of the 8th–9th/14th–15th centuries will shed more
light on the role that the H. urūfīs and similar mystical and messianic
movements of this period played in the contemporary reconstruction
and reconﬁguration of the Muslim world.
Overview of Academic Research and the Purpose of the
Present Book
The earliest mention of a H. urūfī text by Western scholars is probably
the description of the Jāwidān-nāma by P. De Jong and M. J. De Goeje
in the Catalogus codicum orientalium bibliothecae academiae lugduno
batavae, vol. IV (Leiden, 1866), p. 298. The scholarly exploration of
H. urūfī texts began a quarter of a century later, with the works of
Clément Huart and Edward G. Browne. Both scholars were attracted
by the linguistic peculiarities of the H. urūfī manuscripts. In 1889,
Huart published a ‘Notice d’un manuscrit pehlevi-musulman’, where
he described a manuscript from the library of the Hagia Sophia
mosque in Istanbul.70 According to Huart, this text entitled ‘The Book
of Questions Related to the Qurʾān, Preceding the Commentary’
(Kitāb al-asʾila al-muʿallaqa bi-l-Qurʾān min qabl al-tafsīr), was
68 Cf. H. Algar, ‘Bektāšīya’, Encyclopaedia Iranica, vol. 4, pp. 118–122, and S.
Faroqhi, ‘Conﬂict, Accommodation and Long-term Survival: The Bektāshī Order and
the Ottoman State’, in Popovic and Veinstein, ed., Bektachiyya, pp. 171–184.
69 On the Nuqt.awīs, see Kiyā, Nuqt.awiyān yā Pasīkhāniyān (Tehran, 1320 Sh./
1942), and on the possible Nuqt.awī inﬂuence on the emperor Akbar, A. Amanat,
‘Persian Nuqt.awīs and the Shaping of the Doctrine of “Universal Conciliation” (s.ulh. -i
kull) in Mughal India’, in Mir-Kasimov, ed., Unity in Diversity, pp. 367–391.
70 C. Huart, ‘Notice d’un manuscrit pehlevi-musulman’, Journal Asiatique, 14
(1889), pp. 238–270.

written in an unknown dialect of Persian,71 and dealt with esoteric
interpretation of the Qurʾān familiar to Shiʿi sects and based on
kabalistic calculations.72 A few years later, Browne found the frag-
ments cited by Huart in the manuscript of the Cambridge Library
Ee.1.27, which he identiﬁed as the Jāwidān-i kabīr.73 In his catalogue
notice, Browne cites some passages from the Jāwidān-nāma, as well as
examples from the dreams of Fad.l Allāh contained in the last folios of
the Cambridge manuscript.74 He also established a list of names and
locations mentioned in the dream diary, which provided a ﬁrst
assessment of the inﬂuence and geographical extension of the H. urūfī
movement.75 With the discovery of the Jāwidān-nāma, Browne
became more interested in H. urūfī doctrines, which stimulated his
further research. His two articles, ‘Some Notes on the Literature and
Doctrines of the H. urūfī Sect’ and ‘Further Notes on the Literature of
the H. urūfīs and their Connection with the Bektāshī Order of
Dervishes’, contain valuable information on H. urūfī doctrines and
manuscripts as well as on their diffusion and inﬂuence. Browne
summarised his two articles on the H. urūfīs, with some additions
resulting from his personal research and from other studies
concerning H. urūfīs published in the meanwhile, in his Literary
History of Persia (London and Cambridge, 1902–1929).
Browne’s research formed the basis of the academic study of H. urūfī
literature at this early stage. It was developed and ampliﬁed by some of
his colleagues and contemporaries. In his History of Ottoman Poetry
(London, 1900), vol. 1, pp. 336–388, Elias Gibb used the works of
Browne considerably, developing in particular the part concerning the
poet Nasīmī and his follower, Rafīʿī.
In 1909, Huart published and translated into French eight short
H. urūfī works in the E. J. W. Gibb Memorial Series (Leiden and

London, 1909). This edition, entitled Textes persans relatifs à la secte
des houroûfîs, included also a lengthy chapter by Rid.ā Tevfīq (Etude
sur la religion des Houroûfîs). The importance of Huart’s edition is that
it made available a selection of H. urūfī texts to the academic
community for the ﬁrst time. The selected texts in this volume are,
however, by no means representative of the original H. urūfī doctrine. It
is a miscellaneous collection of pieces belonging to different authors
and historical periods, without any attempt at systematisation or
critical assessment. A number of errors, both in the Persian text and
the French translation, were noticed by several scholars.76 The absence
of a critical assessment of the texts which, with the exception of the
Mah. ram-nāma of Sayyid Is.h.āq, represent the works of popularisation
rather than authentic scholarly production of the sect, led both Huart
and particularly Tevfīq, notwithstanding their impressive insight and
intuition, to some inaccurate or altogether wrong conclusions
concerning the original H. urūfī doctrine.77
The publications of Browne and Huart were followed by a period of
relative silence. The only publications which contributed, indirectly, to
the knowledge of H. urūﬁsm during this period were works on the
Bektāshīs, in particular Beiträge zur Kenntnis des Derwisch-Ordens der
Bektaschis by G. Jacob (Berlin, 1908), which includes a German transla-
tion of the Kāshif al-asrār wa dāﬁʿ al-ashrār, the anti-Bektāshī and
anti-H. urūfī polemical writing of Ish.āq Efendi, and The Bektāshī
Order of Dervishes by J. K. Birge (London and Hartford, 1937).
The work of the Iranian scholar S.ādiq Kiyā opened a new stage in
the academic study of the H. urūfīs. In his Wāzha-nāma-yi Gurgānī
(The Vocabulary of the [dialect] of Gurgān), published in Tehran in
1330 Sh./1951, Kiyā summarised a wealth of information on the
H. urūﬁs, from external sources, such as historical works or the bio-
bibliographies of poets (tadhkira), as well as from various H. urūfī
works. The Wāzha-nāma also contains some excerpts from the works
of Fad.l Allāh, written in the cryptic language mixing the dialect of
Astarābād and standard Persian, together with their translation into
standard Persian. But the bulk of the work, as its title announces,

77 For examples, see Mir-Kasimov, ‘Etude de textes h.urûfî anciens’, in particular
p. 35 ff.

consists of an extensive vocabulary of the archaic Astarābādī, or
Gurgānī, dialect used in early H. urūfī writings, including many useful
grammatical notes with examples from H. urūfī texts, essentially from
the Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr of Fad.l Allāh. The importance of the
vocabulary compiled by Kiyā for the study of early H. urūfī texts can
hardly be overestimated.
A few years later, the same author published the results of his
further research on the H. urūfīs in an article entitled ‘Agāhīhā-yi tāza
az H. urūﬁyān’ (‘New Evidence Concerning H. urūﬁs’).78 In this article,
he discussed some recently discovered manuscripts related to the early
history of H. urūfīs and the confusion between the dīwāns of Shams-i
Tabrīzī, Fad.l Allāh and ʿImād al-Dīn Nasīmī.
Concurrently with Kiyā, Helmut Ritter published an insightful and
well-documented article on the H. urūﬁs, ‘Studien zur Geschichte der
Islamischen Frömmigkeit II: die Anfänge der H. urūﬁsekte’.79 Like
Kiyā, Ritter founded his study on a broad selection of H. urūfī works,
including those of Fad.l Allāh and his direct followers. The article
contains a summary of the central positions of H. urūfī doctrine, a
detailed biography of Fad.l Allāh according to the Khwāb-nāma of ʿAlī
Nafajī, and some evidence concerning the divisions and spread of the
H. urūfī community after the death of Fad.l Allāh.
In 1970, an Azerbaijani scholar, Zümrüd Guluzade, published a
monograph based on a number of H. urūfī works, including published
treatises and manuscripts.80 This monograph contains a fair summary
of the relevant research up to the date of its publication. In her
presentation of H. urūfī doctrine, Guluzade outlines some central
themes, such as its theory of love and beauty, the relationships between
macrocosm and microcosm, the name and the named. A signiﬁcant
part of the book is devoted to the study of ʿImād al-Dīn Nasīmī’s
Dīwān, for which the author used 12 different copies, including
manuscripts and printed editions. The author also deals with the issues
of evolution and inﬂuence of the H. urūfī community after the death of

Fad.l Allāh, and its connections, whether attested or hypothetical, with
such groups as the Qizilbash, Nuqt.awīs and Bektāshīs.
Around the same period, Henry Corbin published his work En
Islam Iranien: aspects spirituels et philosophiques, which contains an
insightful description of H. urūfī metaphysics, essentially on the basis of
the source texts published by Huart. Corbin’s deﬁnition of the post-
Mongol Iranian ‘science of letters’ as an ‘onto-logy’, in the sense that,
in this tradition, being is fundamentally the Word, or Logos, is
particularly valid when applied to H. urūfī doctrine.81
The H. urūfîlik metinleri kataloğu (The Catologue of H. urūfī Texts) of
Abdülbâki Gölpınarlı, published in 1973, was a major contribution to
the systematisation of H. urūfī manuscripts. The catalogue contains
descriptions of several dozens of H. urūfī works preserved in the
manuscript collections of the Turkish libraries, including valuable
information on the authors, scribes and history of transmission of the
texts. The introduction contains a well-documented outline of Fad.l
Allāh’s life and work, the works of his followers and the history of the
H. urūfī movement after the death of Fad.l Allāh, based on a broad
selection of H. urūfī texts, mostly manuscripts.
The book of Kāmil Mus.t.afā al-Shaybī, al-S.ila bayna-l-tas.awwuf wa-
l-tashayyuʿ, published in Beirut in two volumes in 1982,82 contains a
substantial chapter on H. urūfī history and doctrines.83 In this chapter,
the author also provides an overview of the Islamic tradition related to
the science of letters and numbers (ʿilm al-h. urūf wa-l-arqām), and the
Islamic messianic, or mahdist, tradition, in an attempt at context-
ualisation of H. urūfī thought.84 Al-Shaybī’s study is founded on several
H. urūfī sources, including published works and manuscripts. In so far
as I can ascertain, he is the ﬁrst scholar to regularly refer to Fad.l Allāh’s
opus magnum, the Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr, in his account of H. urūfī
doctrine. Unfortunately, the author reproduces the central methodo-
logical shortcoming of previous studies, by elaborating and extra-
polating the evidence of Jāwidān-nāma from statements taken from

In 1991, Yaʿqūb Āzhand published a comprehensive monograph
on H. urūfī history, H. urūﬁyya dar tārīkh (The H. urūfīs in History).
The monograph explores a wealth of source material about the
H. urūﬁs, thus developing the research initiated by S.. Kiyā. The author
frames the events related to the H. urūfīs within a broad historical
perspective, and analyses their possible relationships to similar
movements in the social and political context of the time. Available
evidence concerning Fad.l Allāh and his family, and the evolution of
H. urūfī groups after the death of the founder, is presented system-
atically in separate chapters. However, as announced by its title, the
focus of this work is on the history of the H. urūﬁs; the presentation of
H. urūfī doctrine remains very general and, again, founded essentially
on the short works published by Huart and not on the works of Fad.l
Allāh himself.
The book of Muʿīn al-Dīn Mih.rābī, Kalimatullāh hiya al-ʿUlyā,
dukhtar-i Fad.l Allāh-i Naʿīmī-yi H. urūfī: bānū-yi inqilābī wa gumnām
az qarn-i nuhum (Cologne, 1991), is focused on the ﬁgure of one of
the daughters of Fad.l Allāh, mentioned in the sources under the
name Kalimatullāh hiya al-ʿUlyā, who was known for her political
activity as the leader of one of the regional H. urūfī groups. Like the
book of Āzhand, this work deals essentially with H. urūfī history and
does not add any signiﬁcant evidence to our knowledge of H. urūfī
thought.
The works of Ali Mirfetrous, Zindagī, ashʿār wa ʿaqāʾid-i Nasīmī,
shāʿir wa mutafakkir-i h. urūfī ([Stockholm?], 1992), and Histoire des

The most signiﬁcant recent research work on the H. urūfīs has been
produced by Shahzad Bashir, who has devoted to this topic several
articles and a monograph based on a thorough knowledge of the
published and unpublished H. urūfī works.87 His book Fazlallah
Astarabadi and the Huruﬁs (Oxford, 2005) is a short but insightful
introduction to H. urūfī history and thought, which purposefully
avoids the repetition of many clichés uncritically transmitted in several
earlier works.
The last published monograph on the H. urūfīs known to me is
Huruﬁlik: ilk elden kaynaklarla doğuşundan itibaren, by Fatih Usluer
(Ankara, 2009).88 This work covers an impressive range of H. urūfī
texts. However, Usluer’s presentation of H. urūfī doctrine suffers from
the same basic methodological shortcomings that I have already
mentioned when discussing previous works, namely, the absence of
critical assessment and systematisation of the works belonging to
different authors and historical periods.
From the preceding overview of existing studies on the H. urūfīs, we
can conclude that, ﬁrst, the historical research clearly predominates
over the doctrinal. While we have several monographs on the history
of the H. urūfīs, the presentation of their thought remains disorganised
and heavily dependent on external sources and the few published
secondary H. urūfī treatises. The most important H. urūfī works,
including Fad.l Allāh’s Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr, remain unpublished
and insufﬁciently explored.89 This imbalance between the historical
and intellectual aspects of research sometimes results in a distorted
view of H. urūfī thought and the perpetuation of medieval here-

siographical clichés instead of promoting an impartial study of
primary sources.
Secondly, much of the existing research on H. urūfī thought does not
take into consideration the temporal evolution of the doctrine and its
geographical divergence corresponding to the regional ramiﬁcations of
the movement. In other words, it is often tacitly assumed that H. urūfī
doctrine was a homogeneous whole and remained invariable over the
centuries. However, a preliminary comparison of the works of Fad.l
Allāh with those of his followers exhibits possible modiﬁcations and
additions introduced into the original doctrine some 30 years after the
death of Fad.l Allāh.90 This is further supported by the accounts of
early H. urūfī sources on the doctrinal divergence between local H. urūfī
groups.91 An indiscriminate use of sources belonging to different
periods and geographical regions can, therefore, lead to a confused or
even erroneous description of the doctrinal positions.
Instead of unconditionally accepting all works produced by Fad.l
Allāh and his followers as parts of the same doctrinal construction, it
would be safer to admit that only the works of Fad.l Allāh express his
own views authentically. In the present state of research, we simply do
not have enough information concerning Fad.l Allāh’s followers, their
intellectual background and possible afﬁliations and, therefore, cannot
adequately assess the conformity of their works to the original
doctrine, nor the portion of their personal input.92
These observations suggest two complementary directions for
further systematic study of H. urūfī literature. The pressing need is to
restore the doctrine of Fad.l Allāh as fully as possible on the basis of his
own writings. That effort should be supplemented by the study of the
writings of the later H. urūfī authors individually, including their
spiritual and intellectual leanings, and their relationship with the
thought of Fad.l Allāh, both on the basis of biographical evidence and
of comparison of their works with the teachings of the founder.
The purpose of the present book is to contribute to the ﬁrst step of
this ambitious project. It is focused on the most important work of
90 Mir-Kasimov, ‘Notes sur deux textes h.urûfî’, pp. 203–235.
91 See note 49 above.
92 For a summary of information on H. urūfī authors and their works, see Usluer,
Huruﬁlik, pp. 29–106.
Words of Power

Fad.l Allāh, and intentionally avoids any overlap with later doctrinal
literature. Such an approach has several advantages. Most importantly,
it eliminates the possibility of confusion related to the use of disparate
sources which, as we have noted, has been the principal weak point of
previous research. The accurate reconstruction of Fad.l Allāh’s thought
also provides us with a solid basis for the study of the subsequent
evolution of H. urūfī doctrines, and reduces the distance between the
historical and doctrinal aspects of H. urūfī studies.
Among the writings attributed to Fad.l Allāh, the voluminous
Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr has been singled out, both by H. urūfī and
external authors, as the great sum of Fad.l Allāh’s thought. This text
represents the most authentic primary source for research on the
original H. urūfī doctrine. And this is essentially what the present book
is about: it is an attempt to reconstruct the central positions of the
original H. urūfī doctrine on the basis of the Jāwidān-nāma.
The present volume can thus be regarded as the ﬁrst step in the
reconstruction of the Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrine. This step brings before
us a system of religious thought that might appear complex and
difﬁcult at ﬁrst, but I hope it is deprived neither of logical coherence
nor of freshness and creativity in the interpretation of the rich
scriptural material cited in the Jāwidān-nāma.
Puzzle of Fragments: Structure and Language of the
Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr
The work on which the present book focuses is known under the titles
Jāwidān-nāma, Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr or Jāwidān-nāma-yi ilāhī
(The ‘Book of Eternity’, ‘Great Book of Eternity’, or ‘Divine Book of
Eternity’).93 It is the most important text attributed to Fad.l Allāh
Astarābādī and the central reference of H. urūfī doctrinal literature. As
mentioned previously, Fad.l Allāh’s works in general, and the Jāwidān-
nāma in particular, are often cited in the works of his followers with
the extension ilāhī, ‘divine’, added to the title. It seems that Fad.l Allāh’s

nāma in order to emphasise the speciﬁc written form of this word often used in H. urūfī

inspired. The Jāwidān-nāma contains no explicit evidence that would

The exact date of the Jāwidān-nāma’s composition is not known.
One fragment of the work mentions Baku, the capital of Shirwān (in
present-day Azerbaijan), and is dated 2 Rabī‘ al-akhir 796 (4 February
1394).95 This would support the thesis that Fad.l Allāh wrote this
voluminous work (containing between 400 and 500 folios depending

The original text of the Jāwidān-nāma, introduced by the word
ibtidāʾ (beginning) repeated six times, is sometimes mentioned also as
Jāwidān-nāma-yi shish ibtidāʾ (the Jāwidān-nāma of six beginnings).
As mentioned earlier, this work is written in a mixture of standard
Persian with the local dialect of Astarābād, characteristic of the early
H. urūfī works. It should not be confounded with several revised
versions existing both in standard Persian and Ottoman Turkish.97 To
the best of my knowledge, the complete text of the Jāwidān-nāma has
not yet been published. This is, without doubt, at least partly due to the
difﬁculties related to the language and structure of the text, which I will
discuss in the rest of this section.

I mostly used the manuscript of the Jāwidān-nāma located in the
British Library (Oc.Or. 5957). Unless otherwise speciﬁed, all folio
numbers of the citations in this book refer to this manuscript. I was
also able to consult three other manuscripts of the Jāwidān-nāma: in
the Cambridge University Library (Ee.1.27), Istanbul Millet Library
(Ali Emiri Farsça 920), and Basel University Library (M.VI.72), and
compared them with the manuscript of the British Library for the
limited selections of fragments.98
The Jāwidān-nāma is a very curious text indeed. For one thing, it is
not organised thematically, as one would expect from a doctrinal
treatise. It is a corpus of fragments, only loosely, if at all, related with
each other in their actual order of succession. The impression that a
reader receives at the end of the ﬁrst few pages is that of a puzzle. It is
as if the author had cut his work into small paragraphs, mixed them
like a shufﬂed pack of playing cards, and then aligned the paragraphs
one after another in the order they came out of the pack. Already the
ﬁrst catalogue descriptions of the Jāwidān-nāma conﬁrm this
impression. According to the note by De Jong and De Goeje in the
catalogue of the Leiden library, the contents of the work are random to
the point that makes any systematic description impossible.99 Browne
conﬁrmed this opinion: ‘The contents of the work, as stated in the
Leyden Catalogue, are so miscellaneous as almost to defy description
in any brief compass.’100 Gibb made a similar remark: ‘The task of
discovering what were the special features of Fadl-ullâh’s teaching is
rendered yet more difﬁcult by the fact that the H. urūfī books . . . are
utterly unsystematic in their arrangement.’101
98 While there are many minor textual differences between these copies, I have
not come across any signiﬁcant divergence in meaning, and none at all in the order of
fragments. The accuracy with which the words and expressions in the Astarābādī
dialect are reproduced is particularly noteworthy in all copies. This ﬁrst assessment
cannot, of course, ﬁll the place of an accurate critical edition of the complete work.

academiae lugduno batavae (Leiden, 1866), vol. IV, p. 298.

Introduction

These observations clearly show that the Jāwidān-nāma can hardly
be read in its original condition. The text requires a rearrangement
that would render its contents coherently. Our access to the contents
of the Jāwidān-nāma depends, therefore, on the solution to the puzzle
of random fragments.
In the previous sections, we have seen that Fad.l Allāh and his
followers suffered continuous persecutions on the part of the
‘orthodox’ religious establishment. It would therefore be natural to
suppose that Fad.l Allāh wanted to conceal the contents of his works
from the occasional and potentially hostile readers who would use
this material to accuse him and his followers of heresy. Indeed,
taqiyya, or intentional dissimulation of doctrinal positions, has been
practised, especially in Shiʿi milieus, since early times. It is possible
that one of the techniques of taqiyya, called ‘dispersion of the
knowledge’ (tabdīd al-ʿilm), when the text related to a ‘sensitive’ topic
is deliberately dissociated and inserted in different places of a more
‘neutral’ text, may provide an explanation to what we ﬁnd in the
Jāwidān-nāma.102
Some indications in the Jāwidān-nāma seem to corroborate the
supposition that the disposition of the fragments was intentional, and
that it required an effort of reconstruction on the part of the
interested reader. Firstly, the order of fragments seems to be strictly
the same in several manuscript copies of the Jāwidān-nāma.103 This
excludes the possibility that the text was compiled independently by
different persons who would have had at their disposal a corpus of
unorganised notes left by the author. Secondly, by emphasising its
similarity with the structure of the Qurʾān, where verses on similar
102 For tabdīd al-ʿilm, see M. A. Amir-Moezzi, Le guide divin dans le shî’isme
originel (Lagrasse, 1992), index, taqiyya and tabdîd al-ʿilm, especially p. 307. More
particularly, for the connection between the tabdīd al-ʿilm and the ‘science of letters’ in
the alchemical corpus attributed to Jābir b. H. ayyān, see the chapter by D. Gril in Ibn
al-ʿArabī, Les Illuminations de la Mecque, pp. 414–415; P. Lory, Alchimie et mystique
en terre d’Islam (Paris, 1989), p. 125; and P. Lory, ‘Eschatologie alchimique chez Jābir
ibn H. ayyān’, in M. García-Arenal, ed., Mahdisme et millénarisme en Islam, in Revue
des mondes musulmans et de la méditerranée, 91/4 (2000), pp. 73–92, in particular
pp. 82–83.
103 I compared signiﬁcant selections from four manuscripts of the Jāwidān-nāma
mentioned in the text above.

and read together.104
It seems that this tendency to organise the fragments of Jāwidān-
nāma in accordance with some major thematic chapters was present
among the followers of Fad.l Allāh, and resulted in the appearance of
works containing extensive lists of topics and fragments of the
Jāwidān-nāma organised into thematic chapters.105 I have not used
these works because, although they undoubtedly contain a large
selection of fragments from the original text of Jāwidān-nāma, the
exact relationship between the shorter structured versions and the
original long version of the text has not been clearly established. Also,
the division into chapters proposed in these works has the purpose of
serving devotional and not scholarly interests. This division is
therefore not very helpful for the analysis of the doctrinal content of
the Jāwidān-nāma.
For the latter purpose, I found much more useful the anonymous
note in the last folios (481b–483b) of the British Library’s manu-

description of six large sections corresponding to the six ‘beginnings’

(ibtidāʾ), which introduce the text of the Jāwidān-nāma.107 This plan
covers most of the contents of the Jāwidān-nāma. The six sections are

The Master of taʾwīl (s.āh. ib-i taʾwīl), exalted be his glory (jalla
ʿizzahu) founded the Jāwidān-nāma upon six ibtidāʾ, mentioned

these six houses, and each house provides the explanation
concerning the original nature of one category of things. Thus,
the ﬁrst ibtidāʾ is the house of the hours contained in six days

and that what is in between. The third ibtidāʾ is the house of
Adam and Eve. The fourth ibtidāʾ is the house of Hereafter
(maʿād), that of the retribution and corporeal resurrection. The
ﬁfth ibtidāʾ is the house of prophets and laws (anbiyāʾ wa
sharāʾiʿ). The sixth ibtidāʾ is the house of explanations of the
Master of taʾwīl.108
Although we do not know who wrote this note and when,109 the very

presentation of the Jāwidān-nāma’s contents circulated among Fad.l
Allāh’s followers. In a sense, the present book is in line with the same
tendency towards thematic organisation of the corpus of fragments,
arguably suggested by the Jāwidān-nāma itself and developed in
H. urūfī circles. As a starting point of such organisation, I have adopted
