the simple plan of six ibtidāʾ cited above. It could be reformulated as
follows: (1) Time, (2) Cosmogony and Cosmology, (3) Anthropogony
and Anthropology, (4) Prophetology, (5) Soteriology and Eschatology,
(6) Ontological Hermeneutics (taʾwīl). However, a straightforward
application of this plan to the contents of the Jāwidān-nāma proved
impossible in practice.
The principal difﬁculty resided in the fact that almost every fragment
is related not just to one, but to several topics. It is therefore impossible
to sort the fragments out univocally into the six sections suggested by
our plan. The corpus of fragments forms a rich and complex network
of mutual allusions and references. My ﬁrst attempt at division
according to the six ibtidāʾ resulted in six huge compilations, with
many fragments included in several chapters, each of which was
comparable in dimension with the original corpus itself.
This made clear that the organisation of the fragments alone was not
sufﬁcient for obtaining a coherent presentation of the doctrine.110 At
this point, there was a choice between two possible options. The ﬁrst
consisted of admitting that the Jāwidān-nāma should be left as it is. No
‘linear’ presentation, necessarily following a single logical thread, can
fully reﬂect the richness and quasi-inﬁnite semantic potential of the
network of fragments. In other words, it is possible that the Jāwidān-
nāma was, after all, designed intentionally as a corpus of fragments,
to provoke not a ‘reconstruction’, but a steady and careful reading
and gradual assimilation of the text. I will come back to this idea
further below.
The second possibility was to ﬁnd an analytical framework, not
contained explicitly in the text, but deduced on the basis of careful
reading and comparison of fragments and attempts at their thematic
selection and organisation. Only such a framework could provide a
possibility of incorporating the large selections of fragments into
logically organised thematic chapters forming a coherent whole. The
present book results from the exploration of this second possibility.
110 For a more detailed account on the methodological premises underlying my
previous work on the text of the Jāwidān-nāma, see Mir-Kasimov, ‘Etude de textes
h.urūfī anciens: l’œuvre fondatrice de Fad.lallāh Astarābādī’, Revue de l’Histoire des
Religions, 226/2 (2009), pp. 246–260.
Introduction

The analytical framework used to organise the fragments is
essentially based on the idea of a metaphysical ontological language
which, I believe, is the most fundamental thematic line of the
Jāwidān-nāma. Three out of six segments of the original plan of the
six ibtidāʾ have been included as separate parts: Cosmogony and
Cosmology, Prophetology, Soteriology and Eschatology. Time, the
ﬁrst ibtidāʾ of the original plan, ﬁgures as a section among the three
counterparts of the complete divine Word. This position reﬂects, in
my opinion, the central point of the Jāwidān-nāma’s approach to the
issue
of
Time.
Two
remaining
ibtidāʾ
–
Anthropology
and
Ontological Hermeneutics – represent the transversal themes run-
ning throughout the text. Since they are deeply related to a large
spectrum of issues, it is difﬁcult to conﬁne them in separate sections.
Anthropology is the cornerstone of the Jāwidān-nāma; its different
aspects are highlighted through all three parts of the book. Only
those aspects that remained outside the focus elsewhere in the book
are brought together in the Excursus on Knowledge and Love. The
Jāwidān-nāma’s concept of taʾwīl is placed in the context of
discussion on the relationship between the divine and human
word. It is central for Chapters 9 and 10 in Part Two.
Part One on cosmogony and cosmology is presented as a kind of
metaphysical grammar, with its semantics, morphology and syntax,
the latter represented by the structure of three fundamental
counterparts of the original Word, namely the couple Adam/Eve,
Time and Universe. The part on prophetology is centred on the most
fundamental issues related to the prophetic cycle: the descent of
knowledge of the divine Word (tanzīl), the relationship between
divine and human languages, the concept of ‘motherly’ (ummī)
knowledge, and the return of the Word to its source (taʾwīl). Only
prophetic ﬁgures addressing important points related to these issues
are dealt with in separate sections. Other information on the prophets
mentioned in the Jāwidān-nāma and the particular features of their
missions is summarised in the last chapter of this part (Chapter 11).
Part Three on soteriology and eschatology is divided into two
logically complementary chapters: Chapter 12 contains an account on
the ways of individual salvation, while Chapter 13 is focused on
the question of the end of time and the fate of mankind and universe
as a whole.
Words of Power

The quotations included in this book are selected from a large
portion of the relevant fragments. Ideally, only one fragment follows
every analytical segment. Long fragments or short series of fragments
following each other without additional analytical notes are still
admitted when it is necessary to provide a minimal context, or if they
address different aspects of a particular issue.111
To conclude this Introduction, I would like to brieﬂy address the
ﬁrst hypothesis concerning the structure of the Jāwidān-nāma
mentioned a few pages above, namely, the idea that this text was
intended to remain a corpus of fragments, without any artiﬁcially
introduced thematic arrangement. Indeed, we have observed that the
most apparent reason behind the fragmented presentation of the
Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrine would be the taqiyya, the intentional
dissimulation of beliefs from occasional and potentially hostile
reader. Such a measure seems indeed fully justiﬁed by the difﬁcult
historical circumstances in which Fad.l Allāh and his followers lived.
In addition, the argument of taqiyya is brought forth explicitly in
the works of Fad.l Allāh’s close followers.112 If the Jāwidān-nāma
was encoded in order to conceal its real contents, then it seems
perfectly legitimate to apply a procedure of decoding in order to
access these contents.
After a closer examination of the text, however, the thesis of taqiyya
raises some questions. As already noted, one of the structural
particularities of Jāwidān-nāma is the use of a hybrid language,
standard Persian mixed with a little known local dialect of Astarābād.
At ﬁrst glance, this looks like an attempt to introduce a secret language,
which could be understood only by the initiate. But a basic glossary of
the ‘secret’ dialect, compiled by the H. urūfī authors themselves, is easily
available and sometimes even included as appendix at the end of the
manuscript copies of the Jāwidān-nāma. Furthermore, the Jāwidān-
nāma contains a fair amount of fragments either written entirely in
111 The restriction of the number of fragments included in this book has also
several downsides, which I hope to compensate in the future with a critical edition of
the text. One signiﬁcant loss is the representation of the Jāwidān-nāma’s use of
scriptural materials, the import of which can only be conveyed and contextualised by
extensive selections of fragments.
112 Cf. Sayyid Ish.āq Astarābādī, Mah. ram-nāma, in Huart, Textes persans, p. 13 of
the Persian text.
Introduction

standard Persian, or with only an insigniﬁcant addition of dialectal
words that do not necessarily hinder understanding of the text. Why
would an author or his followers wishing to conceal their secret texts
provide the reader with the key to deciphering attached to the
document? And would not such an author use the secret writing
throughout the document, rather than a portion of it? In addition, if
Fad.l Allāh’s concern was to conceal his doctrine, why would he write
the ‘summaries’ easily accessible to anyone, such as the Jāwidān-
nāma-yi s.aghīr and theʿArsh-nāma mentioned above? The only way to
reconcile the existence of such works with the thesis of taqiyya is to
admit that their apparent accessibility is in fact a kind of veil, which
conceals some important points of doctrine behind its more secondary
aspects. This can only be assessed after a thorough study of these
works and comparison with the Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr.
Furthermore, the fragmented, dissociated composition of the text,
the ‘puzzle of fragments’ discussed above cannot really prevent a
superﬁcial reading of the text. On the contrary, it encourages the kind
of reader who does not intend to read the work thoroughly, but wants
just to have a quick random look. This is exactly what a partial
‘orthodox’ jurist would most likely do in order to pick up some
expressions out of their context and use them as evidence against the
‘heretical’ author. We will see that the Jāwidān-nāma contains several
concepts and expressions that, without a careful reading and
comparison of many relevant fragments, are almost sure to be
misunderstood and misinterpreted. Thus, the ‘puzzle of fragments’ is
an obstacle to the deep and accurate understanding of the Jāwidān-
nāma’s contents, but not to a quick superﬁcial reading easily leading to
wrong conclusions, which the taqiyya could be expected to prevent in
the ﬁrst place.
Finally, it can be argued that there is simply nothing to conceal in
the Jāwidān-nāma. As we will see further below, this work does not
contain any explicitly ‘extremist’ or ‘heretical’ ideas incompatible with
Sunni ‘orthodoxy’, at least not to the greater extent than many other
mystical and philosophical works which were largely admitted under
the broad umbrella of the Sunni majority. Many fragments of the
Jāwidān-nāma emphasise the adherence of the author to the
fundamental tenets of Sunni Islam. This would also explain why
Words of Power

anti-H. urūfī polemical literature does not contain any citation from the
Jāwidān-nāma as proof of heresy.113
Without invalidating the arguments for taqiyya discussed above,
these points shed some doubt on the assumption that taqiyya was the
only reason of the linguistic and structural complexity of the Jāwidān-
nāma. But, if it is not taqiyya, what could possibly be the true reason?
Why did Fad.l Allāh not write the Jāwidān-nāma in plain Persian or
Arabic, systematically developing and presenting his thought accord-
ing to a logical plan? The text of the Jāwidān-nāma provides no clear
answer as to its linguistic complexity. We can only guess that the
addition of words and short passages in the local and little known
Astarābādī dialect had something to do with the idea of liberation
from the narrow conventions governing human languages central to
the Jāwidān-nāma, or with the idea of sacredness of a particular
language (Persian? Astarābādī?), not explicitly formulated in the
Jāwidān-nāma but suggested by some fragments. But it seems that the
Jāwidān-nāma does provide an answer to the issue of fragmentation
independent of the ‘political’ concern of taqiyya.
This answer is contained in the particular interpretation of
fragmentation developed with reference to the biblical episode of the
broken tablets of Moses,114 and closely related to one of the most
essential doctrinal principles of the Jāwidān-nāma, that of taʾwīl.
According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the breaking of the tablets was a
necessary act, because it manifested the basic elements of writing, the
disjointed letters. Unlike words and other compound units of
language, disjointed letters are free of any semantic or grammatical
convention of a particular human language. They do not refer to any
concept or object of the visible world; their only counterparts are the
corresponding phonemes. In turn, the phonemes are related to
metaphysical truths, borne by the sounds emanated from the divine
Word. Therefore, the letters, obtained as a result of ‘breaking’ or
‘fragmenting’ a text, are the only possible starting point for ontological
hermeneutics, taʾwīl, independent of the arbitrary conventions of
113 Mir-Kasimov, ‘Takfīr and Messianism’.
114 Exodus 32:19. For the possible relation between the interpretation of the
biblical episode and the fragmented structure of the Jāwidān-nāma, see Mir-Kasimov,
‘Etude de textes h.urūfī anciens’ (the article in Revue de l’Histoire des Religions).
Introduction

human languages, leading from visible form to universal metaphysical
truth.115 Many fragments of the Jāwidān-nāma invite the reader to put
aside the conventional meanings of words, and to transcend the forms
of the letters in order to attain the truth beyond the corresponding
phonemes, a truth without shape, colour or any other sensible
manifestation.
In this perspective, the fragmented character of the Jāwidān-nāma
could be regarded as a ‘sign of perfection’, to use the expression
applied in several passages to the breaking of the tablets by Moses. In
this case, the fragmented composition of the text would have been
intended to remind the reader that, in order to access metaphysical
truths, the arbitrary conventions and concepts of any particular
human language have to be broken and transcended. Such is,
according to the Jāwidān-nāma, the purpose of the broken tablets of
the Law, and of the fragmented structure of the Qurʾān which, in
addition, is the only prophetic Book where the disjointed letters are
included as part of the Revelation, along with the compound words
having a conventional meaning in Arabic.116 It is therefore not
impossible that the fragmented structure of the Jāwidān-nāma reﬂects
Fad.l Allāh’s intention to implement the principle of fragmentation
which, according to his understanding, was in itself an expression of
the fundamental principle of taʾwīl.117
If this is the case, then the ‘puzzle of fragments’ can no longer be
seen as a puzzle at all. The analytical approach should be abandoned,
and the reader, like Moses before the pulverised mountain, should dive
headﬁrst into the ocean of fragments. The exploration of this

After this digression, let us proceed to examine the ﬁrst approach,
the analytical reconstruction of the central doctrinal themes of the
Jāwidān-nāma.
Introduction

Part I
Cosmogony and Cosmology: The Language of the
Creation
The cosmogony and cosmology of the Jāwidān-nāma are based on the
metaphysical theory of the original creative Word. This theory
constitutes the core of the work, which describes the creation and
evolution of the universe as the unfolding of the primordial ontological
language. All objects and beings contained in the universe, at any scale,
from the heavenly spheres down to the tiniest atoms, are essentially the
manifestations of the ontological names derived from the Word. These
names are the instrument of the creation. They convey metaphysical
meanings or truths (maʿnā, pl. maʿānī; h. aqīqa, pl. h. aqāʾiq) which
constitute the principle of existence of any object and being, either
actually existing or only possible.1 In addition, the Jāwidān-nāma
establishes a link between the metaphysical meaning of the ontological
name and the external form (s.ūra) of the named. Therefore, the
structure of the universe with all that is contained in it – spiritual,
mental, imaginary as well as material entities – and its evolution in
time are essentially a structure and evolution of a language. The
universe is ‘spoken out’ and ‘written down’.
This language of the creation has its own semantics, morphology
and syntax. It is constituted of phonemes, which compose meaningful
words. It has its alphabet, by means of which the primordial phonemes
and names composed of them become visible in the external form of
objects and beings that they bring into existence, and thus can be
recognised and read. It also has its own convention that establishes the
1 For the technical vocabulary of the Jāwidān-nāma, see the Glossary.

necessary correspondance between the invisible meanings and the
forms of their visible manifestation, though this convention is not like
any convention proper to human languages.
With the exception of the Excursus (Chapter 4), this part is
organised as a kind of grammar of the ontological language. Chapter 1
brings together the Jāwidān-nāma’s evidence concerning the func-
tioning of the primordial language of the divine Unity, beyond the
differentiation that is the essential condition of creation. At that
original stage, the category of form does not exist, which means that
there are no letters and consequently no writing. The language of
Unity is purely ‘oral’. Its expression is the primordial Word (kalima)
or Voice (s.awt), which contains, in an undifferentiated condition of
eternal Present beyond space and time, inﬁnity of meanings (maʿnā, pl.
maʿānī), names and words. At the stage of Unity, the meaning is
identical and simultaneous to its expression. In other words, the
relationship between the meaning and its expression requires no
intermediary and no means other than the meaning itself. Because of
this focus on ontological meanings, the ﬁrst chapter’s subtitle is the
‘semantics of creation’.
The second chapter – ‘morphology of creation’ – examines the
process of differentiation and emergence of forms. The category of
form is an intermediary between the pure ontological meanings such
as they existed within the primordial Unity and the created universe
with its spatial and temporal dimensions. The introduction of this
category raises a critical issue of correspondance between two
incommensurable levels, that of invisible metaphysical meanings and
that of visible physical objects and beings. The Jāwidān-nāma’s
conception of Balance (istiwāʾ) is conceived as a solution to this issue.
The Balance is essentially what ensures a correspondence between the
primordial ontological meanings and the visible forms, so that the
latter become the loci of manifestation (maz.har, pl. maz.āhir) of the
former. Thus, the ﬁrst manifestation of form is the primordial Point
(nuqt.a), which represents the undifferentiated original divine Word.
As the Word undergoes the differentiation triggered by the Imperative
Be! (Kun), producing a set of distinctive phonemes, which constitute
primary elements of ontological meaning, the Point produces a
corresponding set of primary forms, or primordial ‘letters’ (h. arf pl.
h. urūf). The subsequent stages of creation and evolution of the universe
Words of Power

are thus described in terms of writing: the combinations of ontological
phonemes produce the meaningful names, which constitute the
essence of objects and beings, and manifest themselves in bodies
formed by corresponding combinations of primary letters.
The Jāwidān-nāma’s views on the structure of the universe are
studied in Chapters 3, 5 and 6, which thus constitute the ‘syntactic’
section of our metaphysical grammar. The syntax is divided in three
chapters because, according to the Jāwidān-nāma, apart from the
physical universe, there are two other entities which reﬂect the fullness
of the original divine Word. First of these is the cosmic Human Being,
represented by the primordial couple of Adam and Eve. The Human
Being combines the perfection of the external form and knowledge of
the metaphysical meaning of this form. The form of the human body is
the only form in the universe which is produced not by a partial
combination, but by totality of the primary letters. Since, in
accordance with the principle of Balance, the letters are linked with
the corresponding phonemes expressing the primordial meanings of
the divine Word, the external form of the human body and features of
the human face potentially give access to the totality of divine
knowledge. As a perfect counterpart of the original divine Word, the
form of the human body and its proportions determine the structure
of the physical universe. The second entity equivalent to the original
Word is Time. The basic unit of Time in the Jāwidān-nāma is the
week, which represents the time of creation and therefore contains the
totality of the physical universe. Because they are all perfect
counterparts of the divine Word, there is an essential equivalence
between human bodily form, time and the physical universe.
Cosmogony and Cosmology

Primordial Unity: The Semantics of the Creation
This chapter brings together the Jāwidān-nāma’s developments
concerning the divine Word or language in the state of original
Unity, before the creation of the visible universe. The description of
the properties and functioning of the language in this original
condition is fundamental for the understanding of all other doctrinal
lines of the Jāwidān-nāma, because these properties and functioning
remain fully operational during the creation and throughout the
temporal existence of the universe, though veiled by the diversity of its
visible forms and manifestations, and in particular by the diversity of
human languages.
In the relevant fragments, the language of primordial Unity appears
essentially as a power by means of which the metaphysical meanings
or truths of the transcendental divine Essence are expressed and
manifested. The initial manifestation of the language is the Word
(kalima), which is the ﬁrst emanation of the Essence and contains, in
an undifferentiated condition, all that can be known of the Essence, the
totality of its meanings that can be expressed.1
1 The Jāwidān-nāma’s conception of the kalima, which describes the Word as
being the ﬁrst emanation of the divine Essence, is close to that of the longer version of
the Theology of Aristotle, a partial Arabic translation and adaptation of the Enneads by
Plotinus. It should be noted that, in the Theology, kalima, pl. kalimāt is the Arabic
equivalent of the Greek Logos, pl. logoi of the Enneads. Having circulated in two
different versions, the Theology is one of the foundational texts of the Islamic
Neoplatonic tradition. Unlike the shorter version, the longer version of the Theology
places the kalima immediately after the original One, before the universal Intellect,
universal Soul and Nature. This scheme has been adopted and developed mostly in the
Ismaili tradition and, plausibly under the inﬂuence of the latter, in the Rasāʾil Ikhwān
al-S.afāʾ, and in the works of Andalusian mystics such as Ibn Masarra (d. 319/931) and
Ibn al-ʿArabī (d. 638/1240). On the Hellenistic heritage of Islamic Neoplatonism, the
link between the longer version of the Theology of Aristotle with the Ismaili tradition,

The Jāwidān-nāma further states that the primordial Word consists
of a limited number of indivisible, simple elements, named ‘words’
(Arabic, kalima, pl. kalimāt; Persian, sukhan). As we will see later, this
statement provides a quantitative basis for the formulation of the
fundamental unity of the universe. The number of the primary ‘words’
is expressed by two numerals, 28 and 32. Depending on the context,
any of these numerals as well as their sum can stand for the full Word.2
Because their existence is directly supported by the truth of the
Essence, the ‘words’ represent the ultimate reality (h. aqīqa) of
existence, independent of any other factor. They act as ontological
principles, the raison d’être or archetypes, of all possible realisations of
the universe. The original ‘words’ are uncreated and inimitable; they
and its possible inﬂuence on the Ikhwān al-S.afāʾ and Andalusian mysticism, see
Ebstein, Mysticism and Philosophy, pp. 33–72, and references given there. However,
although its conception of the kalima is essentially concordant with the outlook of the
Islamic Neoplatonic literature afﬁliated to the longer version of the Theology, the
Jāwidān-nāma does not contain the Neoplatonic hierarchy of intellects and souls. In
addition, quotations from the prologue of the Gospel of John and Christian
apocalyptic texts such as the canonical Book of Revelation and the Arabic Apocalypse
of Peter (see further below in this chapter, and Chapters 10 and 13) indicate that the
Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrine of the kalima was inﬂuenced by a combination of the
Neoplatonic philosophy and Christian doctrine of the Word.
2 Hereafter, I will use ‘28/32’ as the most general reference to the full number of
the primary ‘words’. The relationship between the series of 28 and 32 in the Jāwidān-
nāma is complex. Its various aspects will be discussed in this and following chapters.
The 28/32 are simple entities, they represent the most basic constituent units of the
metaphysical language. After the differentiation of the primordial divine Word, these
units manifest themselves as sounds. Therefore, in most cases, kalima would be
rendered more appropriately as ‘phoneme’ than as ‘word’. However, ‘phoneme’
cannot be applied to these units before the differentiation, when they were immersed
in the all-comprehensive Unity of the original Word and can at best be represented as
various aspects of the latter. Also, in some cases, it is not clear whether kalima
characterises a simple or a compound unit. For example, the names taught by God to
Adam (Q. 2:31) are identiﬁed in the Jāwidān-nāma with the 28/32 kalimāt. For these
reasons, I have consistently maintained the formal translation of kalima/kalimāt as
‘word’/‘words’, between single quotation marks in order to emphasise the technical
use of this term. The term ‘Word’, capitalised, singular, and without inverted commas
is used as translation of kalima, when it refers to the primordial undifferentiated
divine Word. See the Glossary: ‘28/32’.
Words of Power

are the source of the creation.3 All names of the original language are
composed of these primary ‘words’. Since the category of form does
not exist within the original condition of Unity, the ontological
language operates at this level with pure metaphysical meanings.4
The characteristics of the original language of Unity are particularly
important for understanding the Jāwidān-nāma’s approach to
ontological hermeneutics, the taʾwīl, which is the central concept of
the work. First, the language of Unity operates at the level of
ontological principles, not with conventional meanings attributed to
the combinations of phonemes in human languages. Second, there is
no differentiation or duality of any kind within the original Unity. The
name of the original language is simultaneous and identical to the
named object, the name and named are one and the same thing.
Thirdly, the ontological language of Unity is universal and rooted in
the ultimate truth of the divine Essence. As such, it constitutes the goal
of the taʾwīl. As we will see in the ﬁnal chapter of this book, the
realisation of the taʾwīl at the end of the prophetic cycle leads to the
uniﬁcation of mankind and to the restoration of the original universal
language. Let us now take a closer look at the relevant data of the
Jāwidān-nāma.
The Jāwidān-nāma apparently adheres to the theological position
according to which the divine Essence is absolutely unknowable. No
effort of human thought or imagination can penetrate the mystery of
the Essence, which can only be described negatively, that is, by what it

is not. The Essence is the absolute Unity, where there is no plurality or

neither past nor future, but only the eternal Present. The Essence

tas.awwur wa khayāl). Meditate thoroughly on [the fact] that
there is [absolutely] no possibility that anybody other [than Him]
attains this [stage] (472a–b).6

There is no doubt that the hand (yad), the hearing (samʿ), the

The same idea is expressed, with some additions and developments, in
many other fragments of the Jāwidān-nāma. This contradiction might
corroborate the thesis that the ostentatiously ‘orthodox’ fragments
were inserted in the Jāwidān-nāma in order to deceive a superﬁcial
reader, that is, by way of taqiyya. However, the conclusion of
Gölpınarlı that ‘anything [in H. urūfī works] said in agreement with the
sharīʿa is taqiyya’ is, in my opinion, much too radical.9 A divergence
from the ‘orthodox’ Sunni theological views does not necessarily entail
a contradiction with the fundamental precepts of the religious law. As
will be seen in the following chapters, a signiﬁcant part of the Jāwidān-
nāma is devoted to the interpretation of these precepts, and the
author’s concern with conciliation of the established mainstream
understanding is discernible in many fragments.
At the level of the divine Unity, the 28/32 ‘words’ are not
differentiated, they cannot be separated from the Essence and are as
inaccessible as it is. Inherring in the Essence, they cannot be described
by any positive characteristic (being invisible, without colour or any
spatial dimension). They are co-eternal with the Essence, but not
identical with it (261a). The following passage is a description, typical
for the Jāwidān-nāma, of the relationship between the Essence and
‘words’ within the state of the divine Unity:
9 Gölpınarlı, Katalog, p. 24 (my translation).
Words of Power

The 28 ‘words’ have no length, no width, no depth, no colour, no
beginning, no end and no limit.10 They are founded on the
essence of the Unity (qāʾim bi-dhāt-i h. ad.rat-i ah. adiyya) as the
light of the sun is founded on the sun. They are united with the
essence of the eternal King; [they are] invisible and indivisible.
Neither imagination (tas.awwur) nor mind (takhayyul) are able to
attain them behind the veils which cover their essence (312b).
In themselves, considered independently of any relationship between
them, the original ‘words’ are also free of any grammatical function:
‘Unrelated, not included in any compound, they [express] neither past
(mād.ī) nor future (mustaqbil), neither positive (amr) nor negative
(nahy) imperative’ (410b). Furthermore, they are absolutely simple
and cannot be divided by any means: ‘Each ‘word’ is simple (basīt.) in
its essence, and cannot be divided by any imagination (wahm),
supposition (fard.), action (ﬁʿl) or reasoning (ʿaql)’ (478b). The original
‘words’ have thus no sensory form, but they bear elementary,
undifferentiated meanings (maʿnā pl. maʿānī), simple metaphysical
truths (h. aqīqa pl. h. aqāʾiq),11 and are capable of expressing the gram-
matical categories in the compound condition.
The Jāwidān-nāma explicitly likens the original ontological ‘words’
to the phonemes of human languages. The meaning of any separate
phoneme is indeed beyond human understanding, but the combina-
tions of phonemes compose meaningful words ﬁtting into the
grammatical categories of language. In the state of Unity, the 28/32
are essentially identical to each other, united within the original Word:
‘All [28/32 original ‘words’] are fundamentally the One Word.
Necessarily, each of them bears, without excess or deﬁciency, the
totality of meanings (maʿānī) and truths (h. aqāʾiq) of the science of the
divine Word (ʿilm-i kalima-yi ilāhī)’ (478b).12
Notwithstanding their number, their presence within the divine
Essence does not disrupt the original unity of the latter, because all 28/
32 are fundamentally one Word:

Any quality (s.ifa) contained in the essence of the ‘a’ is also
contained in the essence of the ‘b’, ‘t’, and that of all other [sounds
corresponding to the letters of the alphabet]. Therefore, there is no

Together, the 28/32 constitute the Name of the divine Essence. This
Name is the eternal Word of God, an attribute privileged among others

Separately, the 28/32 ‘words’ are conceived of as the most basic, simple
attributes of God. All other names and attributes are composed of
them, like the words of any human language are composed of the
limited number of basic sounds or phonemes of the alphabet: ‘ “To
Him belong the most beautiful names,” [Q. 7:180] which are the
[combinations of the] single letters, such as khyʿs. . . . because every
beautiful name is composed of them’ (216b).14

and His attributes by the means of the 28 ‘words’ without

Among all divine attributes, the 28/32 original ‘words’ have a special

concept of ‘Mother’ has many different aspects in the Jāwidān-nāma,
particularly in anthropology and prophetology. We will regularly
return to it in further discussions. At the present stage, let us just note
that the Jāwidān-nāma establishes parallels between the divine
attribute of Mercy, the symbol of the Mother, who is the origin and
the source of existence, and the 28/32 ‘words’. This Mercy is the source
of the divine Word: ‘“Voices will be hushed to the All-Merciful”
[Q. 20:108]: it is from this place [from the All-Merciful] that the Word
comes forth. He [the All-Merciful] is its [the Word’s] essence (dhāt),
and it [the Word] is His attribute identical to Him’ (244b).

Rigour (qahr)’ (149a). They manifest themselves in the material world
‘by the means of the attribute of Beauty (jamāl) or by that of Glory
(jalāl)’ (478b). Among these, the connection with the attribute of
Beauty is an extremely important axiom of the Jāwidān-nāma, the
foundation of the theory of Love which we will discuss in detail in

Words of Power

Because of this particular link with divine Mercy associated with the
‘motherly’ creative power,18 the Word with its 28/32 ‘words’ is the
original and the most direct way of divine manifestation, the locus of
manifestation (maz.har) par excellence of God.19 Each ‘word’ from
among the 28/32 takes part in this theophanic function; each ‘word’ is
essentially the means and the locus of the divine manifestation:
The Word is the locus of manifestation of God (maz.har-i khudā).
It is inseparable from God . . . The Word and Speech (kalima wa
kalām) are the loci of manifestation of God in the sense that if
[the ontological ‘words’] had not encompassed (ih. āt.a) all things,
it would not have been known that God encompasses [all things].
The explanation of the divine Essence and attributes would not
become manifest. This is how they [the ‘words’] are the loci of
manifestation of God (345b).
The original ‘words’ are thus the basis of all the Names of the divine
language. One of the most fundamental features of this language is the
identity of the name and the named.20 Just as the phonemes of the
human languages – for instance ‘a’ which represents simultaneously
the name of a phoneme and this phoneme itself – the 28/32 ‘words’ are
simultaneously the name and the named object:
All the names [of the existing objects and beings] are [composed
of] the 32 divine ‘words’, namely of alif, bāʾ and other [names of
the phonemes]. The named objects [corresponding to these
names are the phonemes] ‘a’, ‘b’ and others. The 32 ‘words’,
which are the names of the 32 [phonemes like] ‘a’ and ‘b’, are
identical to them [to the phonemes]. This demonstrates that the
names are identical to the named objects (asmāʿayn-i musammā
bī). Once established for the single [phonemes], this principle

Primordial Unity

remains also valid for the composed entities. This is how it is
possible to know the divine Essence, because Allāh [the name of
the divine Essence] is identical to the named entity (195a).
Indeed, there is no differentiation at the level of divine Unity. The
forms and the material bodies have not been created yet, and there
cannot be a separation between the name of the object and the object
itself (cf. the citation 472a–b above). The Word is the principle of
existence, and any ontological name composed of the 28/32 original
‘words’ is simultaneously the principle of identiﬁcation of some reality
and this reality itself, the realisation of its actual existence.21
At the level of Unity, therefore, the language is a purely ontological,
creative power: language and being are the same. Unlike human
languages, where a name is attributed to an object on the basis of a
social agreement (wad.ʿ, is.t.ilāh. ) speciﬁc for each particular language,
the name of the divine language is simultaneous and identical to its
object.22 The social agreement changes from one human language to
another, and the same object has different names in different
languages. But in the language of Unity, the name is ontologically
related to the named and cannot be changed arbitrarily: if the name
changes, the named object must change accordingly.
However, the divine language is not totally void of any convention:
an absolute, divine convention governs the combinations of 28/32
simple ‘words’ when constituting compound names: ‘[The 28/32
original ‘words’ are initially] exempt of any attribute (tajarrud); they
are simple (ghayr murakkab) entities. When, according to a
convention (is.t.ilāh. ), they compose into [a compound], they become
the name of an object’ (408b).
The divine convention introducing essential identity between the
name and the named is based on the divine Order and Intention,
which determine the relationship between the name and the named
within the unity of the Essence:
O Seeker of the pre-existent divine Word, be aware that [some]
things existed before [the creation of] Adam, genii and angels,
and [in these times] there were no [social] conventions (is.t.ilāh.
21 According to the Jāwidān-nāma, only the Word has real existence: ghayr az
kalima chīzī dīgar nīst (fol. 464a).
22 See the Glossary: ‘Convention’, ‘Name and named’.
Words of Power

nabūda bāshad). [But] in the essence of the presence of Unity,
there was a name for every existing thing. God named things by
these [essential] names, and therefore a relationship based on the
[divine] command (amr) and intention (gharad.) was established
between every particular thing and its name (50b–51a).
The relationship between the name and the named acquires a new,
more complex dimension after differentiation and the emergence of
the category of form. The differentiation raises the question of
adequate manifestation of an invisible truth or meaning in a
differentiated sensible form, a problem that was absent at the level
of primordial Unity.
The compound names are the basis of the divine manifestation and
the prototypes of all that will exist in the created universe: ‘The
heavens, the earth and Paradise are composed from disjointed
[ontological phonemes] (mujarradāt), which [combine to] become
the names of the things’ (426a). It is the compound names that convey
the divine manifestation into the creation: ‘When they [the 28/32
ontological ‘words’] compose into compounds (murakkab ast), they
express (bayān) their essence (dhāt), their attributes (s.ifāt) and their
divinity (khudāyī)’ (395b).
From these citations, it can be concluded that, according to the
Jāwidān-nāma, the 28/32 original ‘words’ are part of the divine
Essence, the ultimate and transcendental divine Reality. They are
therefore regarded as the elements of essence (dhāt), quiddity
(māhiyya), meaning (maʿnā) and truth (h. aqīqa). The combination
that incorporates the full set of the 28/32 ‘words’ produces the Supreme
Name of the divine Essence, while other combinations, limited to a
lesser number of composants, create all other divine names and
attributes. The 28/32 ‘words’ are therefore the basic elements of the
divine language, very much in the same sense that the phonemes are
the basis of any human language. Since the name and the named are
identical in the divine language, the named object is actualised
simultaneously and immediately with its name, just as a phoneme is
actualised with the utterance of its name. This is possible because the
category of form does not exist at this stage. Within the realm of
divine Unity, all things are pure realities, simultaneous to their names
and inseparable from them; their being has no form, shape or support
other than their existence itself. The 28/32 ‘words’ and the names that
Primordial Unity

they produce are therefore essentially the principle of existence. Free
from any form or spatial dimension, the original Word with its 28/32
‘words’ is before all a sound and a voice: ‘The 32 ‘words’ are the voice
(s.awt) and the echo (s.adāʾ) of the pre-existent Essence (dhāt-i qadīm);
they are inseparable from it’ (148b). These sounds produce musical
melodies shaping the original nature of things. These same melodies
are also the basis of any prophetic revelation:
Every atom of the universe praises God by the means of musical
modes (us.ūl), tones (parda) and melodies (naghma)23 . . . From
the point of view of their original nature (khilqa), all things are
brought into the existence by the musical modes. Their shape and
their movements correspond to the musical modes. Nothing is
excluded from their modes and voices (s.awt). The voice
transformed into melody (naghma) comes down from the
same Essence from which the books of all prophets were revealed.
The prophetic books are composed of the 32 ‘words’ [i.e.,
phonemes/letters]. Every explanation (bayān) [concerning] the
ontological status (hastī) of these 32 ‘words’ ... comes from the
divine presence, [all the more that it is established that] the
composite [books] derived from [these simple words] come from
the divine presence (182b).
This description of a prophetic revelation as essentially sound and
music is important for the understanding of the Jāwidān-nāma’s
approach to the interpretation of the prophetic books. As we will see
later, this interpretation ultimately focuses on the individual letters
and phonemes of the language, rather than on the semantic aspect of
the compound words. Many passages of the Jāwidān-nāma insist on
the fact that it is the phonetic aspect of the word – the sound of the
speech and not its rational and conventional meaning – that is the ﬁrst
emanation of the divine Essence. As the original revelation of the
Essence, the Word contains all that can be known of the divine
Essence. Without the intermediary of the spoken word God would be
absolutely unknowable. The voice and sound of the Word with its

28/32 ‘words’ or aspects are therefore the original carriers of divine

presence outside of this domain, which is only possible if God

purest of all words is the word that leads towards the Essence and
the attributes of the divine presence and towards the Balance
(istiwāʾ) of the Word (174b–175a).24

Although the ‘phonetic’ aspect seems predominant in the Jāwidān-
nāma, the original Word and 28/32 ‘words’ are also described as light.
Sound and light refer thus both to the ﬁrst emanation of the divine
Essence and are fundamentally identical to each other. This is
explicitly stated in the Jāwidān-nāma: ‘The light is the divine Word’
(nūr kalām-i khudā hastī, 317b); ‘God, the Most High, called His Book
“light”, and His Book is His Word. (Therefore) each of His [28/32]
‘words’ is a light’35 (435a). While the ‘phonetic’ description of the
Word is often supported with reference to the Christian texts, the
representation of the Word as light is extensively founded on Muslim
scriptural sources.36 The saying attributed to Muh.ammad – ‘The ﬁrst
thing that God, the Most High, created was my light’37 – echoes the
paraphrase of the beginning of the Gospel of John that the Jāwidān-
nāma attributes to Jesus: ‘The ﬁrst thing that came from the heaven
was the Word.’38 God is light and reveals Himself as light, the light of
the Qurʾān. This light is the Word, and all 28/32 ‘words’ or aspects of
the Word are the one light within the divine Essence.39

Words of Power

Notwithstanding their essential equivalence, there is an important
difference between the representation of the Word as sound and light.
Sound is invisible, while light is the visible aspect of the manifestation
of the divine Essence. The light is one step closer to form, which does
not exist within the divine Unity, but emerges at the moment of
differentiation. According to the Jāwidān-nāma, form (s.ūra) is the
support of knowledge, providing the latter with the visible loci of
manifestation (maz.har, pl. maz.āhir). The metaphysical realities can
only be perceived and known through their loci of manifestation. As
the means of giving access to the knowledge of a transcendental reality,
form is characterised as ‘science’ (ʿilm).40 We will come back to the
more detailed deﬁnition of the science in the Jāwidān-nāma in the
next chapter. At this point, let us just emphasise the relationship that
the Jāwidān-nāma establishes between light and science: ‘The science
(ʿilm) is called “light” (nūr) because [it] is a mark (ʿalāmat) of the Word,
and the Word is light’ (151a); ‘The prayer of the Messenger (of God),
may he be blessed, cited in the Mas.ābīh. :41 “O my God, turn my heart
into light, and my hearing into light, and my tongue into light.”42 To
turn these (organs) into light means to make them locum tenens (qāʾim
maqām) of the Word, because they are the science of the Word.43
Whosoever does not know that, cannot access the Word’ (184b).
This relationship between the light and the science of the divine
Word underlies, in the Jāwidān-nāma, the approach to the well-
known h. adīth material concerning the ‘light of Muh.ammad’.44 It is
noteworthy that the Jāwidān-nāma extensively quotes the version of
this h. adīth according to which at the beginning Muh.ammad and

ʿAlī b. Abī T. ālib were the one light, which was then divided into two

This, together with some sayings attributed to ʿAlī and asserting his

God’ (anā kalām Allāh al-nāt.iq))46 is one of many indications of the
Shiʿi inspiration of the Jāwidān-nāma. The conception of light
occupies a central place in the Shiʿi conception of the Imām as divine
guide: the light is the substance of the Imām identical to the sacred
knowledge transmitted in the line of Imāms.47 In the Jāwidān-nāma
the light is the knowledge of the complete divine Word with its 28/32
aspects, transmitted in the line of the prophets.48
However, it is not the light itself that is the science of the Word. If the
light of the divine Face and of the Word with its 28/32 ‘words’ was not
veiled, it would burn and destroy the creation (fol. 457a). Therefore, the
light is veiled by form, which is the shadow: ‘The 32 ‘words’ [manifested
by the means of visible forms] constitute the veil [that covers] the 32
‘words’ [such as they exist within the divine Essence]’ (198a); ‘These 32
‘words’ are the reverse side and the shadow of those 32 that are founded
on His Essence and inseparable from Him’ (172b); ‘These 32 ‘words’
are the reverse side and the shadow of the light founded on its own
essence. They are inseparable from each other’ (369a).
It is precisely this shadow/form, this black veil, which at the same
time hides and reveals the light that is the science of the divine Word.
Before the differentiation that we will discuss in the next chapter, the
dimension of shadow is represented in the Jāwidān-nāma by several
symbols and images. First of these is smoke:
At the beginning of the creation, the heavens were ‘as smoke’, and
then [God] ‘determined them as seven heavens’ [Q. 41:11–12] . . .
The smoke represents the initial condition [described in] ‘then
He established Himself [in balance] (thumma istawā) upon the
heaven when it was smoke’ [Q. 41:11].49 The balance in the

The undifferentiated smoke contained the potentiality of the 28/32

When the superﬂuous [wood] is removed, the name Allāh

The Point (nuqt.a) symbolises this inﬁnite potential for the realisation
of concrete forms contained within the undifferentiated science. Just as
the original 28/32 ‘words’, the point has no shape and no spatial
dimension. It represents the fundamental unity of the divine Word
and of its 28/32 aspects. But, at the same time, the point is also the
source of any possible shape. It contains, in an undifferentiated
condition, the science of all ontological meanings of the divine Word:
‘All the meanings (maʿānī) and all the truths (h. aqāʾiq) of the divine

science of the ﬁrst and of the last are contained, without determination

As we will see in the next chapter, the ﬁrst forms produced out of
the point are the shapes of the 28/32 letters, that is, simple elements of
form corresponding to the 28/32 ‘words’/phonemes, which are simple
elements of sound. Signiﬁcantly, the science of the undifferentiated
divine Word concentrated in one point is exempliﬁed in the Jāwidān-
nāma by the ﬁgure of ʿAlī b. Abī T. ālib:
Just as the 32 [ontological ‘words’] are together one single light,
the Point is one, as the science of the Word is one. Anything that is
outside the Point exists [only] for the needs of discrimination . . .
Since any [meaning] contained in the bismillāh is also contained
in the [letter] bāʾ of this formula, and any [meaning] contained in
bāʾ . . . is also contained in the point under bāʾ, and he [ʿAlī] is this
Point, he is therefore the name of God (233b–234a).
[ʿAlī said:] ‘Knowledge [ʿilm, ‘science’ according to the
technical vocabulary of the Jāwidān-nāma] is a Point; it is the
ignorant who multiplied it.’50 The ignorant are those who are
unable to see the Point as the locum tenens (qāʾim-maqām) of the
[primordial] Word, and the Word as the locum tenens of 32
divine ‘words’. Necessarily, they ﬁnd themselves in the station of
division and multitude (maqām-i tafriqa wa kathra), not in the
station of the Unity of the original Point. When the scribe
touches [the paper] with his pen, he produces a point. The Word
rooted in the essence of the Unity is the counterpart of this
original Point (320a).
The 32 [ontological] ‘words’ are united in their essence. Their
science (ʿilm), containing [the knowledge of] the entirety of their
attributes and of their essence, is a fundamental Point, which is
the locum tenens of the 32 ‘words’. This is why (ʿAlī) said that the
secret of God is in the point under the bā’ of bismillāh, and [he
said]: ‘I am this Point].’51 This Point is the science of the divine
Word; therefore [ʿAlī] meant ‘I am the science of the divine
Word’ (465b–466a).
As the concentrate of all possible realisations, the Point of the science
is likened in the Jāwidān-nāma to the drop of sperm which contains,
in an undifferentiated condition, the most perfect form of the universe,
that of the human being:

Within the [divine] Unity (wah. da), there is no difference

At the beginning, there was a pearl (durr) in the state of mineral.

every living thing’. This means that everything was brought into

53 Inventory I, no. 38.
Words of Power

Manifestation of the Invisible: The Morphology of
the Creation
In this chapter, we will examine the fragments of the Jāwidān-nāma
that address the issue of relationship between the invisible ontological
meanings or truths of the original language and the category of form
(s.ūra). The Jāwidān-nāma’s solution to the problem of transition from
the primordial Unity of the Word to the multiplicity of forms
constituting the visible universe is based on the principle of ‘balance’
(istiwāʾ) and ‘measure’ (andāza, qiyās, miqdār), and related concepts
of the locus of manifestation (maz.har) and ‘science’ (ʿilm). The goal of
the relevant doctrinal developments is to maintain a certain
correspondence between the condition of the original Unity and the
differentiated condition of the creation despite
their obvious
incommesurability. Without such a correspondence, it would be
impossible to attain the knowledge of the metaphysical meanings of
the original language through the visible forms of its manifestation,
which would mean the impossibility of ontological hermeneutics
(taʾwīl).
The differentiation is based on the category of form, which did not
exist in the state of original Unity. The correspondence between the
forms of objects and beings and their ontological names necessitates
the introduction of an absolute convention based on the divine Will
(is.t.ilāh. -i ilāhī). This divine intervention makes possible the balance
between the semantical level of the primordial language discussed in
the previous chapter and its morphological level, that is, its visible
manifestation in the forms of objects and beings contained in the
visible universe.
According to the Jāwidān-nāma, all available knowledge of the
divine Essence was originally contained in the Word with its 28/32
‘words’, which represent the ﬁrst emanation of the Essence and its

revealed, knowable side. In the previous chapter, we have already seen
that the ‘science’ is deﬁned in the Jāwidān-nāma as the locus of
manifestation (maz.har) of this knowledge. In opposition to the
Essence, which is one and undifferentiated, its locus of manifestation is
differentiated: ‘All words are the one unlimited (bi-lā nihāya) Word,
and all things are the one unlimited thing . . . There is [only] one
Essence and one locus of manifestation. But the locus of manifestation
is differentiated (mutajazzī), while [the Essence] is not’ (179b).
Both differentiation and manifestation are closely related in the
Jāwidān-nāma to the concept of form (s.ūra). The form is the means by
which differentiation is realised at the level of visible manifestation,
because it is by their form that the objects can be distinguished from
each other. The science (ʿilm), which appears in a differentiated locus
of manifestation, is essentially a form by and through which an
invisible reality manifests itself: ‘Without the external shape (hayʾa)
there would be no manifestation of the Word’ (376b). If the Word had
remained uniﬁed as it was at the level of the Essence, the knowledge of
the Essence contained in the Word would have remained inaccessible
to any created being. Only a differentiated manifestation of the divine
truths makes them knowable: ‘The 32 [ontological words] are
differentiated in their external manifestation according to the points
of their emission: ‘The divergence within my community is Mercy.’1
Without this divergence, one single Word would not be able to convey
the divine knowledge (maʿrifat-i Allāh)’ (93b–94a); ‘If it was not by the
intermediary of the science (ʿilm), the Word (kalima) would never
manifest itself. Without the manifestation of the Word, the manifest-
ation of the divine Essence would be impossible’ (316a).
The deﬁnition of ‘science’ as form requires some further explana-
tions. If ‘science’ is understood as an intermediary giving access to the
knowledge contained in the undifferentiated Word, a purely phonetic
differentiation and manifestation of the Word could theoretically fulﬁl
this role without any visible support. Why is science not identiﬁed with
the ‘oral’, phonetic phase, before the Word becomes encoded and
‘written’ in a speciﬁc form? To my knowledge, no passage in the
Jāwidān-nāma gives a straightforward answer to this question.
However, some passages do mention a divine science, that is, a
1 Inventory I, no. 5.
Words of Power

science contained within the divine Unity and apparently independent
of form: ‘In the presence of the divine Glory, the divine Word has
neither “before” (taqaddum) nor “after” (taʾakhkhur). All the objects
of the sensible world (mah. sūsāt), the writings (maktūbāt) and the
intellegibles (maʿqūlāt), the past and the future, are in His science (ʿilm)
and in His Word, without “before” or “after” ’ (95b–96a).
This divine science is clearly distinguished from the science deﬁned
as the locus of manifestation and intended for created beings. But there
is an important link between these two kinds of science: the Jāwidān-
nāma states that the forms representing the visible science are made in
accordance with the divine science. This means that the correspon-
dence between the invisible metaphysical truth or meaning contained
within the divine Essence and the sensible form revealing it in the
world of creation is not accidental, but determined by God Himself.
This idea is close to the concept of ‘divine convention’ and the
principle of identity between the name and the named discussed
above. The thesis of essential correspondence between form and
meaning is central to the Jāwidān-nāma. When God taught the
ontological names to Adam, this teaching was purely ‘oral’, because
there was yet no form corresponding to these names and the writing
did not yet exist: ‘The Pen was, is and will be the writer (nawīsanda) of
the names that God taught Adam. The Pen gave the form to the
names, which [previously] had no form whatsoever’ (28a).
When God was teaching Adam the names, these names were
words without any shape or form. The teaching of the writing,
[mentioned in the verse] ‘taught by the Pen’ [Q. 96:4], and the
attribution of forms to these names took place after [the teaching
of the names themselves], and [the names] were separated by
means of the writing (27b).
In most passages, however, the differentiation of the Word is
accompanied by the emergence of the differentiated forms corre-
sponding to the individual phonemes and names. The following
passage states the simultaneity of the Word and its locus of
manifestation. It afﬁrms at the same time the superiority of the
Word to form and image. The Word can – in accordance with the
principle of correspondence determined by the divine science or the
divine convention – produce a form perfectly expressing the invisible
truth contained in this Word, while the opposite is impossible.
Manifestation of the Invisible

Together with the principle of identity of the name and the named, this
statement is another element of the theory of correspondence between
the invisible realities and the forms which are their loci of
manifestation.
[The ontological] ‘word’ and locus of manifestation (maz.har) are
both pre-existent (qadīm). But the ‘word’ has the power to shape
the corresponding locus of manifestation . . . Thus, the ‘word’
dominates (ghālib) [its] locus of manifestation, since the latter is
subordinated to the original nature (khilqa) of the former, not the
inverse. The ‘word’ can give to its locus of manifestation any
quality (s.ifa) it wishes, while the inverse is not true (389b).
This last citation raises another question related to the deﬁnition of
science as ‘locus of manifestation’. If the locus of manifestation is co-
eternal to the Word, and the Jāwidān-nāma does not seem to claim the
eternity of form, then should we suppose that the Jāwidān-nāma admits
the existence of eternal loci of manifestation which are not necessarily
forms? Some passages of the Jāwidān-nāma seem to corroborate this
supposition. The following statement, for example, refers only to the
phonetic aspect when speaking of the differentiation: ‘If the oneness [of
the divine Word] were not differentiated by the means of articulation
(bi-wāsit.a-yi makhraj) at the moment of [production] of sounds
(as.wāt.) of the words, it would be impossible to understand the
information (maʿlūmāt) [conveyed by these words]’ (211a).
The phonetic aspect is much closer to the knowledge of the truth
than the formal. It constitutes the secret encoded in the forms of
letters: ‘Take your eyes off (qat.ʿ-i naz.ar kun) the exterior [form] of the
letters and points of the Qurʾān, and seek the articulated word (kalima
ki dar talaffuz. mī-āyad). When you attain the knowledge of the latter,
you will reach the secret of the letters and points’ (422a).
The superiority of the phonetic aspect over the formal could be one
of the reasons why science is identiﬁed with the latter. Some evidence in
the Jāwidān-nāma seems indeed to support the idea that the phonetic
level is too lofty and subtle, too close to the original knowledge of the
Word to fulﬁl the role of universal science. The link between science
and form enables the former to reach the lowest layers of the creation,
conveying there the knowledge of the divine Word. This idea is also
expressed by means of alchemical symbolism. Earth is the only natural
element able to maintain form, which is the support of the science. For
Words of Power

this reason, though the most gross and opaque, earth is the noblest of
the four elements. Water, air or ﬁre are not able to keep a given form
and therefore not suitable for the expression of the science. Earth is the
element of Adam and the material which served in the creation of his
body. According to the Jāwidān-nāma, God ﬁrst created the bodily
form of Adam from the earth, as the science or locus of manifestation of
the Word with its 28/32 ‘words’; and only then He taught the meaning
of this form to Adam, that is, the correspondence between the lines of
the human body and face and the invisible ‘names’ of the 28/32 ‘words’
or phonemes. The idea that access to the superior, phonetic level of
knowledge is impossible without it being manifested in corresponding
visible or mental form is constantly repeated in the Jāwidān-nāma. We
will see relevant textual evidence further below. When Satan, made of
ﬁre, refused to follow the divine command to bow down to Adam,
arguing that his ﬁery constitution is more subtle than the earth of
Adam, he was not aware of the science contained in the bodily form of
Adam. Because he refused to bow down, he did not receive this science,
and thus condemned himself to the Hell of ignorance.
Whether the locus of manifestation of an invisible truth is
necessarily a form or not, we have seen that the germ of the form,
the black Point, appeared, according to the Jāwidān-nāma, at an early
stage, before the differentiation, as the counterpart, the shadow or veil,
of the 28/32 ‘words’ uniﬁed within the light of the original Word. It is
therefore logical that the phonetic (emergence of the 28/32 distinct
sounds or phonemes from the undifferentiated Word), and the formal
(emergence of the 28/32 distinct forms or letters from the undiffer-
entiated point) are two aspects of the differentiation which are
interrelated and unfold in parallel to each other starting from this
stage. The 28/32 ontological letters are the most basic elements of
form, the loci of manifestation and, therefore, according to the
deﬁnition of the Jāwidān-nāma, the science (ʿilm) of the 28/32
primordial ‘words’, the most basic elements, emanated from the divine
Essence: ‘The form (s.ūra) of the letters and points is the science (ʿilm)
of the 28 single divine ‘words’ [or phonemes], of which the names [of
all named objects] are composed’ (422a).
Similar to the combinations of ontological phonemes, which
compose the compound names of objects, the combinations of
corresponding letters compose the forms of these objects. In this
Manifestation of the Invisible

perspective, the making of an ontological name is simultaneous to the
making of the corresponding external form. Although their natures are
different and apparently incomparable, there is nevertheless a rigorous
link between the phoneme and the letter, between the metaphysical
truth contained in the sound of the name and the form which is its
locus of manifestation. In the following passage, this link is referred to
as ‘explicit convention’:
[The ontological] ‘words’, exempted (munazzah wa mubarrā)
from any form (shakl wa s.ūra wa paykar), [constitute] the
composite [entities]. In accordance with the [divine] convention
(wad.ʿ-i wād.iʿ) inspired by ‘He taught by the Pen’ [Q. 96:4],
appeared 50 letters and points.2 ‘Recite: In the Name of thy Lord
who created, created Man of a blood-clot’ [Q. 96:1–2] . . . the
names of God are composed of the 28 ‘words’, which are the true
Mother of the divine Book (umm al-kitāb h. aqīqī-yi ilāhī-and) . . .
‘Recite: And thy Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the Pen,
taught Man that he knew not’ [Q. 96:3–5]. The 50 letters and
points possess the science (khudāwand-i ʿilm) . . . because they
are the science of the divine names and the science of the origin
(as.l) of the Word (kalām) of the pre-existent unlimited Essence
(dhāt-i qadīm-i nāmutanāhī) (384b–385a).
The names are thus ontological principles of the objects. By the
process of attributing names, the divine Word penetrates all things,
‘breathing’ the existence into them:
‘And breathed My spirit in him’ [Q. 15:29]: [Like the divine
breath], the names attained all things, exteriorly (z.āhir) and
interiorly (bāt.in). By the means of attribution of the names
(ismiyyat), they attained the interior of all things and manifested
(tajallī) themselves [there]. All things are [therefore] their loci of
manifestation (maz.āhir) (21b).
The external forms of the objects appear only as the expression of the
ontological ‘words’ and invisible truths contained in them. The
ontological name, a particular combination of several divine ‘words’, is
inseparably connected to the object and constitutes its innermost
reality. This name is represented by the sound speciﬁc to each
particular object. This sound is released by inanimate objects when
2 That is to say, the 28 letters of the Arabic alphabet and their 22 diacritical points,
which are, according to the Jāwidān-nāma, the forms of the primordial ‘words’.
Words of Power

they collide, and also expressed in the voice of animate beings. The
only real reason for existence of the external forms is to be the locus of
manifestation, or the ‘science’, of these ontological names; if the names
were withdrawn from the objects, the objects would disappear:
There is no object that would stay out of reach of the names
[conveyed by the 28/32 ontological ‘words’]. No sound or voice,
either generated by the objects or beings or potentially contained
in them, does exceed the 32 divine ‘words’. [These ‘words’ are
inseparable from the objects that are their loci of manifestation].
If you supposed or imagined (bi-fard. wa tas.awwur wa takhayyul)
that the ‘words’ were extracted [from their loci of manifestation],
this would be impossible. And if you [nevertheless] extracted
them in your imagination, there would remain nothing of the
locus of manifestation. For example, when you strike two stones
against each other, they produce the sound ‘chak’, composed of
[the ‘words’] chī and kāf. If you were to remove or to extract these
[‘words’] chī and kāf, that is to say, [the sound] chak from the
stone, there would remain nothing of the stone, nothing at all.
This is the sense of the prophetic words when he said that [every]
piece of stone praises God (443a).
The passages above are related to the fact that every existing form is
composed of the 28/32 basic elements, or letters. They thus convey the
idea that the creation of the visible universe is essentially the act of
writing. As every ontological letter is the locus of manifestation, or
‘science’, of a fragment of the knowledge emanated from the divine
Essence, and embodies an invisible truth or meaning carried by the
corresponding ontological ‘word’ or phoneme, the entire world of
forms is literally a written Book containing the science of the divine
Word. This Book is intended to be read. But in order to be able to read
it – which means, in terms of the Jāwidān-nāma, to be able to spell the
forms according to the ontological letters contained in them and thus
access their ‘phonetic’ quiddity, that is, the divine names on which
their existence is founded – one should know how to decipher this
writing. This implies, ﬁrst, the ability to distinguish the basic forms of
the ontological letters within the compound form of any object and,
secondly, the knowledge of the principle of correspondence between
the 28/32 letters and the 28/32 ‘words’ or phonemes. This principle of
correspondence is the key to reading the Book of forms. Evidence
concerning the Jāwidān-nāma’s understanding of this principle is
Manifestation of the Invisible

fragmentary and allusive. However, in the following few pages I will try
to bring together some indications concerning the Jāwidān-nāma’s
theory of correspondences.
We mentioned above the terms such as ‘divine convention’ and
‘divine science’, referring to the absolute divine Will and Knowledge,
and determining an essential correspondence between the unfathom-
able metaphysical truths of the divine Essence and the ontological
names composed of the 28/32 ‘words’ of the divine Word. With the
differentiation and the emergence of forms, which constitute the veil
and shadow of the phonemes and names, the ‘divine’ convention
governs also the correspondence between the phonetic and formal
aspects of the manifestation of the divine Word. But the emergence of
form introduces a dramatic disruption in the perfect synchronicity
and immediate identity of the name and named, which characterises
the undifferentiated condition of Unity. There emerges therefore a
second convention, related to the external appearance and sensible
perception of the forms, which is the shadow of the primordial and
absolute divine convention based on the divine Will. This second
convention is represented by the rules admitted in human language
and writing:
All things are divine Word (kalima) and divine writing (kitāba).
[In the language] of signs (ishāra) they say: ‘We are the Word of
God.’ In the same way, any apparent line (khat.t.-i z.āhir) [of
writing] says: ‘I [point], according to the [orthographic]
convention (is.t.ilāh. ), to such a thing.’ Whosoever knows this
convention of the apparent line (is.t.ilāh. -i khat.t.-i z.āhir) will also
be able to read [according to the] convention of the divine line
(is.t.ilāh. -i khat.t.-i khudāʾī) [of ontological writing], the line
mentioned in [the verse]: ‘[Thy Lord] taught by the Pen, taught
Man that he knew not’ [Q. 96:4–5] (392a).
As within the divine Unity, the correspondence between the invisible
metaphysical truth and the forms through which it is expressed is
based on the principle of the identity of the name and the named.
However, in contrast to the condition of the Unity where the
relationship between the name and the named is immediate, the forms
are perceived as something different from the name, and the
relationship between the ontological name and the form, which is its
locus of manifestation, is now concealed behind the shadow of the
Words of Power

second, human convention. But, although hidden, the principle of
identity between the name and the named remains valid also at the
level of differentiation and form:
This soot and blackness [of the ink] that has been written on the
leaves (mus.h. af) [of the Qurʾān] is the science (ʿilm) of the 28
divine words (kalima), which are pre-existent (qadīm) and
rooted in the essence of the Reality (qāʾim bi-dhāt-i h. aqq). The 50
letters and points are the pre-existent soot and the blackness [of
the ink] . . . The forms (shakl wa paykar) [of the letters] are
written by the scribe (kātib) in accordance with the science of the
word (barā-yi ʿilm-i kalima) . . . The most difﬁcult question of
the theology (khudāshināsī) and knowledge of the [divine] Word
(kalāmshināsī) is how the external appearance of this soot and
blackness [of the ink] can become in reality the Word of God.
There are several points (muqaddimāt) that must be understood
before [the answer to this question] becomes clear, but ﬁrst of all,
it should be known that the [ontological] name is identical to the
named [object] (441a–b).
We will come back to the discussion of the working of the principle of
identity between the name and the named when discussing the
Jāwidān-nāma’s views on the relationship between the human form
and forms of particular objects contained in the universe, and between
divine and human languages. At this point, let us just note that the
principle of identity remains the basis of the correspondence between
the invisible metaphysical truth and the visible form which is its locus
of manifestation.
Another term mentioned in the Jāwidān-nāma in relationship with
the question of correspondence is divine inspiration (ilhām). The
inspiration is a link between the divine science and the world of forms.
Because this link exists, no form and no line produced in the empirical
world can be fully arbitrary, without any link with the divine science:
According [to the verse]: ‘[By the soul], and That which shaped it
and inspired it to lewdness and godfearing!’ [Q. 91:8], any line
drawn in the [empirical] world, whether it comes from the
human soul or from God, is drawn by inspiration (ilhām), in
accordance with the science of the Word (ʿilm-i kalima wa
kalām). [This line] cannot be without relation to the shape of
[ontological] writing that God established in the universe as the
Manifestation of the Invisible

science of the Word.3 The Word engraved (naqsh) in the locus of
manifestation of the human [form], and various forms of lines
written [on it], cannot be in contradiction (khilāf) to the science
(ʿilm) that God impressed in the universe (199b).
The term ‘measure’ (andāza) is also related, in the Jāwidān-nāma, to the
issue of correspondence. According to the Jāwidān-nāma, all levels of
the universe share a common measure due to the fact that the
differentiation and division at any level of the universe is made in
conformity with the number of 28 and 32 original ‘words’. The heavenly
sphere is divided into 360 degrees, that is six times 28 and 32; time is
measured by hours, each of which is composed of 28 and 32 minutes;
the human body contains 360 bones which is again six times 28 and
32, etc. This homology makes possible the correspondence between all
levels of the creation and links them all to the ontological ‘words’
which are the direct emanation of the divine Essence. Some of the
passages of the Jāwidān-nāma uphold that the verbs ‘to measure’
(andāza kardan) and ‘to create’ (khalaqa, ījād, āfarīdan) are
synonymous.4
‘He created the heavens and the earth . . . ’ [Q. 6:1 and ff.]: The
heavens and the earth were measured (andāza) by the same thing
by which they were created, that is to say, by the Word [of the
divine Imperative] Kun (Be!), as this is mentioned in the Qurʾān.
[The letters] kāf and nūn [of the Imperative contain] six ‘words’,
and each of them [is identical to the] 28 ‘words’. This is known
from the explanation concerning the essential unity (tawh. īd wa
yagānagī) [of the ontological ‘words’]. [Also, one week contains]
six times 28 hours. The heavens, the earth and all that which is in
between, the water and the Throne [which were created within
the week of creation] are thus measured [by the ‘words’ of the
Imperative]. When one thing is measured by another, it is in
order to attain the knowledge of its innermost reality (tā h. aqīqat-
i ān-rā bi-dānand) (88b–89a).
The Measure is thus closely related to the differentiation and the
division. The stages of the differentiation are determined by the divine
Imperative Kun, (Be!), which initiates the creation. According to the

Jāwidān-nāma, the two consonants of the Imperative, K and N,
symbolise the ﬁrst division of the original divine Word, the crucial
transition from One to Two. The names of these phonemes, kāf and
nūn, contain six phonemes, symbolising the six days of creation. From
these six phonemes comes the complete set of 28 and 32 separate
phonemes. Simultaneously, the original Point produces 28 and 32
separate forms corresponding to the phonemes, the 28 and 32 letters.
These phonemes and letters constitute the real ‘alphabet’ of the
creation: they are the basic elements which compose the name and the
external form of any object at any level of the universe:
‘The ﬁrst thing created by God was the Pen. God said: Write!
[The Pen asked]: What should I write? [God] answered: That
what was and what is to come.’5 All [that what was and what is to
come] appeared from the two ‘words’ [kāf and nūn] of the
[Imperative] Kun. Two tongues of the [nib] of the Pen produced
the science (ʿilm) of the two ‘words’ of the [Imperative] Kun.
These two ‘words’ contain 32 and 72 ‘words’ (108a).
Thus, in order to maintain the correspondence between the invisible
and undifferentiated metaphysical truths emanated from the divine
Essence and forms of the created universe, the differentiation which is
the starting point of the creation must be in conformity with a measure
determined by the number of the original ‘words’. An arbitrary
differentiation would not convey the truths unto the creation; but the
‘measure’ makes every form resulting from the differentiation a locus
of manifestation of the corresponding invisible truth, so that the latter
can be seen through the former. This idea is exempliﬁed in the
Jāwidān-nāma by the Qurʾānic episode relating the encounter between
God and Moses in the Sinai, when Moses asked to see God. The direct
vision of God was refused to Moses. According to the Jāwidān-nāma,
the pulverisation of the mountain at the direct sight of God symbolises
in this episode the differentiation, when 28/32 basic forms appear from
the divine Imperative. It is only after this ‘measured’ differentiation
that the vision of God in His locus of manifestation becomes possible:
‘But behold the mountain – if it stays fast in its place . . . ’
[Q. 7:143] . . . The ‘place’ of the mountain and of anything other
(jabal wa ghayr-jabal) in the original nature (khilqa) of things is

[Moses] was (qarār gīrad) in the word of the Imperative, ‘then

the word Kun! uttered [by God]. This is why Moses heard the
divine Word (kalām) [simultaneously] from all directions:6

Another concept essential to the Jāwidān-nāma’s theory of corre-
spondence between the differentiated forms and their invisible
archetypes is the principle of Balance (istiwāʾ). The action of the
balance seems to be very similar to that of the Imperative or of the
‘measured’ differentiation that we have just mentioned. Like the
concept of measure, the principle of balance governs the conformity of
the differentiation and division to the undifferentiated and undivided
divine Reality: ‘Nobody other than God can produce the division
corresponding to the [ultimate] reality (qismat bi-h. aqq). [It is] God
[who] introduces into the original nature (khilqa) of things the right
division (qismat-i rāst), in accordance with the [principle of] balance
(istiwāʾ)’ (218b). This principle originates from the divine attributes of
Balance, Justice (ʿadl) and Equity (qist.), and emanates from the divine
Throne (ʿarsh): ‘The Balance [is extended] to all things from the
Balance of His presence and His Word on the Throne (istiwāʾ-yi
h. ad.rat wa kalām-i ū barʿarsh), in the same way as the orders of a king
sitting on his throne [are extended to] his servants’ (276b). Like the
Measure, the Balance is linked to the Imperative, and its most

According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the Throne symbolises the place of
the ﬁrst and supreme manifestation of God, and is therefore identical
to the Word and to Adam, who is the locus of manifestation of the
complete Word. This ﬁrst manifestation is perfectly ‘in balance’ with
the number 32 characterising the Word. Starting from the Throne,

The passage 102b, already cited above, mentions the state of balance in

Balance introduces differentiation into the initial undifferentiated state

In the beginning [of the creation], the heavens were smoke, and

condition of smoke, or like smoke (wa hiya dukhān ay shabīh

Master of the Word (s.āh. ib-i kalima) (102b).

All created objects are transformed by the line of Balance into the
loci of manifestation of the 28/32 original ‘words’. Any created object
receives, through the line of Balance, the status of the writing and the
aptitude to express the science of the Word. The capacity to reﬂect and
to express the divine ‘words’ communicated to the objects by the line
of Balance makes that any object can potentially speak:
When the line of Balance is drawn on the things, they become the
science (ʿilm) . . . : ‘We have neglected nothing in the Book’
[Q. 6:38], ‘Everything We have numbered in a clear register’
[Q. 36:12] . . . The division by the line of Balance transforms

us speech, as He gave everything speech’ [Q. 41:21] (385b–386a).
