Thus, the line of balance transforms the creation into the Book of God:
‘ “And with Us is a Book speaking truth” [Q. 23:62]. It is known that the
form of the true Book (kitāb-i h. aqīqī) created by God appeared when
the line of balance was drawn’ (184a).
All levels of the universe, from the heavens and constellations down
to the tiniest atoms, are thus interconnected by the invisible thread of
the line of balance starting from the divine Throne. One of the
interesting deductions that the Jāwidān-nāma derives from this fact is
that the entities belonging to the different levels of the universe are not
simply ‘corresponding’ to one another, but are potentially equivalent.
This makes possible their evolution (or involution) when the entities
of one level are transformed or integrated into the entities of another
level. The following passage discusses the transformations of this kind
which are taking place within the food chain:
If a grain of wheat, which has the line of balance in the middle,
were divided into a thousand pieces and then eaten by the
animals, it would reappear in the line of balance [proper to the
form] of these animals. If it were eaten a thousand times, [then]
became a plant and forage, [the line of balance of the grain]
would appear again in the line of balance of a leaf or that of
[another] grain. [Any substance composed of] earth, water, air
and ﬁre seeks a line of balance when it manifests itself in a
mineral, a tree or [another] plant or in an animal. It is impossible
to go astray from the line of balance, because [every stem of] the
forage has the line of balance in its middle, which [divides it into
two halves and thus produces] the science of the two
[ontological] ‘words’ [corresponding to two consonnants] of
the [Imperative] Kun!. It becomes thus the name of the 32 ‘words’
[which] in every particular language [constitute] the science of
this plant. If you strike this plant against something, it will
produce a ‘word’ from among the 32 [ontological] ‘words’. If you
wanted to separate this ‘word’ produced [by the plant from the
plant itself] by imagination (wahm wa tas.awwur) or supposition
(fard.), this would be impossible. If someone extracted this ‘word’
from the plant, there would remain no existence in this plant (ān
nabāt-rā wujūd namānad), because it is identical to this
[ontological] ‘word’. ‘Upon the day the earth shall be changed
to other than the earth, and the heavens’ [Q. 14:48], the things will
be changed to the divine words. You see ﬁrst of all the things and
the bodies (ashyāʾ mīdīdī wa ajsām). But if you look [through the
eyes of] ‘those who possess the knowledge of the Book [or of
Words of Power

writing] (man ʿindahu ʿilm al-kitāb)’, [you will see that] all is the
divine Book [or writing], and the Mother of the Book (umm al-
kitāb) [are] Adam and Muh.ammad, upon them be peace, and the
lines of their faces (456b).14
It was already mentioned that the relationship between the series of 28
and 32 ‘words’ in the Jāwidān-nāma is complex and paradoxical: the
two series either complete each other (28+32=60), or the shorter is
included in the longer (28+4=32). One of the functions of the line of
balance is exactly the transformation of 28 into 32: ‘ “He revealed its
commandment in every heaven” [Q. 41:12]. The commandment to
each heaven was fourfold, 28 [for the seven heavens]. When the line of
balance was drawn, [the 28] became 32’ (74a). In this perspective, the
line of balance reveals the full number of ‘words’ of the divine Word,
which is also expressed in the bodily form of Adam and taught to
Adam by God: ‘Until the 14 [lines of the human face] located on 14
[parts of the face] are not divided [by the line of balance], the 32
[‘words’ taught by God to] Adam will not become manifest’ (320b).
The knowledge of the bodily form of Adam as being the locus of
manifestation of the complete Word gives access to Paradise. And the
eight gates of Paradise also allude to the line of balance:
In Paradise, there will be only seven black [lines] on the faces of
Adam, Eve and [other] humans . . . This is the Supreme
Blackness (sawād-i aʿz.am) which, [multiplied] by the number of
four natural elements, makes 28. [With the line of balance, there
are] eight [lines which, multiplied by four, make 32]. This is why
the gates of Paradise, which is the time (waqt) of the balance and
of the line of balance-‘And the earth shall shine [with the light of
its Lord]’ [Q. 39:69]-are eight, which [refers to] 32 (246b–247a).

Manifestation of the Invisible

It has already been mentioned that, in the perspective of the Jāwidān-
nāma, the creation of the visible universe is essentially an act of
writing. This is perfectly in accordance with general Muslim views,
based on the Qurʾān, of the creation as divine writing. The speciﬁcity
of the H. urūfī approach – which states that this ontological writing is
composed of 28/32 letters representing basic elements of form and
constituting the ‘science’ of the corresponding 28/32 phonemes of the
divine Word – does not prevent the author from extensive usage of
Qurʾānic symbolism, which receives thus a new interpretation in the
context of H. urūfī theories. One of the Qurʾānic symbols associated
with the line of balance is the divine Pen (qalam). The Pen manifests
the writing, just as the line of balance manifests the 28/32 basic forms
of ontological letters in any given form. The Pen thus establishes a link
between this particular form and the invisible name that is manifested
by its means. In addition, the author observes that the tip of any pen is
split into two halves, exhibiting a line in the midst: this is also an
allusion to the line of balance.15
The following passage makes again extensive usage of the symbols
of the story of Moses. At the same time, it illustrates an extremely free,
creative approach of the author to the symbolism of the Qurʾānic text.
This can be seen in the manner he establishes parallels between the
idea of balance and the images such as pen and the staff of Moses. The
pen with its split tip is similar to the staff of Moses, one of the ends of
which is divided in two parts. Just as the pen is dipped into the ink
prior to writing, the staff of Moses is dipped into the sea; a Qurʾānic
verse provides a link between the ink and the sea. Just as the line of
balance generates differentiation and thus displays the science of the
divine Word, the staff of Moses divides the waters of the sea – water
representing the undifferentiated condition – and opens the ‘dry
passage’, that is to say, brings forth the earth associated with form and

halves); fol. 385b–386a (the line of balance produces couples), etc. This is implied also
by the idea of balance itself: balance is usually the balance of two equal parts,
something in the middle. From this point of view, the line of balance seems close to the
Imperative which, as was mentioned before, played a central role in the transition
from the primordial One to Two.

The deﬁnition of form as the science of the invisible Word is not just a
convention in the Jāwidān-nāma. The line of balance, establishing a
correspondence between the visible forms and the elements of the
divine Word, guides the seeker to the real knowledge of the

The account on the Jāwidān-nāma’s theory of differentiation and
manifestation that we have attempted in this chapter would not be
complete without the mention of the negative side of this process. The
transition from the original Oneness of the divine Essence to the
duality of the Imperative which triggers the differentiation and the
creation, implies the emergence of opposites. The light of the divine
Word has the shadow of the form as its counterpart. As mentioned
before, though this shadow is the means of the intelligible perception
of the Word, its science, it is also the veil which hides the Word. In
other words, in the differentiated universe, the science is simultaneous
to its opposite, the ignorance. Indeed, in the passages concerning the
original point cited above, usually with reference to the well-known
saying attributed to ʿAlī b. Abī T. ālib: ‘The knowledge [ʿilm, ‘science’
according to the Jāwidān-nāma’s technical vocabulary] is one point, it
is the ignorant who multiplied it’,21 the Jāwidān-nāma expresses the
idea that the differentiation is made in order to overcome the
ignorance of minds based on discriminative perception, unable to
grasp the undifferentiated metaphysical truth. The science and
ignorance are essentially the same and have the same support,
which is the form of the visible or mental objects. Completely opaque
to the ignorant unable to transcend the superﬁcial conventions, the
same form is perceived by an initiate as a piece of divine ontological
writing. The limit between two opposites is very subtle: it is, exactly,
the line of balance, as narrow as the ‘Straight Path’ (al-s.irāt. al-
mustaqīm) mentioned in the Qurʾān:22
Outside the station of Equity (maqām-i ʿadl), it is impossible to
ﬁnd the path [to the knowledge] of one’s own [self], and to [the
knowledge of all other] things, [because of] darkness and
ignorance (z.ulmat wa jahl). When the things come to the station
of Equity, it will manifest itself in accordance with the words of
the Messenger: ‘[He (the Mahdī) will ﬁll the earth with equity and

Manifestation of the Invisible

Adam and Eve: The Form of the Word
We have seen in the previous chapters that, in the Jāwidān-nāma, the
creation is essentially the unfolding of the ontological Language. It is
described as Speech and Writing. The creation begins with the
differentiation, when the divine Word, originally One, is ‘split’ under
the action of the Imperative KuN, the two consonants of which
symbolise the idea of division, and manifested as distinct basic sounds
or phonemes, the 28/32 ontological ‘words’. At the same time, the
distinct forms of the ‘words’, the 28/32 primary Letters appear as result
of the differentiation of the black Point, the shadow and counterpart of
the undifferentiated Word. Various groups from among the 28/32
‘words’
compose
the
names,
while
the
combinations
of
the
corresponding letters compose the forms and bodies of the named
objects and beings. The names contain the transcendental knowledge
emanated from the divine Essence. The quantum of knowledge
conveyed by any particular name is proportional to the number of
original ‘words’ of which it is composed. This knowledge is encoded
and manifested in the form of the corresponding object in accordance
with the principles of Measure and Balance. These principles ensure
that any existing form is the locus of manifestation of the
corresponding name. As any name is a unit of knowledge, the form
which manifests this knowledge and thus makes it accessible is deﬁned
in the Jāwidān-nāma as the ‘science’ of the corresponding name.1
However, there are three entities that stand out from the rest of the
creation, because they result not from a partial combination but from
the complete set of the 28/32 ontological ‘words’ and letters. Therefore,
these three entities are the differentiated counterparts of the original
divine Word, and they contain not just some particular aspects, but the
1 For all the key concepts mentioned in this paragraph, see the Glossary.

fullest possible science of the divine Essence. As such, though very
different in their natures and ways of manifestation, these three
entities are fundamentally equivalent to each other. They are the
Human Being, Time and Universe.
In this chapter, I will outline the Jāwidān-nāma’s views concerning
the cosmic status of the human being, represented by the primordial
couple of Adam and Eve, in his or her relationship with the divine
names and attributes during the ﬁrst stages of the creation, in
particular during the stage of differentiation which was discussed in
the previous chapter.
As mentioned, the uniqueness of the human bodily form is due to
the fact that this form is the locus of manifestation of the complete
divine Word with its 28/32 ‘words’. This manifestation is, in particular,
concentrated on the human face: ‘All things are, in actuality and in
potentiality (bi-l-ﬁʿl wa bi-l-quwwa), the loci of manifestation of the
[ontological] ‘words’. . . . but the locus of manifestation of the
complete Word and science (maz.har-i tāmm-i kalima wa ʿilm) is the
face of Adam’ (369a); ‘The 32 ‘words’ are the distinctive signs (ʿalāma,
pl. ʿalāmāt) of the human face. Necessarily, the human face is the locus
of manifestation of the complete Word (maz.har-i kalām-i tāmm),
while other [objects and beings] are not the loci of manifestation of the
complete [Word]’ (389b). Since the loci of manifestation of the ‘words’
are the ontological letters, the human bodily shape and, especially, the
human face contain the full ontological Writing. The following
fragment gives a somewhat extended description of the ‘totality’
represented by the human bodily form, that of Adam and Eve:
God brought together all the named [objects] . . . established
them as counterparts of the 32 ‘words’, and made of 32 ‘words’
the names of all [named objects]. He created Adam in accordance
with the number of these [32 ‘words’], and wrote them on the
face of Adam by the hand of His power (yad-i qudrat). He [made
these ‘words’ so that they] expressed themselves from the 32
teeth, from the tongue and face [of Adam] . . . When all things
are bound together by the line of balance, they [produce] the
science of the divine Word (ʿilm-i kalima-yi khudāʾī). Adam and
Eve are, each of them, the locus of manifestation of all 32 divine
[ontological] ‘words’. Their bodies (wujūd) are bound to all
things, as everything is part of them, and [their bodies represent]
the totality (kull). All the heavens and planets with their effusions
Words of Power

(fayd.) face the earth, and they [Adam and Eve] are the spiritual
direction (qibla) of the all. Eve is the foundation (as.l) and the
Mother (umm) – during the prayer over the dead (talqīn-i gūr)
and the Resurrection (qiyāma) everybody is called back to the
Mother – because it is through the original nature of the face
(khilqat-i wajh) of Eve that the original nature of the face of
Adam and the science of the 32 [ontological] ‘words’ manifests
itself. Adam, Eve and the 32 ‘words’ shine from behind the soot
and the smoke [of the ink] of the conventional (is.t.ilāh. ī) writing.
They are the divine Books (kutub-i khudāʾī-yi ilāhī), [the letters
of which] shine through their faces and their bodies. They are the
divine Word (kalima): ‘Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only the
Messenger of God, and His Word . . . ’ [Q. 4:171]; ‘I am the

are bound to their bodies [i.e., of Adam and Eve] from six
[spatial] directions, and thus also [included into] the divine Book:
‘Light upon light’ [Q. 24:35]. The six [spatial directions] are
bound to the bodies [of Adam and Eve] and form their members.
All that face them from the six directions is [part of] their
members and of their bodies. All things are one body of Adam,
and the names of all things come from him. The innermost
meaning (maʿnā) and secret (sirr) of all things manifests itself in
him. In this sense, he is the father (padar) and the spiritual
direction (qibla) of all things: ‘a place holy, and a guidance to all
beings’ [Q. 3:96]. The spiritual direction of all objects and beings,
including angels, is the world of earth (ʿālam-i khāk) (91a–b).
Because it contains the science of the whole set of original ‘words’, the
human face is the counterpart of the supreme name of God: ‘The face
of Adam is the supreme name, in the sense that it is the science (ʿilm)
of the 32 separated divine ‘words’ (kalima-yi mufrada-yi ilāhī)’ (26a).
Therefore, in the whole universe, only human beings possess, at least
in their bodies if not in their minds,3 the complete science of the divine
Word: ‘The human form (s.ūrat-i bashariyya) is the science of the

According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the members of the human body
are the form of the divine attributes. The concept of form as science,
i.e., as the locus of manifestation of metaphysical truth, determines the
Jāwidān-nāma’s approach to the anthropomorphic vocabulary of the
Qurʾān, to the issue of ‘likeness’ between divine and human, a topic of
much controversy in Islamic theology.5 The position of the Jāwidān-
nāma in this regard can be summarised as follows: since Adam was
created as the locus of manifestation of the complete divine Word, the
members of his body are the loci of manifestation of anthropomorphic
attributes of God mentioned in the Qurʾān. The Qurʾānic expressions
such as ‘Face of God’, ‘Hand of God’ and so on thus refer, quite
literally, to the human body.
The Throne of God is the external form (s.ūrat-i z.āhir) of Adam
. . . The innermost meaning (maʿnā) of his form and of his
language is [the fact that they are] the locus of manifestation
(maz.har) of the 32 pre-eternal divine ‘words’ . . . The lines of [the
ontological] writing on the [human] face and [the human body]
in its entirety is the divine [ontological] Writing . . . the [Well-
preserved] Tablet (lawh. ) is a reference to Adam, who is the locus
of manifestation of the pre-existent Word (kalima-yi qadīm). His
face, his hand and his ﬁngers are the science (ʿilm) of the pre-
existent Word because they are the Face of God, the Hand of God
and the Fingers of the All-Merciful (112a–b).
This, however, should not be understood as plain anthropomorphism,
that is, the actual incarnation of divinity in human form. The Jāwidān-
nāma’s deﬁnition of form is crucial in this regard: the relationship
understanding of this science requires a special teaching, which is the purpose of
prophetic missions. This topic will be discussed in more detail in Part Two.

between the divine attribute and the corresponding part of the human
body is the relationship between an invisible, transcendental truth and
its locus of manifestation. There is an essential link between the two,
the link of Balance and Measure, which was discussed in the previous
chapter. But this link does not mean that they are placed at the same
level. Without taking into consideration this speciﬁc deﬁnition of form
as science and locus of manifestation, the statements such as ‘Adam,
created according to the form of the Merciful,6 is the form of God on
the earth and in the heaven’ (125a), ‘The form of Adam is the form of
God’ (139a), or ‘The face of Adam is the Face of God’ (237a), could
indeed be misunderstood as expressions of extreme anthropomorph-
ism (tashbīh, tajassum).
However, as we already have seen above, the Jāwidān-nāma
contains an elaborate theory of correspondences between the
transcendental and formal levels. In other words, whereas the identity
of the realities belonging to the different levels is not admitted in the
Jāwidān-nāma, a certain likeness between divine and human is not
only conﬁrmed, but is also essential to the work. Let us recall that the
Jāwidān-nāma states that
the divine
Essence
is beyond
any
manifestation and is absolutely unknowable; but the Word, the
emanation of the Essence, its revealed part, Deus Revelatus, though
transcendental to the creation, can be manifested in it following the
laws of Balance and Measure outlined above. This means that Deus
Revelatus has a form, a Shadow, a locus of manifestation which
perfectly expresses His innermost reality, just as every ontological
‘word’ and name corresponding to any transcendental truth has a
form, which perfectly expresses this particular truth. Exactly in the
same manner, Deus Revelatus, the Word, which is nothing other than
the totality of the primary ontological phonemes, generates a
corresponding form reﬂecting this totality, that is, its locus of
manifestation: ‘God speaks from behind the curtain of the bodily
form [of Adam], because it is the science of the 32 divine ‘words’, and
it is His Word’ (331b). It is in this sense that Adam, the prototype and
perfect model of human physical form, is essentially the form, the
locus of manifestation and the science of the Deus Revelatus: ‘The
human [body] is the locus of manifestation of the Word, and the Word
6 Inventory I, no. 11.
Adam and Eve

is the locus of manifestation of God, inseparable from God, just as it is
inseparable from the Perfect Human’ (345b). In this speciﬁc sense
then, the form of Adam is the form of God.
The divergence from the plain anthropomorphism resides in the
fact that the locus of manifestation of a certain reality is not this reality
itself. The form that expresses a divine truth is not this truth itself, but
only a means to knowledge of that truth. In other words, the relation
between transcendental reality and its locus of manifestation is
asymmetric and does not work conversely in both directions: the fact
that the form of Adam is the form of God does not mean that Adam is
identical to God. God can see Adam in his totality, but Adam can see
only the form of God, which is the form of Adam’s own body, but he
cannot see the divine Essence; and this is only like to see God:
‘Serve God as if you are seeing Him’ (taʿbud Allāha ka-annaka
tarāhu).7 Since Adam is [made] in accordance with the form of
God (bar s.ūrat-i khudā), when you see him [i.e., Adam], it is [as]
‘if you were seeing Him’, ‘because He sees you’ (fa-innahu
yarāka) ‘in the form of Adam’ (ʿalā s.ūrat Adam), which means
that the name (ism) of God is his [i.e., Adam’s physical] form
(s.ūra) . . . (26b).
This ‘like’, or ‘as if’ expresses the whole distance from plain
anthropomorphism. The way from the name to the named is
immediate because the name creates the named and thus generates
its own form. But the inverse path, from the form to its ontological
principle, is more difﬁcult and cannot be covered without some special
knowledge, which enables the seeker to perceive the form as the locus
of manifestation or ‘science’ and to read it, thus leading him to the
ultimate meaning of this form, to an invisible truth. This speciﬁc
knowledge is akin to the prophetic revelation,8 and will be discussed in

In the previous chapter, we have seen that the category of form,
support of the ‘science’, ﬁrst emerges in the Jāwidān-nāma as a black
Point. This primordial Point contains, in an undifferentiated
condition, the complete science of the original divine Word. The
form of the human body expresses the same complete knowledge, but
in a differentiated condition; the human body is the differentiated
counterpart of the original Point.
The ﬁrst thing that the pen of a scribe produces when it touches
[the paper] is a point (nuqt.a). The Word (kalima), rooted in the
Essence of the presence of the [divine] Unity (dhāt-i h. ad.rat-i
ah. adiyya), is the counterpart of this original Point [produced by]
the scribe [on the] Well-preserved Tablet (lawh. -i mah. fūz.) of
Adam’s face, [in the beginning] of the [lines of the] writing of the
face, which are 28 or 32 with the line of balance (320a).14
Thus, the human form synthesises the complete set of 28/32 original
letters, the basic elements of form resulting from the differentiation of
the Point. In other words, the human body represents the complete
divine ‘alphabet’ of the creation: ‘Adam was created to be the form
(s.ūra) of the 32 [ontological ‘words’], in accordance with the 32 [lines
of writing upon] his face. He is the Word of God (kalimat’ullāh)’ (29a);
‘The graphic form (naqsh) of the letters of the alphabet is similar to the
form of Adam (mithāl-i s.ūrat-i Adam). This is why he [Adam]
represents the science (ʿilm), in the sense that the letters are made [to
represent] the science of the Word (ʿilm-i kalima), and the form of
Adam is the science of [all] the 32 [ontological] ‘words’ on the ‘Straight
Path’ (s.irāt. mustaqīm)’ (153b).
13 Allusion to Q. 2:33, where Adam teaches angels the names he received from God.
14 According to the Jāwidān-nāma, there are seven basic lines on the human face,
which become eight with the line of balance drawn in the middle. Multiplied by four,
which is the number of natural elements (earth, water, air and ﬁre), seven and eight
become respectively 28 and 32. See Chapter 4.
Adam and Eve

It should be noted that the prototypal human being is most often
considered in the Jāwidān-nāma in his dichotomy of the masculine
and feminine aspects, as the couple Adam/Eve. Eve represents the
original form of every human being, male as well as female. In the
couple Adam/Eve, Eve is the form of Adam. In order to support this
position, the Jāwidān-nāma observes that it is the mother who gives
bodily form to the human being; this form is originally that of the
mother. The lines and features speciﬁc to the male body develop only
in adult men. All inhabitants of Paradise have the bodily form of Eve,
and even Adam has in Paradise the form of Eve. The relationship
between Adam and Eve is similar to the relationship between the series
of 28 and 32 ‘words’: the 28 (Eve) represent the foundation potentially
containing the 32 (Adam); this potentiality is realised by the line of
Balance. Adam was created before Eve. Adam’s body contains the
complete science of the divine Word, but this science is inaccessible
without the basic science represented by the bodily shape of Eve. These
positions will be analysed more closely in the following chapters. Let us
just note, however, that even if Eve is not explicitly mentioned in all
passages cited below, any mention of the bodily form of Adam may
equally be a reference to Eve.
The ontological letters required in order to create, to ‘write down’
the actual form of any other being or object, can only be derived from
the alphabet of the human form. Just like the forms of the letters of any
ordinary alphabet are intended to express corresponding sounds, the
human form is intended to express the science of the divine ‘words’:
About the composition of the form (wad.ʿ-i shakl). The forms [of
the names of the letters] alif, bāʾ and tāʾ are made with the
purpose of representing the science (ʿilm) of these words [i.e., the
names of letters] alif, bāʾ and tāʾ. Similarly, God composed (wad.ʿ)
the human form (shakl-i insānī) with the purpose of it to be the
science of the 32 ‘words’ of His [Word] (218b).
But the letters of human alphabets are only a metaphor of the only real
Alphabet, that of the creation represented by the bodily form of Adam:
The letters and the point are the science and the locum tenens of
the Word (kalima). This visible science of the 50 [graphical signs]
is a metaphor (majāz) of the science of the 28 words emitted by
the humans. In reality (h. aqīqa), the science of these 28 words is
the locus of manifestation [which is] the human [body] (maz.har-
Words of Power

i insānī) and [the human] face, which bears 28 [lines of the divine
writing] (316a–b).
Just as the original Point is the source from which any letter is derived,
the human form is the source of any writing based on differentiated
elements. Adam and Eve are, essentially, the original and only real
Book of God, containing potentially any possible book, especially any
prophetic revelation. Again, any prophetic book written in a human
language is only a metaphor of the real ontological writing appearing
on the human body and face:
The divine Book is the visible form of the divine Word
metaphorically (bi-majāz), while in reality (bi-h. aqīqa) it is the
human body that is the Book of God. From the [human body]
you can learn the 32 sciences, which manifest themselves on the
face, and which lead to the 32 [ontological] ‘words’ (318a).
This is why the Jāwidān-nāma identiﬁes the human form, and
particularly the human face, the most expressive part of the body, with
the Well-preserved Tablet (lawh.
mah. fūz.), the archetype of all
prophetic books as well as of the whole creation considered as divine
writing: ‘The Well-preserved Tablet is the place where the Qurʾān and
other [prophetic] books, as well as the [ontological] names of all
things, are ﬁxed. And this person who is the Tablet is the locus of
manifestation of all sciences (ʿulūm), and [this person] is Adam’ (38b).
The form of any created being or object originates from the human
form. As the result of the differentiation of the Word, the human form
emerges from the blackness and smoke of the undifferentiated
condition and irradiates the Balance and the Measure, establishing
thus the correspondence between the creation and the original divine
Reality. In its quality of Well-preserved Tablet, the human form
contains potentially all possible forms of the created universe. Since
the potentialities of all existing things are contained in the form of the
human body, the universe with all that it contains reproduces in its
structure the human body, represented by the primordial couple of
Adam and Eve. All parts of the universe are articulated together as
members of a human body.
The human being is the central ﬁgure of the Jāwidān-nāma’s
cosmology. He/she encapsulates the totality of creation, from
beginning to end:
Adam and Eve

Imagine all things of the three worlds as [if they were] one world,
[established] as the counterpart of the human being (bi-khilāf-i
insān). From the vantage point of the line of balance of the
creation (khat.t.-i istiwāʾ-yi khilqat), you can see that they are all
loci of manifestation of the Word (kalima wa kalām), and that
the human being (insān) is the locus of manifestation of [all] that
[is contained] in all [things of the three worlds], in actuality, in
potentiality, and from the point of view of the [ontological]
science [expressed by the forms of these things] (chi az rū-yi bi-l-
ﬁʿl wa bi-l-quwwa wa chi az rū-yi ʿilmiyyat) . . . Any locus of
manifestation and any [expression of the ontological] science
(maz.hariyyat waʿilmiyyat) that exists in the heavens [exists also]
in [every] single human being: ‘We have neglected nothing in the
Book’ [Q. 6:38], and ‘Everything We have numbered in a clear
register’ [Q. 36:12]
. . .
All the creation, with the inﬁnite
[multitude of] objects [contained in it], is a single human
person. All visible objects are the parts and attendants (ajzāʾ wa
h. awāshī) [of this person] (267a).
Since the human shape is the locus of manifestation of the complete
Word and includes all the 28/32 ontological letters, that is, the totality of
divine science, no other form can contain more science. The human
form is the most perfect form of the universe, and stands therefore at the
limit between the created universe and the eternal, invisible, creative
divine Word. It is the ﬁrst locus of manifestation of the science of the
divine Word, and also the place where this science will return at the end
of times. In many passages of the Jāwidān-nāma Adam is identiﬁed
with the Qurʾānic ‘Lote-tree of the Boundary’ (sidrat al-muntahā,
Q. 53:14): ‘The Lote-tree of the Boundary refers to Adam: “God created
Adam in His form and in the form of All-Merciful.” There is no station
(maqām) above this one . . . The complete science (ʿilm-i kullī) coming
from the heavens attains ﬁrst of all [the Lote-tree] . . . and comes back
to it at the end’ (274a).15 The following two fragments develop the idea
of the human form as the ‘boundary’ of the forms:
The ‘Lote-tree of the Boundary’ mentioned [in the Qurʾān, 53:14]
is, in a sense, [the ‘good tree’ of the verse]: ‘A good word is as a
good tree’ [Q. 14:24]. The boundary (muntahā) is mentioned
because the boundary of the Word (muntahā-yi kalām) is

constituted by the 32 [ontological] ‘words’. In a sense, they are
similar to the human form (mithāl-i s.ūrat-i bashariyya). It is in
this sense that the Lote-tree of the Boundary [is located on the
boundary]. The form of the 32 [ontological ‘words’], which is the
science (ʿilm) of the 32 ‘words’ manifests itself in [the Lote-tree].
And it is the human form that possesses the science of the 32

Boundary (208b–209a).
His [Adam’s] form (s.ūra) is the form of God (s.ūrat-i ilāhīst),

Necessarily, his [Adam’s] form is the boundary form (s.ūrat-i
muntahā). In this form, it is possible to see the presence of Unity

breadth is as the heavens and earth, prepared for the godfearing’
[Q. 3:133] (415b).
The Qurʾānic symbols of the divine Throne (ʿarsh) and Footstool
(kursī) are used in the Jāwidān-nāma to make the link between the
limit position of the human form expressed by the Lote-tree of the
Boundary and the principle of the Balance which, as we have seen,
originates from the Throne. The dichotomy Throne/Footstool reﬂects
the dichotomy of the masculine and feminine aspects of the human
form, which will be discussed in more detail further below. At this
point, let us exemplify this idea through the following citation:
In [the verse] ‘The All-Compassionate sat Himself [in balance]
upon the Throne’ [Q. 20:5],16 God mentions the Throne (ʿarsh) in
order to refer to Adam . . . The Throne is the body (wujūd) of
Adam, because the balance of the divine Word (istiwāʾ-yi kalima-
yi ilāhī) manifested itself in the original nature (khilqa) of his
face. Eve is His Footstool (kursī). There are seven lines [of the
divine writing in the] shape (hayʾa) of the Footstool, compared to
the Throne which [represents] the complete [writing] of
[Adam’s] face (272b–273a).17
Both Throne and Footstool are related to the same concept of the Lote-
tree of the Boundary as the limit:

Adam and Eve

About the Throne. It is said that above [all] things there is the
Throne of God. This is true because, if the things are not limited
on one side, on another side they are limited by the divine
Throne and Footstool. Beyond the Throne and the Footstool is
the world of God (ʿālam-i khudā), that of the divine Word
(kalima-yi ilāhī) (364b).
Adam is the Throne of God, and the Throne is essentially the source of
the Balance. It is from Adam/Throne, the primary locus of divine
manifestation, that the Balance spreads to the rest of the creation, and
thus conveys to every object the ability to express a divine reality:
Adam is the Throne (ʿarsh) of God because . . . he was created in
the form of the All-Merciful: ‘God created Adam in His form and
in the form of the All-Merciful.’ Therefore, Adam is the divine
Throne, and the locus of manifestation (maz.har) of the pre-
existant Word (kalām-i qadīm). The science (ʿilm) of the 28 and
32 [ontological] ‘words’ appears on the tablet of his face. ‘All
things perish, except His Face’ [Q. 28:88], because this science of
the divine Word (ʿilmiyyat-i kalima-yi ilāhī) does not manifest
itself on the face of any creature other than on the face of Adam
. . . The balance of the [divine] presence (h. ad.rat) and of His
Word (kalām) on the Throne and on all things is like a king
sitting on his throne and commanding his deputies. Even if God
and the 32 [ontological] ‘words’ [of His Word] manifest (tajallī)
themselves in everything, nowhere else than on the face of Adam,
which is His Throne, did He found the [perfect] balance (istiwāʾ)
for His manifestation and His writing. [The Prophet] said: ‘In the
night of my heavenly ascension, I saw my Lord in the form of a
beardless youth, in the most beautiful form (ah. san s.ūra)’, because
Adam was [created] ‘in the fairest stature’ (ah. san taqwīm)
[Q. 95:4], as the locus of manifestation of the 32 ‘words’ without
beginning and without end (azalī abadī), from the point of view
of his language and from the point of view of his original nature
(khilqa). His teeth, his forehead, his members and his side are the
science of the complete divine Word (ʿilm-i kalima-yi tāmm-i
ilāhī). This is why Adam is the Throne of God: ‘The All-
Compassionate sat Himself [in balance] upon the Throne’
[Q. 20:5] (276a–b).18
The human form is thus the focal point of the science of the Word.
From this point, the science is irradiated and distributed to the rest of
18 Cf. Chapter 1, note 49.

the creation. In other words, the human form, which summarises and
expresses the supreme Truth or Meaning of the creation, that of the
original divine Word, is like a standard or mould which gives to the
creation a structure appropriate to the reception and visible expression
of metaphysical truths and meanings derived from the divine Word. In
this sense, the human form is what makes the creation meaningful,
literally ﬁlls it with meaning. The action of the principle of Balance
inherent to the human form is applied ﬁrst of all to two general
components of the creation: Time and Universe. As mentioned at the
beginning of this chapter, Time and the Universe are, like Adam, the
loci of manifestation of the complete Word. However, unlike Adam,
Time and the Universe do not possess a proper form. They are
therefore dependent on the human form through which they acquire a
structure corresponding to the science of the Word:
Divided by the line of balance (khat.t.-i istiwāʾ), the body of Adam
is the divine writing and the Well-preserved Tablet (kitābat-i
khudā wa lawh. -i mah. fūz.). From this location, [the ontological
writing is] spread, by the [action] of the line of balance, on all
things, and in particular, on the things [composed] of the four
elements, which are the remnants of the original nature of Adam
(baqiyyat-i khilqat-i Adam), that is to say, the things made of
earth . . . After that, by the division of the world of earth, water,
air and ﬁre (bi-taqsīm-i ʿālam-i khāk wa āb wa hawā wa ātash),
the [division of] the body (wujūd) of Adam was transmitted to
the natural elements (bi-t.abāʾīʿ). After that, [this division attained
the heavens and the heavenly bodies] according to the [verses]:
‘By heaven of the constellations’ [Q. 85:1]; ‘And the moon – We
have determined it by stations’ [Q. 36:39]. The Prophet Idrīs
established that [the moon has] 28 stations, and [that the heaven
of the constellations is divided into] 12 constellations, each
constellation [measuring] 30 degrees, so that [together they
cover] 360 degrees, like [the number] of articulations of Adam, of
his bones, of the parts of ﬂesh and skin [composing his body].
After that, the division [extended] to the nights and days which
are 12,19 just as the constellations (82a).
19 Reference either to the six days of creation mentioned in the Qurʾān (six days
and six nights), or to the 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night.
Adam and Eve

Some details of this process of differentiation and structuring of Time
and the Universe according to the proportions of the human bodily
form will be examined in the following chapters.
Words of Power

Excursus on Knowledge and Love
It is hardly possible to discuss any topic of the Jāwidān-nāma’s
doctrine without reference to human beings. The human being is
the key ﬁgure of the Jāwidān-nāma’s Weltanschauung and, in a
sense, the whole work is essentially an ‘anthropology’. The present
Excursus is focused on two important attributes of the human
being: Knowledge and Love, mentioned only brieﬂy elsewhere in
this book, but important to the understanding of the following
chapters. As we have already seen, the human shape is conceived in
the Jāwidān-nāma essentially as the model for the creation of the
universe, as the source of cosmic Measure and Balance. In the
following chapters, the human being will be considered respectively
as the source and the ﬁnal goal of the prophetic revelations, and the
personiﬁcation of the end of time. Knowledge and Love characterise
human beings in their own existence and their relationships between
each other.
The differentiation between the male and female bodily forms has
an important epistemological signiﬁcance in the Jāwidān-nāma. Man
and Woman are both the loci of manifestation of the divine Word, but
their forms express the knowledge of the Word in two different ways.
In the beginning, we are told, Adam and Eve dwelled in Paradise.
This means, according to the interpretation given in the Jāwidān-
nāma, that they were inseparably united to each other within the
undifferentiated divine Word with its 28 and 32 ‘words’. The
expression of this idea in the following passage is widely based on
the interpretation of the symbolism of the Qurʾānic description of
Paradise:
‘Adam, dwell thou, and thy wife, in the Garden’ [Q. 2:35]. There is
a tree in Paradise: ‘A good word is as a good tree’ [Q. 14:24], that is

to say, ‘dwell in a single word’ (bi-hī [=yak] kalima qarār bi-gīr).
The discourse that God addressed to Adam [in the cited verse of
the Qurʾān] refers to the 32 [ontological] ‘words’, [brought
together] within one single Word. ‘Eat where you desire from this
single word’,1 that is, ‘recognize the [fundamental] unity of all
[things]’. ‘Thou and [thy] wife’: ‘thou’ [refers] to the soul (nafs),
and ‘wife’ means the spouse of the Word (zawj-i kalima) . . . She,
too, dwells in a single Word, because her body is dependent on
[this Word] (wujūd-i khū [=ū] qāʾim bi-khūʾī [=bi-ūst]) (166b).
This quotation suggests that Adam is the soul (nafs) of the Word,
while Eve is its body (wujūd). The idea that Adam is closer to the
initial, invisible stage of the Word, while Eve represents the principle
of embodiment is further developed in other passages. The couple
Adam/Eve is able to reproduce the entire cosmogenesis such as it has
been described in the previous chapters, from the generation of the
invisible and undifferentiated Word symbolised by the drop of sperm,
through the stages of differentiation until its embodiment in the
perfect locus of manifestation, a human form constituted in the womb
of Eve. Thus, Adam provides the original Point, the ‘ink’ of the
ontological writing, associated in the Jāwidān-nāma with the symbols
of smoke and blackness; but it is in the womb of Eve that this writing is
developed and actualised as a concrete human form:2
The sperm (nut.fa) [contained] in the back of Adam is similar to
the soot and blackness (dūda wa siyāhī), which comes from the
inkwell of his back into the original nature of the pen of [his]
penis (khilqat-i qalam-i dhakar), which produces, in the womb of
[Eve] the Mother (dar shikam-i umm), the bodily form of mother
(s.ūrat-i umm), divided [in accordance with] the lines of the
divine [ontological writing]. Whosoever, male or female, comes
[in this world] from [the belly of his or her] mother, comes with
the bodily form corresponding to the form of Mother (bi-s.ūrat-i
umm) (262a).
Any [ontological] ‘word’ from among the 32 divine ‘words’ . . .
is, in the beginning, one point (nuqt.a) . . . [All] that is outside the
point [exists only] for the purpose of differentiation (tamyiz). For
example, the sperm (nut.fa), which [passes] from the back of the

of Q. 2:35.
2 Other aspects of relative position of Adam and Eve with regard to the original

father to the womb (rah. im) [of the mother], does not possess in

The following passages conﬁrm that the sperm of Adam has no
speciﬁc form in itself; the form is given to it in the womb of the
mother, and any human form, male and female, is originally the form
of Eve the Mother: ‘The sperm (nut.fa), produced and emitted from the

The sperm of Adam does not possess this form [of the human
body] in actuality (bi-l-ﬁʿl). It is produced from the form of Eve.
This is why it is said: ‘Truly, Paradise is at the feet of mothers.’
The original nature (khilqa) of Eve is the last in the creation,3 and
the last writing is the writing on the faces of the sons of Adam
[born] from her [from Eve] (57b).
In the womb of Eve, the original point of sperm undergoes
differentiation, reproducing the differentiation of the cosmic Black
Point. The letters and the lines of ontological writing appear
progressively as the foetus develops. At the moment of birth, crucial
because it marks the passage from the interior, invisible (bāt.in) to the
exterior, visible (z.āhir) existence, the half of the lines are fully
developed and visible in the form and facial features of the new-born
baby, independently of its sex:
When a . . . boy [lit. ‘man’, rajul] is born from the belly of his
mother, he already has two times seven [lines of divine
ontological writing on his face]. The other seven [lines, proper
to the adult man], like the moustache and others, develop only in
the external material world (dunyā). One half [of the lines]
appears thus in the womb of the mother (dar bat.n-i umm) and

another in the exterior material world (dar dunyā ki ʿālam-i
z.āhirast). This shows that interior and exterior are governed alike
(ān kas ki murabbī-yi bāt.in ast hamāzan ast ki murabbī-yi
z.āhirast) (213b).4
This original divine writing represented by the form of Eve, and shared
by women, children and adolescents of both sexes, is the foundation
on which develops the more complete writing contained in the form of
adult men, exempliﬁed in the form of Adam. This original writing is
symbolised in the Jāwidān-nāma by the seven facial lines: a hairline,
two lines of eyebrows and four lines of eyelashes. Together with the
seven parts of the face where they appear, they are 14, that is, half the
number 28 symbolising the complete Word. The additional seven
lines, which appear on the face of an adult man, are constituted by the
lines of beard and moustache. According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the
prophetic description of the vision of God narrated in a well-known
h. adīth where God shows Himself to Muh.ammad in the form of a
beautiful youth,5 refers to the revelation of the original divine writing
in its original form, that of Eve. The central idea here seems to be that
the form of Eve is essentially that in which the original divine writing is
revealed and can be seen. This is why ‘the hand of the divine Power’
hinders the manifestation of the additional lines proper to the adult
man in women, children and adolescents. Indeed, if the basic writing
visible on the faces of the latter was hidden by the additional lines, the
more complex writing on the face of an adult man could not be
deciphered:
The original nature (khilqa), which is the starting point of the
degrees [of development] of any human being (insān), is the form
of the mother (s.ūrat-i umm) . . . But the relationship to the
mother is, [in particular], due to the fact that the human being
receives his or her body (wujūd) from the mother, [and this body
has] the shape and the form of Eve (bi-shakl wa s.ūrat-i h. awwāʾ).
This means that the original nature (khilqa) of his or her face [is
constituted] by the [ontological writing ﬁgured by] the hairline,
[two] eyebrows and four eyelashes. All the youth in Paradise have
the form of the Mother (s.ūrat-i umm). The division of other
seven [lines] on the face of Adam is produced by the [original

In Paradise, both Eve and Adam had the bodily form of youth

The following passage highlights the idea that it is by means of the
form of Eve that the original nature of Adam becomes visible:
Why is Mecca not called ‘father of the cities’ (abū-l-qurā)? The
answer is that Eve was the second [being after Adam] to be
created in the location [of Mecca]. [Therefore], the human
original nature (khilqat-i insānī) is better visible in her, because
[Eve] has the shape of the Seven Twofold (shakl-i sabʿ-i mathānī).
In addition, the sperm of Adam reaches the perfection of the
human form in the [womb] of Eve. This is why [Mecca] is called
‘mother of the cities’ (umm al-qurā) (240a).
The fact that it is the form of Eve/Mother and not that of Adam/Father
that is essential for the expression of the divine writing is further
conﬁrmed by the fact that Jesus, the Word of God and a Spirit from
God according to the Qurʾān, took spontaneously a human form in the
womb of Mary, without participation of a physical father: ‘It is said in
the Gospel (injīl) that Jesus is the Word of God (kalima-yi ilāhī),
which came into the womb (bat.n) of the Virgin Mary and became
ﬂesh. This means that [the Word] took the form (s.ūra) of Adam
without [the participation of] the father (bī-padar)’ (421b).
In the light of the passages cited above, it becomes clear why the
form of Adam cannot be understood, or ‘read’, without the key
provided by the form of Eve. Eve is the basic writing starting from
which develop the lines of Adam. Her form is the original
manifestation of the divine writing: ‘It is by the original nature of
Mother (khilqat-i umm) that the science of the divine writing became
vocabulary of which is extensively used in the Jāwidān-nāma, is based on similar
premises.

recognisable on the face of Adam. Otherwise [this science] would not
be available’ (238a–b). It will be recalled that the form of Adam is
deﬁned in the Jāwidān-nāma as the ‘science’ of the complete divine
Word, because this form makes the invisible truths contained in the
Word visible and knowable. From this perspective, Eve is the ‘science
of the science’: she personiﬁes the clear model of division, from which
appear the basic lines of the divine ontological writing without which
the science of the form of Adam cannot be accessed. The knowledge of
the form of Adam means the knowledge of the complete divine
alphabet of creation and knowledge of the Word as the ﬁrst emanation
of the Essence. It gives the possibility of recognising the universal
ontological writing in any existing form, ‘reading’ the creation and
discerning its ultimate metaphysical meaning. In the Jāwidān-nāma,
this is the highest knowledge that can be attained by a created being.
Such knowledge is proper to the condition of Paradise; and since it is
the form of Eve that leads to the realisation of this knowledge, all the
inhabitants of Paradise have the form of Eve. With regard to this point,
the Jāwidān-nāma refers to the Qurʾānic descriptions of Paradise
which mention the houris and youths which, according to the
interpretation that we have seen above, represent the form of the
Mother with its seven basic lines of writing. The meaning of this form
was revealed to the Prophet Muh.ammad when God appeared to him
in the form of a beautiful young man. We have encountered this
interpretation above in passage fol. 69a–b. Another example is given in
the citation below:
‘Paradise is at the feet of Mothers.’8 The Mother will appear [in
Paradise] because, by her original nature (khilqa), it is possible to
recognize the original nature of man’s face (wajh-i mard), and
reach thus the 32 [original] ‘words’ of the divine line [of
ontological writing]. It is said that whosoever goes to Paradise . . .
[goes there in the form of] youth (amrad), because he or she has
reached the original nature of the Mother (khilqat-i umm) . . . All
the houris [of Paradise represent] the original nature of Mother.

[ontological] writing in the ‘Mother of the Book’ (umm al-

He/she discovers then the secret of: ‘God gave us speech, as He
gave everything speech’ [Q. 41:21]. [Such a person] becomes a
reader of the lines of the divine [ontological] writing (233b).
The idea that the form of Eve expresses the basic writing leading to the
understanding of the complete writing represented by the bodily shape
of Adam brings us naturally to the Jāwidān-nāma’s description of
Adam and Eve as the original Book of God. Several passages above
identify the form and the face of Eve/Mother with the Qurʾānic
expressions ‘Mother of the Book’ (umm al-kitāb) and ‘Seven [of the]
Twofold’ (sabʿ min al-mathānī). The ‘Mother of the Book’, generally
understood as the heavenly archetype or source of the Qurʾān, is also
one of the names of the opening sura of the Qurʾān (Fātih. at-ul-kitāb,
or Fātih. a), and the deﬁnition of the Seven Twofold as the seven verses
of the Fātih. a is common in Islamic exegetical literature.9 We have seen
that, according to the Jāwidān-nāma, the human body, represented by

‘Fātih.a’, and U. Rubin, ‘Oft-repeated’, Encyclopaedia of the Qurʾān, respectively vol. 2,
pp. 188–192, and vol. 3, pp. 574–576.

the primordial couple of Adam and Eve, is the original and the most
complete Book of God, the unique locus of manifestation containing
the full ontological alphabet, and the ‘Well-preserved Tablet’. Adam
and Eve are the prototype of any divine revelation, of all the prophetic
books, and especially the Qurʾān which contains the most complete
revelation of the divine Word. The human being is the ‘speaking’
Qurʾān, equivalent to the written ‘silent’ Qurʾān.10 The following
passages remind us of this idea:
The ‘Mother of the Book’ (umm al-kitāb) is, in reality, the writing
that God wrote on the face of Adam, as well as in the universe
(kāʾināt) with all the shapes and forms [contained in it], in the
prophetic books, and in every existing line, in accordance with
the [verse]: ‘taught by the Pen’ [Q. 96:4] . . . [The human shape]
is therefore the ‘Mother of the Book’ and the ‘mother of the lines’
[of the ontological writing] (umm al-khut.ūt.), the foundation (as.l)
compared to which all [other objects and beings] are branches
(farʿ) (175a).
[God] made Adam and Eve the loci of manifestation of the
Word (maz.har-i kalima wa kalām). He made their bodies and
faces the lines [of writing of the ontological] ‘words’, the Well-
preserved Tablet (lawh. -i mah. fūz.). [Expressions such as]: ‘We
have neglected nothing in the Book’ [Q. 6:38], and ‘With Him is
the knowledge of the Book’ [Q. 13:43] refer to them. (28a)
Other passages contain additional details concerning this analogy
between the human body and the structure of the Qurʾān. The 14
letters which appear in various combinations at the beginning (the
‘head’) of some suras symbolise the 14 basic lines of writing on the
human face (either seven ‘lines of Eve’ counted with the seven parts of
the face where they are located, or 14 lines of hair on the face of an
adult man, obtained by the addition of the seven basic lines of Eve and
of the seven lines formed by the beard and moustache of Adam):
[ʿAlī’s utterance]: ‘I am the speaking Word of God’ refers to
Adam as master of the Face (khudāwand-i wajh). The complete
science (ʿilm-i tamām) [represented by the] 14 [lines on his face]

This explains the anthropomorphic appearance of the Qurʾān at the
end of days mentioned in an apocryphal h. adīth:
The Messenger, peace be on him, said that during the
Resurrection (qiyāma) the Qurʾān will appear in the form of a

of] 29 letters. Similarly, the divine [ontological] writing on the

Qurʾān will be represented (mumaththal) [by a form], it will be
made known under the form of a man (bi-s.ūrat-i rajul) (221a).
A perfect human form is a perfect, complete divine Book. Not only the
Qurʾān, but also any other prophetic book where the divine Word is
written symbolises the human body and face. This is particularly true
when speaking of the Book given to Moses and believed to have been
written by God’s own Hand:12
The only true book (bi-h. aqīqat mus.h. af faqat. h. aqīqī) is the form
of the humanity of the Perfect Human (s.ūrat-i bashariyyat-i
insān-i kāmil) . . . The perfect Adam is the true ‘clear book’ and
‘clear register’ [mentioned in the verses]: ‘Everything We have
numbered in a book and in a clear register’ [free combination of
Q. 78:29 and 36:12], because all things are the loci of
manifestation (maz.har) of the 32 [primordial ‘words’], but he
[i.e., Adam] is alone the locus of manifestation of [the complete
set of the] 32. He is therefore the Book of God that He wrote with
His own hand. Such is the shape of the perfect humanity (shakl-i
bashariyyat-i kāmil), [represented] by the human form (hayʾat).
This is why it is said that God wrote the Torah with His own
Hand (162a–b).
The next passage deﬁnes the human face as ‘living pages’ of the holy
writing:
Starting from the visible silent pages [of the Qurʾān], which begin
by ‘She who opens the Book’ (fātih. at-ul-kitāb) with her seven

verses which are the ‘Seven Twofold’ (sabʿ mathānī), from the

This is an allusion to another extra-Islamic reference used in the
Jāwidān-nāma, namely to the sealed Book mentioned in the
Revelation of St John.14 The seven seals of the ‘Book of Life’ are
identiﬁed in the Jāwidān-nāma with the seven lines of the basic divine
writing on the face of Mary, identical to the original writing on the face
of Eve:
Learn, O true seeker, what is the ‘Book of Life’ (mus.h. af-i h. ayāt)
under the seven seals received by the Lamb with seven horns. O
seeker, learn that the face of the Virgin Mary bears seven [lines
of the divine ontological] writing: hairline, two eyebrows and
four eyelashes. This divine writing constitutes the ﬁrst seven
seals (423a).
If both Adam and Eve are the Book of God, Adam represents more
speciﬁcally the complete Book, while Eve is the ‘opening chapter’
without which this book cannot be read. Hence the identiﬁcation of
Eve with the Fātih. a, which is believed to contain the summary of all
the truths contained in the Qurʾān.15 The seven verses of the Fātih. a
symbolise the seven basic lines of divine writing on the face of Eve with
the seven parts of the face where they appear. Eve thus possesses the
‘Seven Twofold’, and she is literally the Mother of the human Book:
‘Eve is the Mother of the Book, with reference to the Book of face
(kitāb-i wajh)’ (352b):
The Mother of the Book, that is to say, the origin of the Book (as.l-
i kitāb), consists of the seven lines of the face of Eve. If these seven
lines did not exist, the 32 lines of the face of Adam would not
appear. Truly, the Mother of the Book consists of the seven lines
of the face of Eve, and ‘Paradise is at the feet of mothers’16 (405b).

The form of the ‘youth’, in which God appeared in the vision of the
Prophet Muh.ammad,17 is also the form of the Mother of the Book:
‘During the night of the heavenly ascension, God showed Himself [to
Muh.ammad] in the form of the Mother of the Book’ (29a).
[The Fātih. a] is recited during the prayer and without it the
prayer is not valid. It is named ‘Mother of the Book’ because it
really has the form of the Mother (s.ūrat-i umm), who is Eve . . .
The inhabitants of Paradise, like youth and young servants, have
this form, and [it is in this form that the Prophet Muh.ammad
contemplated God during his heavenly ascension]: ‘I saw my
Lord in the form of a beardless youth.’ This form [represents] the
original division (mabdāʾ-yi qismat) [according to which is
divided] the face and the writing on the face of Adam. This is why
[it is called] ‘Mother of the Book’ (24b).
Several passages of the Jāwidān-nāma underline the statement that
Eve is the last being produced in the order of the creation.18 If Adam is
the summary of the creation, Eve is the summary of the summary; her
form is derived from the form of Adam and contains the basic
ontological elements necessary for the understanding of the latter:
‘ “And from it created its mate” [Q. 4:1]. If the shape (shakl) of Adam,
who is a man, did not exist, the science (ʿilm) of the 32 [primordial
‘words’] would not appear in [the form of his] wife. [This science was
transmitted] from the face of Adam and appeared in the original
nature (khilqa) of Eve’ (185a); ‘Eve is the last created (makhlūq-i
ākhir). She has on her face seven lines of the divine [ontological
writing]. Otherwise, it would be extremely difﬁcult to read the
complete divine lines [of writing] on the face of Adam’ (119a–b).
As the last created, the form of Eve concludes the descent of the
divine Word. For this reason, it is the form of Eve, and not that of
Adam, that is the clearest manifestation of the Word. This idea is also
expressed in the Jāwidān-nāma with reference to the symbolism of the
divine Throne (ʿarsh) and Footstool (kursī), which we have discussed
earlier. According to a h. adīth, at the end of days God will step down
from His Throne onto His Footstool, and it is upon the Footstool that
He will be visible. The Jāwidān-nāma suggests a link between this
17 Inventory I, no. 30.
18 See note 3 above.
Words of Power

h. adīth and the Prophetic vision of God in the form of a beautiful
youth:
The Messenger said: ‘Upon the day when God will come down
onto His Footstool.’19 This means that [God will come down]
from the Throne (ʿarsh), which is Adam and his bodily form
(s.ūra), to the bodily form of his wife, who is the last [in the order
of] creation (ākhir-i khilqa). It is she who is referred to as the
‘Footstool’ (kursī). According to another tradition, the verse
of the Footstool20 will appear in the form of a youth (s.ūrat-i
amrad) (57b).
The position of Eve as the last point of the descent of the Word means
also that her bodily form corresponds to the deepest, innermost level
of the Word. The following passage identiﬁes the seven lines on the
face of Eve with the seven levels of meanings or truths in the Qurʾān:
‘The Qurʾān has an exoteric and an esoteric [level], and its
esoteric [level] has another esoteric [level], and so on up to seven
esoteric [levels].’21 The limit of the seventh esoteric level is the
[ontological] writing on the face of Eve, who is created the last,
after all [other] objects and beings (ākhir khilqat-i hame ashyāʾ).
First were created the four elementary natures, heavenly bodies
and all that which is useful for humans. After a long delay, Adam
was created, peace be upon him. After Adam, Eve was created.
After all the members and organs of the body of Eve, the seven
lines [of the ontological writing] were written down on the face of
Eve . . . The Prophet said that the Qurʾān has an exoteric [level],
and this exoteric level has up to seven esoteric [levels]. [These
seven esoteric levels] are the seven lines [of ontological writing]
on the face of Eve, who is the last created creature (ākhir-i
makhlūqāt) (307a–b).
From this deepest source the truths are manifested, just as the human
form of the new-born human being, the ‘living Book’, is manifested
from the womb (bat.n) of Eve. Eve is the source and the principle of
manifestation of the truths or meanings of the Word, just as the
innermost (bāt.in) truth of the Qurʾān is the source of its sensible
manifestation in the form of a Book:
19 Inventory I, no. 49.
20 Ayat al-kursī, Q. 2:255.
21 Inventory I, no. 40.
Knowledge and Love

The ‘Seven Twofold’ (sabʿ-i mathānī) [i.e., the seven verses of the
Fātih. a] are called ‘Mother of the Book’ (umm al-kitāb) because
they are the mother of all the meanings (mādar-i hame maʿānī).
All the meanings are [contained] in the ‘womb’ (bat.n) [of the
Seven Twofold], and are born from them (wa azh khū bi-zhāyad
[= wa az ū bi-zāyad]) (24b).
The last point of the descent is also the ﬁrst point of the return to the
origin. The form of Eve and the basic lines of the divine scripture on
her face are the starting point on the way back to the origin of the
divine Word. Every human being receives his or her bodily form from
the mother, and it is in this form of the mother that he or she will enter
the Paradise of the divine Word. On the Day of Judgment, human
beings will be addressed by their mothers, and if they did not realise
the basic writing contained in the form of the Mother, they will not be
admitted to Paradise. The revelation of this basic writing related to the
form of the Mother is the mission of the ‘motherly’ prophets
(ummiyīn), whom we will discuss in more detail in Part Two.
The ﬁrst station of a descendant of Adam [on the path] of
religion is that at which the sperm (nut.fa) of Adam and Eve
takes, in the womb (rah. im) of Eve, the form (s.ūra) of Adam and
Eve, and comes [in this form] into the external world. Since
[every human] obtains the shape of Adam’s human nature
(shakl-i bashariyyat-i Adam) from the mother (umm), he or she
necessarily enters the world of return (ʿālam-i maʿād) and
Paradise in the form of Eve. It is this form that is referred to by
the [symbol of] youth (amrad). [This is why], in the prayer over
the dead, [the deceased person is addressed as]: ‘O son of Eve!’
(yā ibn H. awwāʾ). [The verse]: ‘One day We shall call together all
human beings with their (respective) Imāms’ [Q. 17:71] can be
understood along the same lines (57b).22
Whosoever, male or female, who comes into existence from his
or her mother, has in the beginning the form of the mother
(s.ūrat-i umm). At the end, [humans] will be again in the form of
the mother in Paradise . . . because they will reach the original
nature of the mother (khilqat-i umm). Otherwise, they will not be
in the form of the mother and will not be among the inhabitants
of Paradise (262a).
22 The Qurʾānic imāmihim, ‘their Imāms, their leaders’ in this verse, is usually

Words of Power

Many ideas concerning the relationships between the male and the
female bodily forms and facial features with regard to the expression of
the knowledge of the Word that we have discussed above are
concentrated in the Jāwidān-nāma’s interpretations of the h. adīths
related to the terms derived from the Arabic root rh. m. Let us examine
these relationships brieﬂy.23 The Jāwidān-nāma refers essentially to
the h. adīths which establish the relationship between the Merciful (al-
rah. mān) identiﬁed with Adam, and the womb (al-rah. im) identiﬁed
with Eve.24 There is, therefore, an essential link between the divine
Mercy and the fundamental ‘motherly’ knowledge contained in the
human form produced in the womb of Eve. Notwithstanding the
unavoidable repetitions in the fragments cited below, they add some
new elements to the topics discussed in this chapter.
Adam is the Supreme Name (ism-i aʿz.am) [of God]: ‘I am God
and I am the All-Merciful (al-rah. mān). I created the womb (al-
rah. im)
and
I
gave
it
a
name
derived
from
My
own
name.’25 . . . ‘The womb is attached to the Throne and says, “If
someone joins me, let God join him, but if someone cuts me off,
let God cut him off’26 . . . From a certain point of view, ‘mercy’
(rah. ma) refers to Eve, because she is the Mother, and God
[appeared before Muh.ammad] ‘in the form of a beardless youth’
[which is the form of Eve]. The ultimate purpose of this shape
(shakl) is [to represent] the shape of God. It is from it that Eve
had been ‘derived’. It is the mercy and the womb (zahdān) of
every science (ʿilm) attached to the Throne of God, that is, to
Adam. Whosoever joins her, God appears to this person in the
form [mentioned in the h. adīth]: ‘I saw my Lord in the most
beautiful form, that of a beardless [youth].’ . . . Eve is the name of
mercy of the All-Merciful (ism-i rah. mat-i rah. mān), from which
the womb (rah. im) was derived (256a–b).
The link between the womb and the vision comes from the fact that the
womb expresses the original nature of the Face. The womb is attached

This is why, when Eve asked God to give her the same bodily shape as

The matrix (rah. im) is the womb (zahdān) and refers to the

We have seen that Mercy is closely related to the ‘motherly’ form of
Eve and the fundamental ontological writing expressed by this form.
The following fragment highlights this essential link between Mercy
and writing:
The visible blackness of the letters of the Qurʾān is a mark
(ʿalāma) of the divine Word (kalām-i ilāhī) . . . This mark of
human writing is related to the divine writing [symbolised by
the] Throne (ʿarsh) . . . The starting point (ibtidāʾ) of the creation
of the human body (badan-i insānī) and shape (hayʾa) is the
Word (kalām): ‘And We have brought to them a Book that We
have well distinguished, resting on knowledge, a guidance and a
mercy unto a people that believe’ [Q. 7:52]. ‘Mercy’ is a disposition
(h. āl) related to the Book [or writing, kitāb]. Therefore, [in the
27 Inventory I, no. 12.
28 Inventory I, no. 12.
Words of Power

verse]: ‘My mercy embraces all things, and I shall prescribe it for
those who are godfearing’ [Q. 7:156], ‘My Mercy’ means ‘My
writing’ [or ‘My Book’] (rah. matī ay kitābī) (206b–207a).
When Eve/womb seized the All-Merciful and asked to be given the
bodily shape of Adam, God refused in order to preserve the basic
writing on the face of Eve without which the writing on the face of
Adam would not be accessible. This basic writing is formed from the
sperm of Adam in the womb of Eve, and appears on the face of any
new-born baby. Eve is therefore literally the Mother of the human
Book, and the Fātih. a, the opening chapter of the Qurʾān, reproduces
the structure of this original divine writing on the face of Eve:
The seven [fundamental] lines are those that are produced by the
sperm (nut.fa) of Adam in the womb (rah. im) of Eve. They
complete the shape (paykar) [of the embryo], in which it comes
into the external [world]. These seven lines [on the face] of Eve,
[featured by] the hairline, two eyebrows and four eyelashes are, in
a sense, identical to the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitāb). With
the seven parts of the face where they are located, there are 14
[lines]. God prevented the appearance of the seven [lines featured
by the lines proper to the face of an adult man on the face of Eve,
but she does possess the seven locations corresponding to these
lines on her face]. Three times seven makes 21 divine ‘words’.
[The Fātih. a also] is composed of seven verses, which include 21
‘words’ [i.e., letters] from the [complete set of the] 32 divine
‘words’.29 [The Fātih. a] is thus the [exact] counterpart of the face
of Eve. This is why [it is said]: ‘Paradise is at the feet of mothers.’
The Messenger gave [to the opening chapter of the Qurʾān] the
title Fātih. a – ‘She that opens the Book’ (fātih. at al-kitāb) –
because she [Eve] introduces the division of the lines on the face
of Adam . . . She is also named ‘Mother of the Book’ (umm al-
kitāb), because it is impossible to read the lines [of the ontological
writing] on the face of Adam without reading ﬁrst the lines on the
face of Eve (437b–438a).
It seems that the relationship between the masculine and feminine
bodily forms in the expression of metaphysical knowledge can be
characterised as ‘inclusive’, which means that Eve is considered in this
perspective essentially as a part of Adam. She represents the

fundamental and visible half of the knowledge, the seven lines of
writing which express the original nature of Adam. These seven lines
have to be completed by seven others in order to attain the full shape of
the Word which is that of Adam, just as, as we will see in the next
chapter, the six days of the creation have to be completed by Friday to
attain the full number of six times 28 hours. This kind of relationship
between the bodily forms of Eve and Adam seems to be conﬁrmed by
the following passage:
In order to read the divine writing, Adam needs the original
nature (khilqa) of Eve, who is the Mother and who introduces the
division [which reveals] the line [of divine writing] (muqassim-i
khat.t.-i khudāʾī) . . . Eve [also] needs the original nature of the
face of Adam, because she does not possess the complete [divine]
writing on her face (247b).
Knowledge and Love are closely related in the Jāwidān-nāma. In the
following passages we will see that the love-inspiring beauty is deﬁned
essentially as the distinctive feature of the manifestation of knowledge.
In this context, love is essentially the desire to know, to discover the
ontological writing of the divine Word in any object and being and,
ﬁrst of all, in the human being who is the only complete manifestation
of the Word. But the relationship between two lovers seems to be in
the Jāwidān-nāma ‘complementary’ and not ‘inclusive’. In other
words, this relationship is described as the relationship between two
‘youths’, each of which possesses the ‘form of the Mother’ containing
one half of the complete knowledge of the Word. Their union
produces the complete entity which is greater than any of them taken
separately.
The source of Love is God and His Word: every manifestation of the
Word is beautiful and inspires love. Since, according to the Jāwidān-
nāma, every existing object and being is essentially the locus of
manifestation of some elements of the divine Word, the whole of
creation is beautiful; love is everywhere.30
Every existing thing is part of the divine writing, originally recorded
on the ‘Well-preserved Tablet’ and in the Mother of the Book of the
faces of Adam and Eve. Since beauty is the distinctive mark of the
manifestation of this writing, the elements of human beauty can be
30 See, for example, fol. 102b.

found in everything. The faces of Adam and Eve are the source of this
beauty, and whosoever understands its innermost meaning realises
union with God and enjoys the everlasting life:
Starting from the Well-preserved Tablet (lawh. -i mah. fūz.) and
lines [of the divine writing] on the faces of Adam and Eve,
[contemplate] all existing objects and beings, seek a mark of the
beauty of the beloved one in everything, and read [in this beauty]
the line of the divine [writing]. When you meditate on the line of
the Mother of the Book (taʾammul-i khat.t.-i umm al-kitāb),
remember this h. adīth where it is said that God has a beverage,
and when the saints drink it ‘they seek, and when they seek, they
ﬁnd’ [and] ‘they attain the union, so that there is no more
difference between Him and them.’31 This beverage [comes from
the] reservoir of Kawthar [of] the face of Adam [divided by] the
line of balance [into the] 32 ‘words’ of water, 32 ‘words’ of air, 32
‘words’ of ﬁre and 32 ‘words’ of earth: ‘a fountain at which do
drink those brought nigh/ as they are given to drink of a wine
sealed whose seal is musk’ [Q. 83:28, 25–26]. This water and this
beverage are sealed with the musk . . . the blackness of which is the
blackness of the lines of the curling lock (zulf), eyebrows (abrū)
and eyelashes (muzha). Whosoever drinks water in the reservoir
of Kawthar will never more know the thirst (462b–463a).
In the following passages, the beauty of the human face and body as
the locus of manifestation of the complete Word is highlighted.
Everything in a human being is beautiful and the human face is the
manifestation of the complete knowledge of the divine Word. Love is
essentially a link between the locus of manifestation and the
manifested truth of the Word. The discourse on beauty and love in
the Jāwidān-nāma is clearly marked by the technical vocabulary of
Persian mystical poetry, which acquires a speciﬁc meaning in the
context of H. urūfī anthropology.32 ‘Love [is inspired by] a curling lock,
eyebrows, eyelashes, and [other] features [of the face], which are the
science (ʿilm) of the 28 or 32 [ontological] ‘words’’ (217a).
