Knowledge and Love

God made the human shape (shakl-i insān) the science (ʿilm) of
the Word. [Indeed], His command ‘Be!’ (Kun!) has no other
locus of manifestation (maz.har). That is how this Word fell in
love with its own [locus of manifestation], and with the form of
the beloved one (s.ūrat-i maʿshūq). Since [every feature] of the
form of the beloved one, such as hair, eye, eyebrow, amorous
glance, stature, lip, teeth and mouth (mū wa chashm wa ghamza
wa qadd wa lab wa dandān wa dahān), is created in accordance
with the science of the [ontological] ‘words’ (ʿilm-i kalima), and is
locum tenens (qāʾim-maqām) of a ‘word’, the Word came into
the locus of manifestation of the lover and fell in love with the
lover and with itself. The amorous glances that the beloved one
makes with her eye and eyebrow, her elegant movements and
talk, her playfulness (shīwa), her qualities, her graceful walk
(khirāmīdan). Nothing of all this would appear if her being was
not governed by the Word; [nothing would appear of] this . . .
joyfulness (shūkhī), grace (raʿnāʾī), tenderness (nāzukī), elegance
(lat.āfat) that ravish the heart of the lover (199a).
In the Jāwidān-nāma, love is before all a transforming force. In
Chapter 6, we will see that a human being can integrate the lower
forms of existence into his or her body through the food chain by
means of a sacriﬁce accomplished with love. Similarly, the heavenly
bodies are also attracted by the beauty of the human form and aspire to
become part of it. Although they cannot enter into the food chain
leading to integration into the human body, their attraction and love is
expressed in their eternal rotation around the earth, which is at the
same time the location of the human body and the essential element in
its constitution. Let us note that, in the passages related to this idea, the
human form is often represented by the form of the female body, that
of Eve who is the Mother of the Book:
During the night of the heavenly ascension, the presence of Unity
(h. ad.rat-i ah. adiyya) appeared to the Messenger in the form of a
youth (amrad): ‘I saw my Lord in the form of a beardless
youth.’33 [In accordance with the verse]: ‘The All-Compassionate
sat Himself [in balance, istawā] upon the Throne’ [Q. 20:5],34 this
[form of the youth] is the form of the divine Throne (s.ūrat-i
ʿarsh-i ilāhī), the science (ʿilm) of the 32 divine ‘words’, and the
Well-preserved Tablet (lawh. mah. fūz.) of God. This form is
33 Inventory I, no. 30.
34 Cf. Chapter 1, note 49.
Words of Power

indeed the locus of manifestation (maz.har) of the 32 and 28
divine ‘words’. Just as a human being falls in love with the human
form (s.ūrat-i insān), all existent beings (mawjūdāt), the heavens,
heavenly bodies and angels spin around the earth and the centre
of the earth, in order to attain this human form. The angels [are
able] to descend from the heavens in human shape. But the
heavenly bodies and planets, in their [circular] movement
around the human shape, cannot produce for themselves this
human form, with its beauty and the science (ʿilm) of the line [of
ontological writing represented by the] curling lock and other
[attributes of human beauty] (305a–b).
‘On the day when We shall call all men with their Imām (bi-
imāmihim)’ [Q. 17:71], this is to say, ‘with their mothers’ (ay bi-
ummahātihim), who are the [ontological] ‘words’ and the ‘Seven
Twofold’ (sabʿ mathānī) of God. All moving things (hama ashyāʾ
ki h. arakat mīkonand) are in love with this form (shakl wa s.ūrat)
of the mother. They [received] all that they possess in their
original natures (khilqa) from the mother. They strive therefore
to reach the form of the mother. Some of them [eventually] reach
it, but some of them [perpetually] turn around and educate it.
[The latter] never reach this station (maqām); they will eternally
turn around it in their love (261b).
Although the form of Adam and Eve exists potentially in the heavens,
which is divided in accordance with its proportions, the actual
realisation of this form exists only on the earth:
All objects [and beings], angels, heavens, plants, minerals, natural
elements and [other] creatures (mawjūdāt) have their faces
turned in the direction of the world of earth and to the human
condition (ʿālam-i khāk wa bashariyya). They are all in love with
[this world], and accomplish the ritual circumambulation (t.awāf)
around the centre of the earth . . . . They want all to reach the
complete form of Adam (s.ūrat-i tāmm-i Adam), who attained the
science (ʿilm) of the 32 divine ‘words’, and became their locus of
manifestation (maz.har). The innermost meaning (maʿnā) [of the
form of Adam] is the [reason] of the perpetual movements of all
things, but it is out of reach of any existing entity (mawjūd), with
the exception of the world of earth . . . The form (shakl) [of
Adam and Eve] exists in the heavens in potentiality (bi-l-quwwa),
[contained in the] 360 degrees and minutes, as it already has been
mentioned, and in the division of the sphere of constellations
(falak al-burūj), which [determines] the division of all [other
Knowledge and Love

heavenly] spheres: ‘his length is 60 cubits in the heaven’.35 But
this form, which is produced [only] as potentiality in the
heavenly spheres, appears in actuality (bi-l-ﬁʿl) in the world of
earth, water, air and ﬁre (274a–b).
Love is thus fundamentally the desire to attain the complete
knowledge of the Word, and this is possible only by means of the
human bodily form, the only form which contains the complete
science of the Word. This is why the human form is the object of
universal love par excellence. From this point of view, the love between
two human beings acquires a particular signiﬁcance. The passages of
the Jāwidān-nāma related to this topic consider generally each lover as
a ‘youth’, that is, a young woman or a young man who has not yet
developed the facial lines proper to the face of an adult man. Each lover
is therefore a locus of manifestation of the ‘motherly’ lines, which
represent the half of the lines of the full Word. The love between two
humans is a way of transformation alternative to that taking place in
the food chain. If the lower forms of existence can be brought to the
fullness of the Word after being assimilated as food in the body of
Adam, the two lovers realise the same fullness in their amorous union.
According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the deepest motivation of human
love is the desire for such realisation. As long as this motivation is
unconscious, it manifests itself as ordinary, ‘profane’ love. But, unlike
any other being, human beings can bring to consciousness the real
reason of their love. This is possible because they are originally made
as the loci of manifestation of the full Word, and because the
knowledge of the Word was taught to Adam and transmitted from
him to his descendants. In this case, ‘profane’ love (ʿishq-i majāzī) is
transformed into ‘sacred’ love (ʿishq-i ilāhī), leading to knowledge of
the divine Word. This part of the Jāwidān-nāma’s discourse takes over
the concepts and terminology widely used in Suﬁsm and Persian
mystical poetry: at the extreme point of intensity of the ‘profane’ love,
the lover progressively loses the conscience of his or her ego and its
needs. This can lead to symbolic death, or sacriﬁce of the ego by means
of which the profane love is transformed into a sacred one. Only then

of Adam’s body, corresponding to the 28 and 32 primordial ‘words’.

can the lover read the lines of the divine writing in the features of the
beloved:
[The lover] sacriﬁces himself to the beloved (maʿshūq). [In order
to access] the reality of profane love (h. aqīqat-i ʿishq-i majāzī),
[one should let] the reality kill [one’s self]. By the love of a human

(khwāb wa khwārid wa nām wa nang wa nāmūs wa h. ayāt). In a

of the All-Merciful.’36 The profane love contains within it the

the presence of Unity (ʿilm-i kalām-i h. ad.rat-i ah. adiyya). If he

his love remained profane, he was not conditioned by lust
(shahwa), which [would have prevented him from] becoming an
accomplished lover of this beauty (304b–305a).37
The story of Joseph and the wife of al-ʿAzīz (biblical Potiphar), known
in the Muslim tradition under the name of Zulaykhā, exempliﬁes, in
the Jāwidān-nāma, the sacred dimension of love. The love ﬁrst
manifested itself at the profane level as a carnal desire. Joseph was then
imprisoned which, in the interpretation of the Jāwidān-nāma, means
that he stayed away from the object of his love until his passion was

puriﬁed of any lower component. Joseph thus realised the sacred
character of his love for Zulaykhā:
Each of them [Joseph and Zulaykhā] possess, in their original
nature (az rū-yi khilqa), seven [lines of the divine ontological
writing on their faces]: the hairline, [four eyelashes of] eyes, and
[two] eyebrows . . . with the seven locations [of these lines on the
face] . . . [This is why] they fell in love with each other: ‘For she
desired him; and he would have taken her’ [Q. 12:24]. Because this
was a natural attraction (mayl-i t.abīʿa), Joseph said: ‘Surely the
soul of man incites to evil’ [Q. 12:53], and he had to be put in
prison, which means restraint and abandon of carnal desires
(h. abs wa tark-i hawāʾ), until the demon of the carnal ego
(shayt.ān-i nafs) left him. [His love was then transformed into
the] divine love (mah. abbat-i khudāʾī) (199a).
The story of Joseph is ‘the most beautiful story’ (ah. san al-
qis.as.) . . . because it is about love, the beauty of Joseph and his
attraction (mayl) to the form (s.ūra) of Zulaykhā, which is the
science of the divine Word (ʿilm-i kalima-yi ilāhī). Since Joseph
was [himself] the science of the divine Word, they were
involuntarily and irresistibly [attracted to each other]: ‘For she
desired him; and he would have taken her’ [Q. 12:24]. Zulaykhāsaw
the beauty and the line of the divine [writing] on the face of Joseph,
peace be upon him. Zulaykhā lost self-control (ikhtiyār) [in
contemplating] the science (ʿilm) of the divine Word . . . [Their
mutual] attraction was therefore, [in fact], attraction to the divine
writing (kitābat wa khat.t.-i ilāhī). The imprisonment of Joseph,
peace be upon him, refers to the obstacle of the carnal desire
(shahwat-i jismānī) [created] by his own lower self (nafs) (306b).
The realisation of the sacred dimension of love means, in the context
of Jāwidān-nāma, essentially the capacity to discern and to read the
lines of the ontological writing, the Seven Twofold, on the face of the
beloved. Through the beauty of the beloved, the lover is able to
understand the ultimate meaning of his or her own physical form as
the locus of manifestation of the divine Word:
Zulaykhā fell in love with Joseph, because she saw in Joseph the
locus of manifestation of the Word (maz.har-i kalima). Joseph
was the locus of manifestation of the Word in the sense that,
[among the heavenly bodies mentioned in the verse]: ‘I saw
eleven stars, [and the sun and the moon]’ [Q. 12:4], he was the
14th, and it is before him that the sun and the moon bowed
down. They bowed down because Joseph is superior to the moon

and the sun. Since a copy of the science of the Word (mithāl-i
ʿilm-i kalima) appeared in him and on his face, he said: ‘O my
Lord, Thou hast taught me the interpretation (taʾwīl) of tales’
[Q. 12:101] . . . The perfection (kamāl) of Zulaykhā was in her
attraction (mayl) to Joseph, [since this attraction was provoked
by the fact] that Joseph was the locus of manifestation of the
complete Word (maz.har-i ʿilm-i tāmm) (217a–b).
The divine writing [which determines the form of a] houri
consists of the Seven Twofold (sabʿ mathānī).38 Her inner word
(kalima-yi bāt.in) [becomes visible] in the movement of her eyes
and eyebrows. It is said: ‘Thou shalt not speak, save by tokens, to
men for three days’ [Q. 3:41]. ‘[Speak by] tokens’ (ramz) means
speak by the eyes and eyebrows. There are two kinds [of such
speech]. One of them is the divine writing (kitābat-i khudāʾī).
Another is the inner word composed of the Seven Twofold of
God, the movement of which [produces] the shape (shakl),
amorous gestures (shīwa) and qualities (shamāʾil) underlying the
beauty and mutual love and attraction [of humans]. [The
humans] are provided from birth with the beauty of the Seven
Twofold of God, bestowed upon them by their mothers. In
Paradise, [their appearance] will be in accordance with this writ-
ing, line and beauty. Zulaykhā saw the Seven Twofold on the face
of Joseph. She saw also the innermost truth (h. aqīqa) [of] her own
form (s.ūra). And Joseph saw in Zulaykhā his own beauty. This is
why they felt attraction to each other, as it is said: ‘For she desired
him; and he would have taken her’ [Q. 12:24]. This was an essential
attraction (mayl-i dhātī), [in accordance] with the innermost
truth (h. aqīqa) of their gender and their beauty. The attraction of
the houri and youth in Paradise is of the same kind (238a).
The passage from profane to real love is, therefore, a way to self-
realisation:
‘They cut their hands’ [Q. 12:31]: they were so seduced by the

[inspired by] the divine line and writing. [But] if someone
interprets (taʾwīl) the divine writing on the basis of [personal]
spiritual realisation (az sar-i tah. qīq) . . . [he or she will ﬁnd] the
key of all heavenly provision: ‘And in heaven is your provision’
[Q. 51:22]. [Such a realisation is attained by] the meditation

that the original nature of the 32 [primordial ‘words’] appears on
the faces [of the houris]. If the original nature of the male lines
did not exist, the science of the 32 [ontological] ‘words’ could not
be known from the original nature [of the houris]. The reason of
the presence of youth (amrad) in Paradise is that the houris
possess seven [lines], and the [youth] possess seven lines, too.
This is why, [since the science of the 32 primordial ‘words’ comes
into the original nature of woman from the] original nature of
man, when a marriage is concluded between a man and a woman,
God requires, according to the religious law (sharīʿa), that the
man, not the woman, provides the necessary expenses for living
(nafaqa), including food and clothes (376a).
The beauty of any existing form is the mark of the words of the divine
Word which manifest themselves through this form. Several forms can
be loci of manifestation of the same ontological words; in this case,

they have the same ‘expressive capacity’ in the terms of the divine
Word, which means, according to the deﬁnition of the Jāwidān-nāma,
that they are equal in beauty. This conception is the basis of the
symbolic relationships between things, by means of which one thing
can symbolise another. For example, the beauty of a human face can be
described as a beauty of a precious stone, because both human face and
precious stone express some aspects of the divine Word:
The houris, the youth . . . [beautiful humans, precious stones] or
other beautiful forms are beautiful because they are created in
accordance with the science of the Word (ʿilm-i kalima). It is the
Word that manifests itself (tajallī) in the loci of manifestation
(maz.har) [perceived then as beautiful forms]. The same Word
manifests itself in ruby, musk and other [attributes of Paradise].
Both [the human form and these noble substances] are brought
into existence by the word [of the divine command] ‘Be!’ (Kun).
This is why, in the world of spiritual disclosure (ʿālam-i kashf), a
human can be seen in different forms (s.ūra), such as the form of a
ruby or another precious stone. This is how Moses heard a voice
coming from the tree: ‘Verily I am God!’ [Q. 20:14] (364b).
The h. adīth according to which there is a market in Paradise where the
forms (or beauty) are sold refers,42 in the interpretation of Jāwidān-
nāma, to this same fact.43 This kind of symbolism is at work in sacred
texts, in ecstatic visions, as well as dreams. The true love leads to the
understanding of the innermost meaning of beauty as the manifesta-
tion of the divine Word in His writing. The accomplished lover is
therefore able to discern the divine Word in any object and being,
including those appearing as dream images. This is why love is closely
related in the Jāwidān-nāma to the power of dream interpretation.44
The following passage illustrates this idea again with reference to the
Qurʾānic story of Joseph:
The story of Joseph is called ‘the most beautiful of stories’,
because it is said: ‘[O my Lord . . . ] Thou hast taught me the
interpretation of tales (taʾwīl al-ah. ādīth)’ [Q. 12:101]. The
knowledge [of the innermost meaning] of tales (ʿilm-i h. adīth),

which are words (kalima), refers [to the science of the divine

From this point of view, the power of dream interpretation is just
another aspect of the general idea of interchangeability of forms based
on their essential equivalence as loci of manifestation of the
ontological words. The same idea underlies the Jāwidān-nāma’s
theory of evolution/involution of forms which will be discussed in
Chapter 6. The accomplished lover understands this fundamental
unity of all existing forms, and is therefore able to permute or
‘substitute’ visible forms for the 28/32 original ‘words’ which
constitute the source and ultimate meaning of any form:
‘The saint practising substitution (abdāl) is the person before the
eyes of whom I take form and shape (mus.awwar wa mushakkal
wa mumaththal bāsham).’45 [This person] substitutes the 28
visible and silent ‘words’ [i.e., the forms of the letters of the
alphabet, kalima-yi z.āhir-i s.āmit] by the 28 [ontological] ‘words’
without beginning (azalī), without end (abadī) and without form
(bi-lā shakl wa bi-lā mithāl wa s.ūrat), [i.e., the primordial
phonemes of which the visible letters are the loci of manifesta-
tion]. He substitutes the 28 [letters written with ink composed] of
soot and blackness by the 28 ‘sciences’ (ʿilm) of the faces of Adam
and Eve46 . . . and he further substitutes these 28 of Adam and
Eve by the 28 and 32 [primordial] ‘words’ without beginning and
without end. In order to reach the secret of [the verse]: ‘Upon the
day the earth shall be changed to other than the earth’ [Q. 14:48],
you must recognise in the object of substitution (mubdil),
represented [ﬁrst] by the 28 visible [letters], and [then] by the 28
‘sciences’ of the face of Adam an [additional] level of depth (bat.n-
i dīgar), [that is to say,] the 28 and 32 divine ‘words’ without
beginning and without end (301b–302a).

transmitted and gradually revealed by perfect Lovers in the line of the
prophets, which will be discussed in Part Two.

Knowledge and Love

Time: The Receptacle of the Word
The chapter on Time is the ﬁrst in the list of the six ‘beginnings’
(ibtidāʾ) of the anonymous plan included in the British Library
manuscript of the Jāwidān-nāma that has been discussed in the
Introduction. The reason for that is speciﬁed in the citation below.
Time encompasses the whole creation. Time introduces universal
measure and division:
The ﬁrst ‘beginning’ (ibtidāʾ) is the house of the original nature of
the hour (khāna-yi khilqat-i sāʿa) of the night and of the day, of
three, six, seven, 10 and 40 days and nights (shabānrūz), of
month and year, times and centuries . . . [The author wanted] to
place [the ‘beginning’ on] time before [other ‘beginnings’] in the
divine Jāwidān-nāma (Jāwidān-nāma-yi ilāhī), because all that
exists in the created world is brought into existence within the
hour (dar sāʿa). The [author] considered that the explication [of
time] is the basis of all other questions. Indeed, the questions
arise when there is a disagreement in the approach to a given
topic. And there is no opposition whatsoever among any groups
belonging to any religion or nation in what concerns the six days
[of the creation], the seven days [of the week], the months and
the years. All [of mankind] agrees [on this topic] (482a).
The term usually applied in the Jāwidān-nāma to characterise the
relationship between Time and the rest of the creation is z.arf/maz.rūf,
‘container/contained’. I took the point made by the author by placing
the ‘container’ before the ‘contained’, the chapter on Time before the
chapter on Universe. However, I thought that it is more suitable to
situate our discussion on Time after the description of the ﬁrst stages
of the differentiation of the original Word and the chapter on the
cosmic role of Adam, which provide a frame necessary to the better
understanding of the passages related to the issue of Time.

Like the category of Form, the category of Time does not exist at the
level of divine Unity. This idea was already expressed above, in the
account on the condition of the primordial Unity and the ﬁrst stages of
differentiation. The Unity is the eternal Present, where the categories
of ‘past’, ‘future’, ‘beginning’ or ‘end’ do not apply:1 ‘Time does not
exist for God’ (96a).
Similar to Form, the category of Time emerges as the result of the
differentiation of the original Word by the Imperative KuN!. The two
consonnants of the Imperative, K and N, are the ‘two ﬁngers of the All-
Merciful’, the divine attributes of Beauty and Glory; and the names of
these phonemes, kāf and nūn, contain six phonemes:
[The Prophet], peace be upon him, said: ‘The hearts are between
the two ﬁngers of the All-Merciful.’2 ‘Two’ [refers here to] the
attributes of Beauty (jamāl) and Glory (jalāl), which are the two
[ontological] ‘words’ (kalima), kāf and nūn [of the Imperative
Kun!], containing six ‘words’. The past and the future are
subordinated to these [six ‘words’] (291b).
The reason for which the six letters of the Imperative contain ‘the past
and the future’ is the parallel that the Jāwidān-nāma establishes
between these six letters and six days of the creation mentioned in the
Torah and in the Qurʾān. As we have seen, the Jāwidān-nāma states
that in the course of the differentiation, the 28/32 separate phonemes
were produced from the two primordial phonemes of the Imperative.
This generation of the separate phonemes represents the crucial
passage from the primordial Unity to the condition of multiplicity. In
the course of this passage, the two phonemes of the Imperative
produce six phonemes contained in their names,3 and each of these six
then produce 28/32 basic phonemes which eventually generate the
inﬁnite variety of ontological names. An additional postulate, namely
the identiﬁcation of the six phonemes contained in the Imperative
with the six temporal units, the ‘days’ of the creation, allows the author
of the Jāwidān-nāma to apply the same schema of differentiation to
the temporal dimension.
1 Cf. supra fol. 472a–b.
2 Inventory I, no. 18.
3 KN = kāf + nūn = kāf + alif + fāʾ + nūn +wāw + nūn.
Words of Power

Indeed, since Time is produced by the Imperative, the different-
iation of Time develops in perfect accordance with the differentiation
of the Word. But there is an important detail that should be mentioned
at this point. It seems that the Jāwidān-nāma operates with two
different concepts of Time: ‘ontological’ Time, that is, Time considered
as the product of the Imperative and closely related to its division into
28/32 ‘words’, and ‘physical’ time determined by the movement of the
heavenly bodies.4 The ‘measure’ of the ontological time is entirely
determined by the six phonemes of the Imperative. It cannot
be determined by the movements of the sun and the moon because,
at that early point of creation, the heavens did not yet exist. The six
days of creation mentioned in the Bible and the Qurʾān refer,
therefore, to this ontological Time structured in accordance with the
six phonemes of the Imperative, and not to the ordinary terrestrial
days of 24 hours.
[The creation was accomplished] in seven days, according to the
Prophet Muh.ammad, and in six days according to the Torah,
which says that the heavens and the earth were created in six
days, and on the seventh day God rested.5 This [description of
the creation in the Torah] is a witness to the truth of
[Muh.ammad’s] message ‘whom they ﬁnd written down with
them in the Torah’ [Q. 7:157]. If they ask, ‘What does this mean?’,
the answer is that the six days during which, according to the
Torah, God created all things, cannot be taken literally, because
there was then no [physical] time (waqt wa zamān).6 [Indeed, the
latter is determined by] the movements of the [heavenly] spheres
and by the cycles of the sun and of the moon [which were not yet
created]. There remains only one [explanation, namely] that ‘six
4 The division of ‘ontological’ and ‘physical’ time is not explicitly stated in the
Jāwidān-nāma. I introduce it because it seems to be supported by the textual evidence,
and I believe that it provides a logical extrapolation of the essentially symbolic thought
of the author, giving us an insight into the central ideas of his theory of Time.
5 Seven days are not explicitly mentioned in any of the Qurʾānic accounts of the
creation. The Jāwidān-nāma reads them into the interpretation of the Qurʾānic
expression ‘Seven Twofold’ (sab’ min al-mathānī, 15:87), and in the statement: ‘Every
day He is upon some labour’ (Q. 55:29). We will see an example of such interpretations
further below. The biblical reference is Genesis 1 and 2:1–3.
6 The same idea is expressed at the beginning of the fragment in fol. 287a: ‘The
expression “six days” [in the Q. 25:59] refers to the duration of six days’ (murād az
sittat ayyām muddat-i sittat ayyām khwāhad būd), and in fol. 65a cited below.
Time

days’ refer to the measure or quantity (miqdār) represented by six
days (298a–b).
Each phoneme of the Imperative has as its counterpart the full set of 28
ontological ‘words’. The ‘measure’ of the creation is therefore six times
28, which makes 168 hours. After the creation of the heavenly bodies
and the emergence of the regular cycle of day and night, this ‘measure’
of ontological time is divided into the seven days of 24 hours
(168=6×28=7×24). The ontological Time introduces the measure and
proportion of the Imperative and 28 ontological ‘words’ into the
creation, into anything that is created and exists within Time:
The Word [of the Imperative], kāf and nūn, [is composed of] six
‘words’. In accordance with the [principle of] unity, every ‘word’
[from among these six is equivalent to] the 28 ‘words’. [This
makes] six times 28 hours, which demonstrates that He [God] . . .
set the 28 ‘words’ as a measure (andāza) to all objects and beings.
[They are all] created in accordance with the number of the divine
‘words’: ‘His command, when He desires a thing, is to say to it
‘Be!’ and it is’ [Q. 36:82]. Time (zamān) has been created and
divided by the 28 [ontological] ‘words’, which are the receptacle
(z.arf) of everything. And the things have been created in
accordance with the number [which determines the structure] of
the Time, itself contained (maz.rūf) [within the 28 ‘words’] (77a).
The original parallelism between the Word and Time becomes more
apparent as the revelation of the Word progresses from one prophetic
mission to another.7 In the mission of Muh.ammad, it is exempliﬁed by
the fact that Muh.ammad received both the Qurʾān and the ‘Seven
Twofold’ which, in this context, are interpreted in the Jāwidān-nāma
as seven days and seven nights of the week:
‘We have given thee seven of the Twofold’ [Q. 15:87]. [These are]
the seven days and nights of which are composed all the years
and months, ‘and the mighty Qurʾān’ [Q. 15:87], [composed of
the] single letters and their combinations. This means: as long as
will last the seven nights and days, the nights being related to the
seven planets, the time of the right guidance (zamān-i hidāya), of
the prophecy (nubuwwa), and of the religious law (sharīʿa), are
entrusted to you [Muh.ammad] (299a).
7 The link between the cycles of the Word, Time and Revelation will be discussed
in more detail in Parts Two and Three.
Words of Power

The Qurʾān, revealed in the Arabic language, contains 28 letters, the
number of the complete Alphabet of the creation. It expresses the
complete divine Word, and is contained in the receptacle of the ‘Seven
Twofold’ which correspond to the temporal dimension of the Word:
If someone asks why the seven days and the seven nights which,
according to you, are the Seven Twofold (sabʿ mathānī) and the
receptacle (z.arf) of the Qurʾān, were given to Muh.ammad and
not to other prophets (payghambarān), the answer is that the
Seven Twofold, which are [identical to] the seven nights and
seven days, are six times 28 hours. They are therefore [identical]
to the six ‘words’ of the kāf and nūn [of the Imperative], each of
which contains 28 ‘words’ . . . This is what was given to
Muh.ammad. All the Time, the hours, the nights and the days, are
contained in seven days and nights. During these seven days,
‘Every day He is upon some labour’ [Q. 55:29]. Time (zamān) and
all that is contained within these seven days and nights is
[included in] six times 28 hours, because the 28 ‘words’ are the
foundation of the Word [or Speech] (as.l-i kalām), by the means
of which God spoke to him [to Muh.ammad], with reference to
the [Imperative] Kun (12a).
Even if the prophetic mission of Muh.ammad is usually linked in the
Jāwidān-nāma to the full revelation of the series of 28 original ‘words’,
corresponding to the 28 letters of the Arabic Qurʾān, and it is on this
series that the Jāwidān-nāma’s theory of correspondence between the
measure of the week and the Word seems to be founded, the series of
32 are not totally excluded from this approach. In Part Two, we will see
that, according to the Jāwidān-nāma, the mission of Muh.ammad also
contains implicitly the series of 32, preﬁguring thus the full revelation
of the divine Word made in the time of Adam. These 32 appear in the
division of the physical time of six days mentioned in the Qurʾān and
the Bible: 144 hours of the six days can be represented as four times 28
plus 32 hours. We have already seen an example of such calculation
above, in fragment fol. 75b–76a, and will come back to it later in this
chapter. The presentation of the week as six times 28 hours also
contains implicitly the series of 32, because each hour is composed of
60=28+32 minutes. We will see several examples of this division based
on the number 60 in the next chapter.
More generally, the measure introduced into the creation by the
means of Time establishes a perfect correspondence between any
Time

object existing within Time and the divine Word: ‘Any object is a
‘word’ of God’ (74b). The idea that Time is the receptacle (z.arf) of the
creation containing all that was accomplished within six days, is
repeated throughout the text of the Jāwidān-nāma:
Hour, day, days and nights are the receptacle (z.arf) of all things,
according to [the verse]: ‘He created the heavens and the earth in
six days’ [Q. 7:54]. [God] divided the time according to the
number of His ‘words’ and of His Word (kalām), brought into
existence by the Word [of the Imperative] ‘Be!’ (Kun!) . . . All
that is [contained] in the six days [of the creation], and ‘in a day
whereof the measure is ﬁfty thousand years’ [Q. 70:4] . . . is
divided according to [the division of] time (85b).
The idea of Time as the receptacle of creation is further developed in
the passages that establish a link between the six days of the creation
containing, as we saw, 28 hours each, and six spatial directions (four
cardinal points, nadir and zenith): ‘One week consists of seven days and
nights, or six times 28 hours. Every existing [object or being] possesses
six directions, and every direction of this [object or being] faces
28 hours, which represent the time of existence of this existent
(zamān-i wujūd-i ān mawjūdast)’ (272b). Every existing object is thus
literally encompassed by Time. Each of six sides of every object faces
one of the six ontological days and its 28 hours corresponding to the
complete set of 28 original ‘words’ of the divine Word. Therefore, by
the intermediary of Time, every object faces the divine Word in every
possible direction. Since the locus of manifestation of the divine Word
is the body and the face of Adam, which expresses the anthro-
pomorphic attributes of God, any side of any object ﬁnds itself before
the Face of God:
Anything that has been created . . . possesses six directions
(jahat). Every direction [of any existing thing] was thus brought
into existence by the 28 divine ‘words’. Every direction was
educated (tarbiya) by the 28 divine ‘words’. Time (zamān), which
governs (murabbī) every direction of [any particular] thing, is
divided into 28 [parts], according to the number of the 28 divine
‘words’.8 Whatever the direction that faces a human being or
8 For the technical terms associated with the root rbb, see T. Mayer, Keys to the
Arcana: Shahrastani’s Esoteric Commentary on the Qur’an (Oxford, 2009), in
particular pp. 42 and 160.
Words of Power

[any] other creature, he/she/it faces something that is divided in
accordance with the number of the 28 divine ‘words’, and created
by them: ‘So set thy face to the religion, a man of pure faith – God’s
original upon which He originated mankind’ [Q. 30:30],
‘Whithersoever you turn, there is the Face of God’ [Q. 2:115].
This makes clear that every direction [of any existing thing] is
divided into 28 [parts] . . . and the six [directions, divided into]
28 [parts, are in fact subjected to] one [and the same division
into] 28 [parts], just as one hour refers to the 168 hours of the
week (95b).
Friday, analogue of the Jewish Sabbath, occupies a particular place in
the Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrine of Time as a link between ‘ontological’
and physical time. Being added to the six other days, the 24 hours of
Friday complete the ontological ‘measure’ of the week and bring it to
the signiﬁcant ﬁgure of 6×28=168 hours.9 This establishes the perfect
correspondence between the time of creation and the means of
creation, the Imperative, each of its six phonemes being a counterpart
of the 28 original ‘words’:
‘And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days,
and His Throne was upon the waters’ [Q. 11:7]. [With] Friday
(jumʿa), which is the ‘day of increase’ (yawm al-mazīd),10 [the
week of the creation] counts 168 hours, or six times 28 hours, in
accordance with the number of the divine ‘words’, which are the
receptacle of Time (z.arf-i zamān ast) (85b).
The ‘conversion’ of the six phonemes of the Imperative into Time thus
results in exactly seven days of 24 hours. The Jāwidān-nāma argues
that this position is in accordance with the Qurʾān. Indeed, it is not
said in the Qurʾān that the creation was completed within six days; it is
only said that ‘the heavens and the earth and all that is between’
(Q. 25:59) were created during this period. But the Qurʾān does state
that the Throne of God was ‘over the waters’ when He created the
heavens and the earth.11 This suggests, according to the Jāwidān-
nāma, that the Throne and the waters existed before the creation of the

(1960), pp. 163–168.

Time

heavens and the earth. It is at this point that the Jāwidān-nāma’s
polemical discourse against the Jews is situated. The Bible mentions
explicitly that there was an additional, seventh day of the creation. This
is true and conﬁrms the Qurʾānic evidence which, without any explicit
mention of the seventh day, clearly indicates that some time in
addition to the six days was necessary for the creation of the Throne
and the waters. But the Jews misunderstood Moses when they said that
the seventh day was the day of rest:
Moses said that on the Sabbath (rūz-i sabt), which is the seventh
day [of the week], there remained no more work for God, in
accordance with ‘the pen was dry’ (jaffa al-qalam). He said this
with reference to the things that were created within the six days,
that is to say, four times 28 hours and one time 32 hours
[=144=6×24]. Because Time (zamān) was created according to
this [measure], there remained nothing [outside of Time]. As to
the meaning that some people, following the Jews, [attribute to
this statement of Moses] when they imagine that God did
nothing [on the Sabbath], God [Himself] said: ‘We cursed the
Sabbath-men’ [Q. 4:47], ‘Every day He is upon some labour’
[Q. 55:29]. The resurrection (qiyāma) and the retribution (jazāʾ)
will take place on Friday (jumʿa), which is the seventh [day], as well
as the manifestation of the Essence (z.uhūr-i dhāt), the blow of the
Trumpet (nafkha) and other [eschatological events] (75b–76a).
This is why the passage in fol. 298a–b cited previously asserts that the
creation lasted seven days, and this would be in perfect accordance
with the Torah if the Jews had not misinterpreted Moses’ message. The
six days of ontological Time cover the seven days of physical time,
leaving no place for the biblical ‘day of rest’.12

Words of Power

The Throne and the Footstool represent Adam and Eve in their
‘limit’ position between the creation and the invisible divine Word. In
this position, Adam and Eve support and convey the Balance which
links these two incommensurable dimensions together. Let us recall
that the primordial Water also refers in the Jāwidān-nāma to a kind of
limit and transition. The passages where water is interpreted as the
natural element characterising the undifferentiated, germinal state of
the world at the very beginning of the creation, the substrate which,
though invisible itself, contains potentially any possible shape, just as
the point contains potentially the form of any possible letter, were
quoted in Chapter 1:
In accordance with [the verses]: ‘And it is He who created the
heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the
waters’ [Q. 11:7], and ‘His Footstool doth extend over the heavens
and the earth’ [Q. 2:255], the creation of the Throne (ʿarsh) and
of the Footstool (kursī) did not take place within the six days.
Since ‘Every day He is upon some labour’ [Q. 55:29], [their
creation] took place on Friday. The Messenger has said indeed
that the divine Throne will manifest itself on a Friday, which is
the day of the creation of Adam. We have already explained
above [the meaning of the] Throne [=Adam] and Footstool [=
Eve]. Since ‘His Throne was upon the waters’ [at the moment of
the creation of the heavens and of the earth], it is clear that the
Throne, the Footstool and the Water were created before the
creation of the heavens and of the earth. When the six days were
increased (mazīd shawad) with [the addition of] Friday, God
sent Gabriel who brought the Friday to the Messenger in the
form of a mirror (dar s.ūrat-i mirʾāt), and said: ‘We call it the
Day of Resurrection, the day of increase.’13 Friday with six
[other] days and nights [of the week], which are the basis (as.l) of
months and years, makes [a week of] six times 28 hours, in
accordance with the number of six ‘words’ of [the Imperative]
kāf and nūn . . . Any existent thing has six directions (jahat),
and every direction is governed (or ‘educated’, murabbā) by 28
hours, and these 28 hours are divided in accordance with the 28
divine ‘words’ (287a–288a).

Time

Until this point, doctrinal developments concerning Time, its
relationship to the Imperative and its link with the six spatial
directions were mostly based on the series of 28 original ‘words’,
identiﬁed with hours. Friday opens new perspectives in the structure of
time which restores the balance between 28 and 32.
The textual evidence of the Jāwidān-nāma suggests that the
relationship between Friday and six days of the week has some
similarity with the relationship between the series of 28 and 32. This
relationship is either ‘complementary’, the two series completing each
other (28+32=60, particularly in the passages concerning the structure
of the heavenly spheres), or ‘inclusive’, when the series of 28 is
contained in the series of 32 (28+4=32, often found in the passages on
anthropology and prophetology). In the same manner, Friday is either
added to complete the six days up to the six times 28 hours, or
considered as a day encompassing and synthesising the six other days.
It also seems that the Jāwidān-nāma distinguishes between these two
paradigms using two different traditional names of Friday. The passages
related to the ﬁrst, ‘complementary’ paradigm, often refer to Friday as
the ‘the day of increase’ (yawm al-mazīd), as in the fragment in fol.
287a–288a cited above. The expression ‘master of the days’ (sayyid al-
ayyām), which will be contextualised in the passages below, could be a
mark of the second, ‘inclusive’ approach, designating Friday as an
independent measure of Time summarising the time of the six days.
The fragments cited above referred mostly to the ‘complementary’
perspective, which apparently supposes that the time of Friday is
essentially homogeneous to the time of other six days. If the time of
Friday were measured on a scale different from that applied to the six
days, it would not be possible to add them together in order to bring
the measure of the Time of creation in accordance with the measure of
the six phonemes of the Imperative. We observe that this perspective is
based essentially on the series of 28. The series of 32 interfere here only
indirectly: 15 rakʿa of the Friday prayer complete the 17 rakʿa of the
prayer on the ordinary days in order to match the complete number of
32 original ‘words’:
A week is [composed of] seven nights and seven days, according
to the number of the ‘words’ [that God taught] Adam: ‘He taught
Adam the names, all of them’ [Q. 2:31]. [Indeed, a week contains]
six days and Friday, and the obligatory prayer [contains] 15
Words of Power

[rakʿa] on Friday . . . and 17 [rakʿa in all other days of the week],
so that [the number of the] 32 [‘words’ of the complete Word] is
achieved through the [weekly cycle of the] prayer (89a).
The ‘inclusive’ perspective supposes, on the contrary, that the time of
Friday and the time of the other six days belong to different scales. If
the ‘complementary’ paradigm clearly privileges the series of 28, the
‘inclusive’ one restores the usual parity between 28 and 32. Many
passages of the Jāwidān-nāma refer indeed to the six ordinary day
cycles of 24 hours as an independent and full measure of time which is
in accordance with the original 28/32 ‘words’ without being completed
by the 24 hours of Friday: ‘In a sense, six nights and days [represent] a
complete number (ʿadad-i tāmm), because they [contain] four times 28
hours and one time 32 hours’ (64b). Since the period of six days is
explicitly mentioned in the Qurʾān, it should be signiﬁcant not only as
‘ontological’ time measured with days of 28 hours, but also in its most
direct sense, with reference to the empirical reality:
[God] created the heavens and the earth in six days, which means
in accordance with the measure of duration (miqdār-i muddat) of
the six days. Their measure of duration is four times 28 and [one
time] 32 hours . . . Everything existing, in [present], past and
future, [exists] within the measure of duration determined by six
days, [established by] the 28 and 32 [ontological] ‘words’ (65a).
On the other hand, with reference to the etymological meaning of
Friday – jumʿa, ‘day of assembly and congregational prayer’, from the
Arabic root jmʿ expressing the idea of gathering, coming together,
synthesis, and therefore interpreted in the Jāwidān-nāma in this broad
sense as the ‘day of synthesis’ – Friday is not an homogeneous
extension to the sequence of six days, but rather a counterpart of six
days, representing a speciﬁc measure of time summarising and
synthesising the creation and the Word: ‘Friday is the time where all
divine ‘words’ are brought together (jamʿ)’ (207a). This special status
of Friday can be better understood with reference to the stage of
creation where the Jāwidān-nāma situates Friday: the creation of the
physical universe is accomplished in six days, while Friday is the day
when the Throne/Adam is created. The latter, as we have seen earlier,
Time

is the model and synthesis of the entire universe.14 If the creation of
the universe was accomplished within the measure determined by the
period of six days, the creation of Adam on Friday introduces its own
speciﬁc measure, determined this time by the period of 40 days. Just as
the measure of week, the measure of 40 days essentially establishes a
correspondence between the 28/32 original words, the principle of
creation, and the created entity, which is, in this case, the body of
Adam:
According [to the divine saying]: ‘I kneaded the clay of Adam
with My two hands during 40 days’,15 the creation of Adam took
40 days and nights, or 16 times 28 and 16 times 32 hours.16 The
time (zamān) is divided in the same way as his [Adam’s] original
nature (khilqa), his names,17 and the [ontological] writing on his
face, in accordance with [the principle of] unity (tawh. īd): ‘Do not
insult time, for I am time’18 (84a).
Closely related to the Imperative, Time is essentially the measure of the
creation, realisation and actualisation. It is the means of transition
from non-existence into existence, from potentiality into actuality:
The pre-existent Word (kalām-i qadīm) of God, by the means of
which He spoke to prophets (anbiyāʾ) and to angels, and [their]

contradiction which appears between, on the one hand, the passages
which state that the Adam/Throne existed before the creation of the
universe, and the measure of the time of six days was fashioned
according to the proportions of the bodily form of Adam and, on the
other hand, the passages that state that Adam was created on the last,
seventh day of the creation, his bodily form being thus contained
within the ‘receptacle’ (z.arf) of Time. These apparently contradictory
passages could be based on the supposition that the pre-existent form
of the Throne/Adam is contained in Friday as an image is contained in
a mirror, and becomes visible only with the accomplishment of the
Time of the creation, that is, at its end:

In analogy with the measure of the week, the measure of 40 days also
produces the form of Adam, and is therefore also related in the
Jāwidān-nāma to the possibility of the vision of God. But if the
measure of the week refers rather to the eschatological vision of God at
the end of time, the vision at the end of 40 days, exempliﬁed by the
story of Moses’ encounter with God, is probably related more to the
individual mystical experience. Because 40 days is the period of time
necessary to produce the form of Adam, the only form of the complete
visible manifestation of the divine Word, the encounter with God and
the contemplation of His visible aspect are not possible before the
period of 40 days:

In the next chapter, we will see how the universe, another general
entity equivalent to the complete divine Word, is organised in

Time

The Universe: Diversity in the Unity of the Word
In the anonymous plan of six ‘beginnings’ that was mentioned in the
Introduction, the contents of the Jāwidān-nāma to be included in this
chapter on the universe are described as follows:
The second ‘beginning’ (ibtidāʾ) is the house of ‘the heavens, the
earth and all what is in between’ [Q. 25:59 and ff.] . . . [It is] about
the heaven containing seven heavens, nine heavenly spheres
(aﬂāk), 12 constellations, 360 degrees, minutes, seconds and so
on until the 10th [fractions of degree], with angels dwelling in the
heavens and on the planets; about earth, clay . . . mountains,
provisions, wild beasts and birds, and all that is generated for
humans from the four elements . . . From the beginning to the
end of the divine Jāwidān-nāma, every explanation (bayān)
[related to these topics] enters in this house (482a–b).1
For several reasons, it is proper that this chapter appears after the
chapter on Time. First, it includes ‘the heavens, the earth, and all that is
in between’, that is, the contents of the six days of the creation
excluding Friday which is the day of Adam, the Throne and the Water.
Second, as we have seen in the previous chapter, Time is structured
and measured in accordance with the divine Imperative, and it
conveys the same structure and measure to all that is contained in it.
There is therefore an essential homogeneity between physical time and
the movements of the heavenly spheres and bodies. Seven days of the
week, the basic measure of the complete time, have seven planets as
counterparts. Twelve hours of day and 12 hours of night correspond to
12 constellations of the Zodiac. Twelve months of a year with its 360
days correspond to 12 constellations in the 360 degrees of the heavenly
sphere:
1 The full Persian text of this anonymous note is reproduced at the end.

In accordance with [the verse]: ‘By the heaven of the constella-
tions’ [Q. 85:1], the 12 constellations (of the Zodiac) cover 360
degrees . . . or six times 60 [degrees]. There are 12 hours in a day:
‘an hour of the day’ [Q. 10:45].2 Six days and seven days are
[established] upon the same measure (qiyās). Following the
divine order, seven days are related to the seven stars (kawākib)
[i.e., the seven planets]. Six days are related to the creation of the
heavens and of the earth, and one day is related to the creation of
the Throne and the water (78a).
One year [contains] 12 months and every month [contains] 30
days, [which makes] 360 days and 360 nights . . . For what reason
does God mention in His book that a year is composed of 12
months?3 When you read the Well-preserved Tablet [of the face
of Adam], you will discern these 12 lines [of the divine
ontological writing], similar to the 12 constellations. Every
constellation [covers] 30 degrees, and the 360 degrees [corre-
spond] to 12 months. Every month [contains] 30 days. There are
thus 360 days [in a year] (83b).
This close structural homogeneity between Time and the Universe is
the basis of the astrological developments of the Jāwidān-nāma, to
which we will come later in this chapter. There is also a close link
between this chapter and the chapter on the cosmic dimension of the
human bodily form (Chapter 3). It would be impossible to describe the
Jāwidān-nāma’s vision of Time and Universe without some previous
acquaintance with its anthropology. Let us recall here the Jāwidān-
nāma’s schema of the generation of forms, which we have examined in
Chapter 2. The primordial Word is the ﬁrst manifestation of the divine
Essence, unknowable in itself. The Word is what makes knowable a
number of aspects, attributes or names of the Essence, and carries thus
all available knowledge of the Essence. The Jāwidān-nāma states that
there is a limited set of 28/32 simple basic aspects, from the number of
which all other names and attributes are composed. At one of the ﬁrst
stages of the creation, there appears the category of Form. Before the
beginning of differentiation, the germ of the form is represented by a

Words of Power

black Point, the shadow of the unique and undifferentiated divine
Word. The essential correspondence between the invisible Word and
the black Point is guaranteed by the principles of identity of the name
and the named, measure and balance. If the Word is the manifestation
of the Essence, the Point is the manifestation of the Word made visible.
All knowledge contained in the Word is expressed in the Point and can
be accessed through the Point. The Jāwidān-nāma deﬁnes the science
(ʿilm) as the locus of manifestation of a metaphysical meaning (maʿnā)
or truth (h. aqīqa). Therefore, the Point is the science of the Word. In
the process of the differentiation, the 28/32 basic aspects emerge from
the Word as distinct simple elements of sound, or primordial
phonemes, named ‘words’ (kalima, pl. kalimāt). As a result of the
parallel process, 28/32 simple elements of form emerge from the single
invisible Point. The relationship between the primordial phonemes
and the corresponding elements of form is governed by the same laws
that establish the correspondence between the primary Word and
Point. These elements of form corresponding to the primordial
phonemes are the ﬁrst Letters (h. urūf). The complete set of the 28/32
letters focalises in a unique form, which is the science of the entire
divine Word and a differentiated analogue of the black Point. As such,
this form gives access to the complete available knowledge of the
divine Essence. This unique form, summarising the full divine
‘alphabet’, is that of the human being, originally represented by
Adam.

of

from
the
comprehensive combination of the ontological letters, but only from
their partial combinations. All objects and beings are thus fragments of
the total science represented by the form of the human body:
The human being (insān) is the locus of manifestation (maz.har)
of the 32 [ontological] ‘words’ . . . because God made manifest
the distinctive signs (ʿalāma pl. ʿalāmāt) of the 32 ‘words’ in the
original nature (khilqa) of the humans. Other objects [and
beings] are not enabled to such a manifestation, and the science
(ʿilm) cannot be manifested in them in its entirety (162a).
Our discussion of Adam and Eve in Chapter 3 concluded with the
citation of passage fol. 82a, where Adam is described as the Well-
preserved Tablet of God, the sum and archetype of the divine
ontological writing. Considered from this angle, the human form is the
matrix of the creation. This form is the standard and the source of the
The Universe

measures and proportions that are given to time and to the universe
contained in the time, from the highest heavens down to the spheres
corresponding to the four elementary natures, and then to all the
diversity of particular forms: a structure in accordance with the
original Word and its 28/32 ‘words’.
The idea of correspondence between the human microcosm and the
macrocosm is the basis of all Jāwidān-nāma’s developments concern-
ing the universe. It seems possible to distinguish two general aspects in
the relevant fragments. The ﬁrst aspect deals with the similarities
between the human bodily form and the structure of the universe,
including heavenly spheres, constellations, planets and natural
elements, together with the Jāwidān-nāma’s astrological and alchem-
ical developments. The second aspect focuses on the relationships
between the human form and all particular forms of objects and beings
existing within the universe, including the theory of evolution and
involution of forms between the most perfect, which is that of the
human body, and the lower realms of animals, plants and minerals. In
our account of the Jāwidān-nāma’s discourse on the universe, we will
follow this twofold division of broad topics.
The link between the human bodily form and the general structure
of the universe is associated with such symbols related to the cosmic
dimension of the human form as the ‘Lote-tree of the Boundary’
(sidrat al-muntahā) and Throne/Footstool (ʿarsh/kursī). In Chapter 3,
we discussed these symbols characterising the human bodily form as
the limit between the world of the pure, invisible, divine Word and the
universe of created forms. Both the Lote-tree and the Throne/Foostool
were described as the place which receives the ﬁrst effusion of the
divine ontological Word, from which this effusion is distributed to the
rest of the creation in accordance with the principle of balance
inherent to human form and with the proportions of human body
corresponding to the basic structure of the divine Word. The symbols
of Throne/Footstool, from which God governs the creation (as a
mighty king governs his realm),4 underlines this role of the human
form as the principle of organisation of the entire creation.
In this cosmic dimension, as the form of the complete divine Word,
the human form can only have as counterpart the universe as a whole.
4 Cf. fol. 276a–b above.
Words of Power

Indeed, only the universe as a whole is the locus of manifestation of the
complete Word, and therefore fully commensurable with the human
form; no particular form contained in the universe can possess this
capacity. We already have seen the application of this idea to the
temporal dimension: only the complete measure of Time contains the
proportions of the human body and can produce the manifestation of
the human form. The universe as a whole is represented in the
Jāwidān-nāma by the heavenly spheres and, most particularly, by the
highest heaven.
Most passages of the Jāwidān-nāma seem to identify the Lote-tree
of the Boundary and the Throne/Footstool with the eighth heaven and
the constellations located in it.5 ‘It is said that above the seven heavens
there is the Lote-tree of the Boundary. This is a reference to the sphere
of constellations (falak al-burūj), because beyond [the Lote-tree] there
is no star-source of effusion (kawkab-i fayyād.)’ (131b). ‘The Lote-tree
of the Boundary . . . located above the seven heavens is the form of
Adam (s.ūrat-i Adam), which is in the form of the heaven of
constellations (dar s.ūrat-i falak al-burūj)’ (126a).
Indeed, just as the Lote-tree, Throne and Footstool, the eighth
heaven is the limit of the world of forms, since there is no form beyond
it. The eighth heaven encompasses seven planetary heavens and can
thus be considered as the outer ‘shell’ of the universe, its most
comprehensive shape. Both the human form in its cosmic dimension
and the eighth heaven are essentially the embodiments of the complete
Word with its 28/32 ‘words’. The human form and the eighth heaven
are, therefore, perfectly homogeneous.
Just as in the case of Time, this homogeneity is demonstrated by the
elaborations on numerical correspondences, corroborated by relevant

the Jāwidān-nāma allude to something ‘above’ the eighth heaven. Other passages

h. adīth, the height of Adam ‘in the heaven’ is 60 cubits.7 The heavenly

Why has God divided the heavenly spheres (aﬂāk) in 32 and 28

Because, according to a h. adīth, the human being (insān) has 360

Every 60 degrees are [composed of] 28 and 32 degrees: ‘his height
is 60 cubits in the heaven’. The heavens, just as the time of a week,
are created in accordance with the face of Adam (97b).

Words of Power

Such correspondence between the proportions of the human physical
form and the structure of the heavenly sphere means that the eighth
heaven reﬂects the complete divine Word ‘written’ into the the cosmic
Book of Adam’s bodily form:
‘I swear by the fallings of the stars, and that is indeed a mighty
oath, did you but know it. It is surely a noble Qurʾān in a hidden
Book . . . ’ [Q. 56:75–78]: the ‘fallings’ (mawāqiʿ) of the ‘stars’ of
the seven planets cover 360 degrees, where is [contained] the
noble Book of the shape of Adam (kitāb-i karīm-i shakl-i Adam):
‘The book of the pious is in Illiyun’ [Q. 83:18] (125a).
Since the eighth heaven encompasses and governs the rest of the
universe, its division implies necessarily a similar division of all the
lower levels of the universe. The standard represented by the bodily
form and the facial features of the human form is thus conveyed and
deeply engraved in the structure of the universe. The seven planetary
heavens correspond to the seven basic features of the human face,
which become eight with the line of Balance.9 The movement of the
planets and the 28 stations of the moon also reproduce the essential
proportions of Adam’s body and of the divine Word.
From the centre of the face of the Adam’s earth and [from] the
line of balance of the face of Adam, pass [to the contemplation] of
the seven heavenly spheres . . . and the seven planets (sayyāra)
[revolving in] them, 14 [together]. The phases of the moon
[divide] the sphere of constellations [into] 28 [parts]. [The sphere
of constellations contains] 12 constellations, and [every] 60
minutes [of each degree are divided into] 28 and 32: ‘his height is
60 cubits in the heaven’. The animals, plants and all other things
[of the sublunar world] are divided according to the same line of
balance that [governs] the division into degrees in stars and
heavenly spheres. All the degrees and the fractions of degree are
created by the line of balance of Adam. The form of the
perfection (s.ūrat-i kamāl), which contains all heavenly bodies,
is divided in accordance with [the bodily form of] Adam
(135b–136a).
9 As discussed in Chapter 4, seven basic, ‘motherly’ features of the human face are
related to the series of 28 original ‘words’ (7×4=28), while eight ‘fatherly’ features
represent the complete Word and are related to the series of 32 ‘words’ (8×4=32).
The Universe

Despite this homogeneity, there is an important difference between the
cosmic Human and the universe. It is true that both these entities
reﬂect the complete Word with its 28/32 aspects or ‘words’, and both
contain the complete ‘alphabet’ of the creation. In addition, because
they have exactly the same structure as the human body, the heavenly
spheres are endowed with intelligence. But even if the original ‘words’
and letters of the creation are potentially contained both in the human
being and in the universe, only the human being has the capacity to
actualise these words in his speech. The cosmic Human, represented
by the primordial couple Adam/Eve, can express the Word potentially
contained in his/her bodily form and in the universe. Some passages of
the Jāwidān-nāma (for example, fol. 279a), suggest a relationship
between this capacity of speech and the knowledge of the names taught
by God to Adam (Q. 2:31). These names are identiﬁed in the Jāwidān-
nāma with the 28/32 original ‘words’. Because he received this
teaching, Adam is not only a passive embodiment, or ‘science’ of the
Word, he also has the knowledge of the innermost meaning of his own
form and of any other form contained in the universe, and is able to
express this knowledge actively. We will come back to this issue in the
part on prophetology. From this point of view, Adam is the ‘speaking
Word’, while the universe is the ‘silent Word’. ‘The 28 divine ‘words’
and 32 divine ‘words’ manifested themselves from the divine Throne,
which is Adam. These 32 divine ‘words’ did not manifest themselves
from any other thing because, in relation to Adam, all [other things]
are silent (s.āmit). [Only] he is the speaking Word [of God] (kalām-i
nāt.iq)’ (437a).
All heavenly spheres are divided in accordance with the 360 parts
of bones, ﬂesh, skin, fat and blood vessels [of the human body].
The heavenly spheres are thus divided in accordance with the
original nature of the possessors of intellect (bi-khilqat-i dhawī
al-ʿuqūl), in the sense that they [the spheres] convey the same
knowledge as Adam, but they do not produce in actuality (bi-l-
ﬁʿl) the speech of the 28 and 32 [ontological] ‘words’ of Adam,
which [is contained in them] in potentiality (bi-l-quwwa). They
are like a man endowed with understanding (mard-i mudrik), but
whose tongue has been cut off; he cannot produce the divine
word [in actuality], but in potentiality (bi-l-quwwa) [this word] is
produced in him (451b–452a).
Words of Power

We have already observed that the Jāwidān-nāma supposes often a
ﬂexible, interchangeable relationship between some central concepts
of its doctrine. The series of 28 and 32 can be either ‘complementary’
or ‘inclusive’; the time taken in its ontological dimension is the
receptacle of the creation, while the physical time is governed by the
movement of the heavens and heavenly bodies; Adam as the locus of
manifestation of the divine Word is the standard which introduces
measure and proportions into the time, but he was also created on the
last day of creation and contained within the temporal receptacle of
‘40 days’. We ﬁnd the same ﬂexibility in the relationships between
Adam and the universe. On the one hand, the cosmic Adam, the divine
Throne, is located at the highest ‘limit’ position of the universe. He is
identiﬁed with the eighth heaven encompassing the whole universe,
and he is the standard according to which the universe is shaped and
structured as the counterpart of the original Word. On the other hand,
however, Adam is located at the lowest level of the universe, in the
world of earth from which his body is made. He is produced by
the rotation of heavenly spheres and planets. His fate is governed by
the heavens and the effusions he receives from the heavenly bodies,
constellations, stars and planets. In this perspective, Adam is con-
sidered not as equivalent, but as part of the universe, he is contained
within the universe as any other object and being.
In the following chapters, we will meet other examples of this
ﬂexible relationship. Adam symbolises the archetype, the whole cycle
of prophecy, all prophets being contained potentially in his loins, and
at the same time he is the ﬁrst particular prophet. In his heavenly
ascension, Muh.ammad meets Adam in the ﬁrst heaven as a particular
prophet, and at the last heaven in the form of the Lote-tree of the
Boundary in his cosmic dimension. The Jāwidān-nāma’s interpret-
ation of the fall from Paradise (Chapter 12), when Adam and Eve lose
the knowledge contained in their own bodily forms, is another factor
of separation between the absolute, cosmic condition of the human
being and his evolution within time and space. The point upon which
these two apparently contradictory approaches or dimensions
converge is the idea that the lowest position is also the central one,
and the earth, the grossest of the four elements, is also the noblest. In
the following paragraphs we will explore the relationship between
these two dimensions of the human being with regard to the general
The Universe

structure of the universe. This will also bring us to the Jāwidān-nāma’s
astrological and alchemical doctrines.
The following quotation describes the emergence of the bodily form
of Adam in relation to cosmic cycles, structured in accordance with the
division of the eighth heaven with its constellations. From this
perspective, the body of Adam is produced by the rotation of planets,
heavenly and elementary spheres:
The 12 constellations of the eighth heavenly sphere are situated
in front of the [ninth] sphere without constellations (falak-i
at.las), [introducing there] the division in 360 degrees. All that is
situated in front of the degrees of the sphere of constellations,
above or under it, is divided into 360 parts. Water, earth, air and
ﬁre are also divided in 360 degrees, [and so on] until Adam, his
original nature (khilqa) produced by their [i.e., of the heavenly
spheres’ and bodies’], rotation and movement (sayr wa safar),
and his body (wujūd), is divided according to the same principle.
[This is why] the Messenger [i.e., the Prophet Muh.ammad] said
[that the human body has] 360 articulations, corresponding to
the [same number of] the parts of ﬂesh, skin and fat. The lines of
the human face are divided in the same way, as well as the hours
of the day and the time (zamān), in conformity with the [divine]
writing (80a).10
Not only do the movements of spheres and heavenly bodies produce
the human form, they also inﬂuence the fate of any human being and
that of his descendants. We ﬁnd here the same terminology as that
which was applied to the relationship between time and the six spatial
dimensions: ‘The heavens are created in accordance with [the model
of] his [i.e., Adam’s body], because they educate (murabbī) [or govern,
patronise] him’ (97b); ‘All heavenly spheres, planets and stars revolve
around him [Adam] in ritual circumambulation (t.awf). The sphere of
constellations (falak al-burūj) was divided into 360 degrees, because it
is his [Adam’s] executive (kār-kun)’ (8b).
Look in the Mas.ābīh for the h. adīth according to which human
beings (insān) have 360 bones, or six times 60. Every [series of]
60 is [composed] of 32 and 28, just as the degrees of the sphere of

to the Jāwidān-nāma, the basis of the division of the heavenly spheres, of time and of
the human body.

constellations which are also 360, because they are related to the
education (tarbiyya) of Adam and his descendants (294a).
It is said in a h. adīth that the body of Adam was created with
360 bones, or six time 60, every [series of] 60 is [composed] of 32
and 28. The ﬁngers of Adam’s hands and feet are created
according to the same proportions.11 The sphere of constellations
is [divided into] 360 degrees because it is the educator [or

why] it contains six times 60 degrees (288a).
The inﬂuence of the heavens is transmitted by their effusions (fayd. pl.
fuyūd.). As we have seen, the cosmic human form, symbolised by the
divine Throne, and identiﬁed with the eighth heaven receives the ﬁrst
effusion of the divine Word and transmits it to the rest of creation.
Effusions coming from the heavenly spheres, constellations and
planets affect human beings as well as any other objects and beings.
The character of the effusions varies depending on the disposition of
planets in the spheres. Every degree and every fraction of the degree of
the heavens is the source of a particular effusion:
The complete effusion (fayd.-i tāmm) comes from the eighth
heavenly sphere, which has the form (s.ūra) of Adam. The form of
everything that has a line of balance (khat.t.-i istiwāʾ), like plants,
animals, minerals, and fruits is similar to the form of Adam.
When [one of] the seven moving stars [kawkab-i sayyār, i.e.,
planets] attains one of the 360 degrees, [the number of which is
proportional to the] 28 and 32, and one of the minutes of this
[degree composed of] 28 and 32 [minutes], and [one of the]
seconds [of this minute], it produces a different effusion [which
affects in its speciﬁc way] minerals, plants, human beings (insān),
animals . . . and all existing beings and objects (mawjūdāt)
(104b–105a).
These heavenly effusions are associated with the divine attributes of
Rigour and Grace, personiﬁed as angels who ﬁll the heavens and
accompany every atom of the universe, fulﬁlling the divine command
and decree:
If someone asks ‘whosoever possesses knowledge of the Book’ (man
ʿindahu ʿilm al-kitāb) [Q. 13:43] what is the meaning of the
[verse]: ‘No! I swear by the fallings of the stars’ [Q. 56:75], one of

It can happen that the effusion of the heavenly sphere (fayd.-i

Paradise of delights. The death will never ﬁnd them, ruin and old

As there is a perfect parallelism between the constitution of the human
body and the structure of the universe, human beings are able to
receive the full range of the heavenly effusions. This idea is the basis of
the Jāwidān-nāma’s astrological passages:
The [bodily] form (s.ūra) of Adam is close to God. The seven
planets (kawkab-i sayyār) travel within the form of Adam (sayr
dar s.ūrat-i Adam karand). All heavenly spheres under and above
the sphere of constellations are divided in accordance [with the
sphere of constellations which is equivalent to the form of
Adam]. They have therefore all the form of Adam. The four
natural elements within the form of Adam are divided similarly
into 28 and 32 parts . . . The division of the heavenly spheres and
[in particular] of the sphere of constellations [is made in
accordance with the division of Adam’s body] because their
ominous or auspicious inﬂuence (badh. ālī wa nīkh. ālī) affects
(muʾaththir) Adam and his descendants (8b–9a).
Since the heavenly spheres are structured in accordance with the
division of the original Word into 28/32 ‘words’, and the 360 degrees
of the sphere are six times 28 and six times 32, every degree is in front
of an ontological ‘word’, and possesses special characteristics which are
activated when a planet passes through this degree. It emits then an
effusion, with properties depending on the properties of the given
degree and on those of the planet which activates its inﬂuence:
The seven moving stars (kawkab-i sayyāra) [i.e., planets] move in
the 360 degrees of the heavenly sphere. Every degree is a locum
tenens (qāʾim-maqām) of an [ontological] ‘word’ (kalima) from
the [28/32 ‘words’] of the divine Word (kalām-i ilāhī), the
[complete] locus of manifestation (maz.har) of which is Adam.
Every degree and every minute [of the heavenly sphere] conveys
[to the planets] a speciﬁc condition (h. āl), dignity (sharaf),
afﬂuence (bāl) or decline (hubūt.), so that [the properties of the
planets’ trajectories] are divided in accordance [with the division
of the heavenly sphere]. In this manner, the planets actualise the
condition (h. āl) corresponding to the part of the seven heavenly
spheres which they reach (129b–130a).

The heavenly sphere covers all domains of human life. This follows
naturally from the perfect correspondence between the human body
and the heavenly sphere. The inﬂuences affecting particular aspects of
the human life come from the corresponding astrological houses
(khāna). The following passages describe the astrological houses in
some detail:
Adam was created [in accordance with the proportion]: ‘his length
is 60 cubits.’17 . . . which consist of 28 and 32, extended [as the
multiples of 60] to the 360 degrees. From the point of view of this
proportion, Adam is equivalent to the heavens. Adam, peace be
upon him, is the surface of the earth (adīm-i ard.). The earth (khāk)
and the four natural elements reﬂect, in [every] particular place, a
[particular heavenly] image (s.ūra). Thus, at the moment of birth
(mawjūd) [of a human being], one constellation is related to the
personality (nafs), the second to the possessions (māl), the third to
something else, as well as the fourth and the ﬁfth, and until the
eighth which is the house of death (khāna-yi murg), the ninth
which is the house of knowledge (ʿilm) and the travels (safar), the
10th [related to] authority (salt.ana), the 11th [related to]
expectations (umīd) and the 12th [related to] enemies (ʿadū) . . .
If a child [is born] with the ascendant in Aries (t.āliʿ-yi h. amal), [this
constellation] will be related to his or her personality. The second
[house] of his or her [horoscope], which is the house of
possessions, will be in Taurus (thaur). And if a child is born with
theascendantinTaurus,thesecondhouseofhisorher[horoscope,
related to] possessions will be in Gemini (jawzāʾ). Thus, every
constellation from among the 12 constellations [of the Zodiac can
potentially convey] the meanings [related to] the personality of
the ascendant, to the house (bayt) of possessions, to the house
(khāna) of the lifetime (ʿumr) and honours (jāh), to the house of
knowledge, to the house of authority, or to the house of enemies
and expectations. [This demonstrates the principle of] Unity
(tawh. īd): all [constellations] are fundamentally one (127a–b).

Jāwidān-nāma relatively to spiritual growth. The good fortune helps
and rewards spiritual progress towards the knowledge of the divine
Word encoded in the human bodily form, while the ominous stars
hinder this progress. The stars also create impenetrable barriers to

After affecting humans, the effusions and inﬂuences of the heavenly
bodies are further transmitted to the lower levels of the universe. This
is possible because of the homogeneous structure of the universe:
anything existing within the universe is shaped in accordance with the
same standard of the original Word. The only difference between the
human body and the external form of any other particular object is
that the former contains the whole set of 28/32 original letters and is
thus in perfect harmony with the heavenly spheres, while the latter
contains only a fragment of the ‘ontological alphabet’ and its receptive
and expressive capacities with regard to the heavenly inﬂuences and
the ontological ‘words’ are therefore limited. The relationship between
the heavenly effusions attaining the remotest parts of the universe and
ontological ‘words’ will become more clear when we discuss, a few
pages below, the process of ‘nomination’, the attribution of ontological
names to particular objects. Another important statement which
regulates the relationship between the human body as the form of the
complete Word and the forms of particular objects within the universe
is the idea that every object is a part of the cosmic body of Adam. The
following passage describes the diffusion of heavenly inﬂuences
through humans to the lower levels of existence:
[The heavens are divided into 28 and 32 degrees] in accordance
with the innermost reality of the human being (h. aqīqat-i insān).
[Both heavenly degrees and human bodily form] possess
(khudāwand) the [complete set of the] 32 [ontological] ‘words’.

If astrology is about the relationships between the human form and the
heavenly spheres, alchemy refers to the same kind of relationship
between the human form and the spheres of the four natural elements.
The elementary structure refers particularly to the human form and
the universe as supports of the divine ontological writing. As we have
seen, in the context of the Jāwidān-nāma, this writing is essentially the
locus of manifestation of the invisible truths emanated from the
supreme divine Reality, that is to say, the ‘science’ which makes these
truths accessible and knowable in the world of sensual perception. Like
the ink and material on which the Qurʾān is written down, the human
bodily form is constituted by four elements. But while the Qurʾān
contains a speciﬁc revelation given to one particular prophet, Adam is
the heavenly Book written with the universal divine writing, the Book
which is the source of any prophetic message:
Both the [heavenly] writing and the writing of the Qurʾān are
referred to as the Book of God. The visible writing of the Qurʾān
[that is, the ink] contains the four natural elements: earth, air,
water and ﬁre. It cannot exist without them . . . And this is so
because the divine writing, which is Adam, contains these four
elements (248a–b).

maintained by the power of love. The all-encompassing love makes the
