The sphere of earth, the principal element in the constitution of the
human body, is located at the lowest level of the universe. Earth is,
indeed, the grossest of the four elements. But, because of the
concentric structure of the universe, the lowest location is also the
central one. According to the Jāwidān-nāma, this location conﬁrms
the superiority of earth above all other elements. Indeed, in the context
of Jāwidān-nāma’s theory of form as the locus of manifestation and
the ‘science’ through which the knowledge of invisible truths can be
attained, characteristics which look negative at ﬁrst glance, turn into
positive qualities. Because it is the grossest of all elements, earth is the
only element able to maintain a given form. Because it is the most
opaque, and does not allow any light to pass through, earth produces
shadow and darkness, that of ink and the writing, closely related, as we
have seen earlier, to the science of the Word: ‘The grossest and darkest
bodies (ajrām wa ajsām-i kathīftar wa z.ulmānītar) become the shape
(shakl), ﬁgure (paykar) and science of the divine Word (ʿilmiyyat-i
kalima-yi khudāʾī)’ (259a). Many passages underline that earth is
therefore the element of the science of the divine Word par exellence,
the only element able to express the science: ‘The earth (khāk) has the
aptitude to receive (qābiliyyat) the science of the [divine] words
The Universe

(ʿilmiyyat-i kalimāt) . . . the [ontological] word [corresponds to the
element] that is heavier (thaqīltar) [than other elements] . . . ’ (364a–b).
The following fragments emphasise the exceptional position of
earth among the natural elements. Earth is the element of form and
science:
Earth is the place where humans dwell (maqarr-i insān). God
made it so that part of earth (juzw-i zamīn) and human body
(wujūd-i insān) [both] receive the distinctive marks (ʿalāma, pl.
ʿalāmāt) of the 32 [ontological] ‘words’. [Satan] said: ‘and him
Thou createdst of clay’ [Q. 7:12], because water, air and ﬁre do not
possess the aptitude (istiʿdād) to receive the form [bearing] these
[marks] (167b–168a).
Among the four elements [lit. ‘pillars’, arkān], earth is part of
the human body (badan-i insān). [Every] ﬁgure and form (s.ūrat
wa paykar) is made of [earth]. [Earth] has the aptitude to receive
(qābiliyyat) the human form, [and the human body] is part of the
earth. [It is only earth that] has the aptitude to receive the science
(ʿilm) of the 32 [ontological] ‘words’, unlike water, ﬁre and air
(211a–b).
Like a precious treasure, earth is locked in the centre of the heavenly
and elementary spheres. Though it is the grossest element, it is also the
most subtle with regard to its property to manifest all the forms of the
creation. This is why the earth is at the centre of the universe, and all
heavens and planets turn around the earth in a ceaseless ritual of
circumambulation and worship:
Consider the forms of objects and beings (s.uwar-i makhlūqāt)
from the point of view of their original nature and disposition
(khilqat wa jibillat). You can see that the point of earth (nuqt.a-yi
khāk) is surrounded by water, water is surrounded by air, air is
surrounded by the heavenly sphere (falak), and the heavenly
sphere is surrounded by another sphere, and so on. It is the
custom of kings and treasurers to keep the most precious gem of
their treasury in a chest put inside another chest, and that chest in
the third, and so on without limit, because of the nobility,
splendour and perfection of this gem. Earth is this precious gem.
Though it is the grossest (kathīftar) [among the four elements], it
is the most subtle with respect to [its capacity to produce] the
external manifestation [of forms] (z.uhūr) and its receptive
aptitude (qābiliyyat) . . . God [created] earth with the purpose to
[produce] the form of [His] vicegerent (khalīfa), Adam: ‘God
created Adam in His form.’ By their essence (dhāt) and their

Since earth represents the science of the Word, it is only natural that

The heavenly effusions that we discussed earlier reach the body of

Adam is created from earth, as well as from air, water and ﬁre.

Earth communicates to other elements the capacity to express the

God gave to earth the aptitude to receive the form (shakl wa

Words of Power

It is because ﬁre was structured in accordance with the model of earth
that it was able to speak to Moses from the Burning Bush: ‘The ﬁre that
Moses saw had been divided in accordance with the [division] of earth
(bi-tabʿiyyat-i khāk). This is how it [was able to] speak’ (213a).
While earth is, without doubt, the central element in the Jāwidān-
nāma’s alchemy, other elements also have a speciﬁc role in the text. As
stated in the passages quoted above, though essentially made of earth,
the body of Adam contains all the four elements. Just as earth, each
element has its particular role and symbolic meaning.
We have already met the element water in Chapter 1, where it
symbolised the undifferentiated condition of the Word and its
germinal potential. Water is the element which was at the origin of
the creation. More speciﬁcally, through the identiﬁcation with sperm,
water is the origin of life. The sperm is further likened to the
ontological ‘ink’ with which the creation is written: ‘It is said in the
Torah that [God] created a pearl (jawhar), and when He looked at it
with the look of His Glory (ʿizza), it became water. From [this water]
were created the heavens and earths. Water is the origin (mabdāʾ) of
the creation. The clot of blood [of the embryo] is produced by sperm,
which is water’ (101a).25
[Just as] the substance (mādda) [by the means of which] the
visible lines [of writing are produced] is dark water (āb-i tīra)
[i.e., ink], the substance [by the means of which] He engraves
(naqsh) [His ontological writing] is water, which becomes sperm:
‘and of water fashioned every living thing’ [Q. 21:30]. This is the
same water upon which [is established] the Throne. It is by the
knowledge (shinākhtan) [of the Throne] that life manifests itself
in any [being] because, among all creatures, [only] he [i.e., the
Throne, symbol of Adam], as the locus of manifestation of God
(maz.har-i khudā), possesses the complete science (ʿilm) and the
complete [set] of ‘words’ (alfāz. wa kalimāt) (201b).26

Water is the support of the divine Throne, which in turn is the support
of the divine Balance. The Throne, as we have already seen, symbolises
Adam and the element earth:
If someone asks . . . why God created the Throne and water on
Friday, outside the six days [of the creation] . . . the answer is that
[the Throne] is the support (maqarr) of the Balance of the divine
Essence (istiwāʾ-yi dhāt-i h. ad.rat-i ah. adiyya), and water is the
support of the Throne. It is this water that is part of Adam’s body
(badan) (94b).
Previously, we have already noted the close association of water and
Throne/Adam: they are not part of the ‘heavens and earth and all that
is between’, but located within a special measure of time, represented
by Friday. This exceptional position of water and earth is due to the
fact that all material forms of the universe are produced by these two
elements without the participation of air and ﬁre, which are not able to
maintain a given form and have no relation to the category of form at
all: ‘[The Prophet Muh.ammad said:] “I was a prophet when Adam was
between water and clay”:27 . . . air and ﬁre are not mentioned, because
they have no aptitude to receive form’ (183b–184a).
The ritual ablution (wud.ūʾ) is done with water or earth. One of
the meanings [of this regulation] is that in the form (s.ūrat wa
naqsh wa paykar) taken by Adam’s body (wujūd), the parts of
earth and water are predominant, not those of ﬁre and air. And it
is this form that is the copy of the science of the 32 [ontological
‘words’ of the divine Word] (171b–172a).
Earth is the most excellent part (juzw-i aʿz.am). It is followed by
water, because it is with water that earth can be kneaded: ‘I
kneaded the clay of Adam with my two hands [during] 40
days’,28 ‘and His Throne was upon the waters’ [Q. 11:7], not ‘upon
the ﬁre’ (ʿalā al-nār) or ‘upon the air’ (ʿalā al-rīh. ) (311b–312a).
Indeed, according to the well-known h. adīth that we have already
discussed in Chapter 5, the body of Adam was kneaded with water.
Water is therefore as essential to the body of Adam as earth, which is
the element of form and structure. Earth, air and ﬁre, which take part
in the constitution of the human body, were kneaded with water:
27 Inventory I, no. 29.
28 Inventory I, no. 27.
Words of Power

‘Earth, air and ﬁre were kneaded with water, while “His Throne was
upon the waters” [Q. 11:7]’ (129a). It is by the mediation of water that
the form and structure inherent to earth and, with them the aptitude to
receive and to express the science of the divine Word, are conveyed to
air and ﬁre.
Let us also remind ourselves here that water has the property to
reﬂect and to show, like a mirror, the form of Adam. This speciﬁc
property creates an additional link between Friday as the day of
creation of Adam and water. We have already cited the relevant
passage above, in Chapter 5, fragment fol. 88a–b.
Fire is an ambiguous element in the Jāwidān-nāma. In its positive
aspect it represents the Light, which is the manifestation of the original
Word.29 This light contains all possible knowledge of the divine
Essence and attributes, and is the source of prophetic revelation: ‘It is
the unique light (nūr) of theophany that shines in all loci of
manifestation (maz.āhir), and comes in the appearance (maz.har) of
prophets (anbiyāʾ) and saints (awliyāʾ), in order to bring tidings of the
divine Essence and attributes, of the Resurrection, origin and return
(dhāt wa s.ifāt-i khudā wa qiyāma wa mabdāʾ wa maʿād)’ (168a).
Through the symbol of smoke representing the undifferentiated
science of the Word, ﬁre is also associated with the ‘science’ and its
principal element, earth. This ﬁre enters, together with other three
elements, into the constitution of the human body. It also reveals the
face of Adam, which is the sum of the science of the Word: ‘Those who
worship ﬁre (ātash and nār) and sun . . . it is in their [light] that the
children of Adam can contemplate the face of Adam and read the
writing of [the human] face’ (244a).
The topic of similarity between ﬁre and human body as sum of the
science of the original Word is also developed with reference to the
symbolism of the Tree, which brings together several Qurʾānic images:
the Lote-tree of the Boundary which we have already discussed in
several places above, the Burning Bush of Moses, and the parable of
the good word likened to the good tree. ‘Moses heard the speech
(khit.āb) of God [coming] from ﬁre and tree, and the good word is a
29 Cf. Chapter 1.
The Universe

tree.30 The Lote-tree of the Boundary that Muh.ammad reached
during the night of his heavenly ascension indicates Adam, and the
ﬁre [of the Burning Bush] is the ﬁre of Adam’s body (ātash-i wujūd-i
Adam)’ (72a).
But ﬁre has also a negative aspect, which makes it the exact opposite
of earth. This aspect is much more present in the text of the Jāwidān-
nāma, and we have already had several opportunities to mention it.
Fire is the most subtle of the four elements, and the less able to
maintain any given form. Thus, if earth, the grossest element, is the
element of the ‘science’ expressed through form, ﬁre is the element of
ignorance, associated with the rebellious attitude of Satan:
Satan can take human form (s.ūrat-i insān) because his part of ﬁre
is subordinated to earth, which is the science of the 32
[ontological] ‘words’, and [can therefore] enter into the
constitution [of a body of] earth. Satan said: ‘Thou createdst me
of ﬁre, and him Thou createdst of clay’ [Q. 7:12]. This means: ‘I
am luminous (nūrānī), while he is dark (z.ulma), and I do not
possess the aptitude to receive form (shakl wa paykar), while he
does.’ But it is precisely this aptitude (qābiliyya) that is the source
of perfection (ʿayn-i kamāl) (149b).
Water, air and ﬁre do not have the aptitude to become the
science of the 32 [ontological] ‘words’. Satan said that this person
[i.e., Adam] was created of earth and not of ﬁre. But he [i.e.,
Satan] was not created as locus of manifestation of the 32
[ontological] ‘words’. Necessarily, whosoever is not the locus of
manifestation of the original nature of the science (maz.har-i
khilqat-iʿilm) of the 32 [ontological ‘words’] belongs to the world
of Satan and to his original nature. Among the four natural
elements, there is none more remote [from the aptitude to
express the science of the Word] than ﬁre (390b).
As stated in this passage, not only ﬁre is the element of ignorance, but
also ignorance leads to the ﬁre that is the original element of Satan,
that is, to Hellﬁre. Fire has the property to delete the lines of the divine
writing on the human face. We will see further development of these
ideas in Part Three.
30 Allusion to Q. 14:24: ‘A good word is as a good tree – its roots are ﬁrm, and its
branches are in heaven.’
Words of Power

The fourth element, air, is generally associated in the Jāwidān-nāma
with the Breath of God, which conveys spirit and soul into created
objects and beings, thus bringing them into existence. We have already
met this idea in Chapter 2, passage in fol. 21b. Let us return to this
short passage because it contains some points important for the topic
we are discussing presently:
‘And breathed My spirit in him’ [Q. 15:29]: in the same manner,
the [ontological] names reach the exterior and the interior of all
things by the means of attribution of names (bi-h. asb-i ismiyyat).
They realise the manifestation (tajallī) [of the divine truth] inside
all things (dar bāt.in-i ashyāʾ), and [therefore] all things are their
loci of manifestation (maz.āhir) (21b).
Another example of the same conception is given in the following
passage, where God seems to speak in the ﬁrst person:
This breath (nafkha) will be My breath, which will remain
eternally (tā abad) in the world, so that the 32 [ontological]
‘words’ become known, and the secret of [the verse]: ‘God’s
original upon which He originated mankind’ [Q. 30:30] revealed. I
am in any locus of manifestation (maz.har) that emerges among
the loci of manifestation of the existing [objects and beings]
(mawjūdāt). [They] and all the rest, they are My breaths in the
loci of manifestation (390a).
These passages link air/breath to the revelation of the 28/32 ‘words’ of
the divine Word through the created things, each of which is a divine
Breath within a given locus of manifestation. The ﬁrst citation speciﬁes
that this Breath carries the ontological names which are, according to
the Jāwidān-nāma, principles of the existence of things. The second
citation alludes to the same idea. From these two passages it can be
concluded that, in the alchemy of the Jāwidān-nāma, air/breath is the
medium through which the ontological names, composed of some
number from the total set of 28/32 original ‘words’ or phonemes,
attain the sensible forms which are their loci of manifestation. The
form of any particular object or being is therefore a visible expression
of the original letters which compose its name. These letters, and the
metaphysical truths represented by the corresponding phonemes or
‘words’, can be known through the physical shape of an object. Any
The Universe

given object or being is therefore the ‘science’ of the ontological name
which was blown into it and brought it into existence.31
It should be stressed again, however, that the ontological name of
any particular object or being contained within the universe includes
only a limited, incomplete group of original phonemes from the total
number of 28/32. This total number cannot be achieved by a particular
form, but only by a global entity such as a heavenly sphere. The only
and unique physical form containing the full ontological alphabet, the
Supreme Name of God, is the form of the human body: ‘Similar to the
human being (insān), who is the locus of manifestation of all the 32
[ontological] ‘words’, [any other object or being] is the locus of
manifestation of some [of these ‘words’] . . . ’ (384a).
The human body – and more speciﬁcally, its archetype, the bodies of
the primordial couple Adam/Eve – are the source of the names which
reach particular objects and beings. Starting from the body of Adam/
Eve, the particles of the divine Word reach everything in the universe,
thus realising divine omnipresence. This means that every possible
metaphysical truth revealed through the form of any particular object
in the universe is also – and originally – revealed through the human
form. The human body contains a universal science which provides
access to the knowledge of any particular form:
Divine omnipresence (ih. āt.a-yi khudā bar hama ashyāʾ) is
realised by the means of his [Adam’s] presence in all things.
When the 32 [ontological] ‘words’ reached the things, with the
[ontological] names attributed to them (barā-yi ismiyyat),
everything became the locus of manifestation (maz.har) [of the
corresponding ontological name]. Adam comprehends the full
[set] of [ontological] names in their entirety (jāmiʿ-yi jamīʿ-yi
asmāʾ), and the complete science of the [Supreme?] name (ʿilm-i
tāmm-i ism) . . . [Other] objects [and beings], such as animals,
plants, and others, possess [only] a part of the original nature
(khilqa) of Adam. This is why it is possible to reach the

innermost secret (sirr) [of all objects and beings] by the original

wings, but they are nations like unto yourselves. We have neglected
nothing in the Book’ [Q. 6:38] (351b).
This brings us to the second aspect of the relationships between the
micro- and macrocosm that we mentioned at the beginning of this
chapter, that is, to the relationships between the human bodily form as
the personiﬁcation of the complete Word and the forms of particular
objects and beings, each of which is the locus of manifestation only of
several ‘words’ or phonemes of the original Word. The attribution of
ontological names to objects, which we discussed earlier, is one of the
central concepts of this kind of relationships.
At this point, it is interesting to note an example of symbolic and
semantic association based on the references to scriptural materials
that the Jāwidān-nāma suggests between the concept of breath and the
human body. This association is constructed on the notion of Mercy
related to the Arabic root rh. m.32 The link between the 28/32 original
‘words’ and the divine attribute of Mercy has already been mentioned

from this source is identiﬁed with the heavenly effusion which was
discussed earlier in relation to astrology. Other fragments mention the

connection with the emanation of the original words.33 This suggests
that the names blown into things and bringing them into existence are
the ‘breath of the Merciful’; this suggestion is further supported by the

well-known h. adīth according to which Adam, the source of all names,

This analogy based on the concept of Mercy is developed still further.
In Arabic, the words ‘mercy’ (rah. m) and ‘womb, matrix’ (rah. im) are
homographs derived from the same root rh. m. A well-known h. adīth
has God saying: ‘I am God and I am the All-Merciful (rah. mān). I
created the womb and I gave it a name derived from My own name.’34
We have seen in Chapter 4 that the womb is further identiﬁed with
Eve, who is also referred to in the Jāwidān-nāma by the Qurʾānic
expression ‘Mother of the Book’ (umm al-kitāb). This is not a metaphor:
for our author, Eve is literally the Mother of the Book, ﬁrst because
her own body and face bears the fundamental lines of the divine
ontological writing, and secondly because it is she who gives birth to
humans, and any human is the original and universal Book of God,
containing the complete set of letters of the divine ontological writing.
The human form, and more speciﬁcally, the female body and facial
features, are thus simultaneously the source of divine Mercy and the
matrix wherein the names are generated and shaped: these two aspects
refer in fact to the same reality. Several fragments suggest the
connection between Mercy, womb and attribution of the names.35

Words of Power

In Chapter 3, we discussed the symbol of the divine Throne/
Footstool, one of the representations of the cosmic couple Adam/Eve,
as the source of the Balance, ensuring the essential correspondence
between the invisible archetypes, ‘truths’ or ‘meanings’, and the forms,
which are their loci of manifestation. In the same chapter, we have
seen the role this symbol played in the relationships between the form
of the human body, Time and the Universe. With regard to the
particular objects and beings, the line of Balance, starting from the
proportions of the human body, reaches any particular thing
simultaneously with its ontological name and guarantees the perfect
correspondence between this name and the visible shape of the thing:
‘The line of balance of the face of Adam, extended to all things, reached
all things together with the 32 [ontological] ‘words’, by means of the
attribution of the [ontological] names (az rū-yi ismiyyat)’ (328a–b).
In other words, the line of the Balance ensures, at this level, that the
shape of any particular object is the adequate locus of manifestation of
its ontological name. This brings us again to the Jāwidān-nāma’s
deﬁnition of ‘science’ and writing, which we have discussed in several
places previously. Due to the correspondence introduced by the line of
Balance, the sensible shape of any object expresses its ontological
name, indicating the fragment of metaphysical truth associated with it,
in the same way as ordinary writing expresses the words of the
language which lead to their meanings:
O seeker of the innermost secret of the truth of the divine science
(sirr-i h. aqīqat-i ʿilm-i ilāhī), [know] that the 32 divine ‘words’
and 28 divine ‘words’ reach all things by means of attribution of
the [ontological] names (az rū-yi ismiyyat), and [therefore] all
things are their science (ʿilm) and their loci of manifestation
(maz.har) . . . because any work of creation contains an indica-
tion to its creator, and to the Word of the Creator (har mas.nūʿ
dalālat kard bi-jahat bar s.āniʿ wa bar kalima-yi s.āniʿ) (297a).
Another central concept of the Jāwidān-nāma’s ‘linguistics’ of the
creation closely related to the deﬁnition of the form of any particular
object as ‘science’, writing and locus of manifestation of its name, is the
principle of identity of the name and the named. We have already
come across this notion when discussing the properties of the divine
language (Chapter 1), and the differentiation and emergence of form
(Chapter 2).
The Universe

Applied to the forms of particular objects, the identity of the name
and of the named means that the sensible form of any object is the
manifestation of its ontological name. In other words, the identity of
the name and the named postulates a link between the object and its
ontological name, a relationship which is stronger than simple
correspondence: form cannot exist without its name. This is only a
natural consequence of the Jāwidān-nāma’s ‘linguistic’ conception of
the creation, where the sensible objects are only shadows of the
invisible truths actualised through the combinations of original
letters.36 But many passages of the Jāwidān-nāma repeat again and
again that no object can exist without its name. This is, without doubt,
to prevent any confusion between the ontological names and the
names attributed to the objects in human languages. The ontological
name refers to the universal language of the creation, resulting from
the differentiation of the original Word into 28/32 ‘words’ or
phonemes, each of which is an immediate emanation of an aspect of
the divine Essence. Unlike the names of the objects in human
languages, which are purely conventional and have no essential link
with the named object, the ontological name is inherent to the object
and constitutes its innermost reality.37 It is the primordial Word that
brings the universe and every single object and being contained in it
into existence. The Word and 28/32 original ‘words’ resulting from it
are the only principle of existence, the only entities that exist as such.
The existence of any other thing is dependent on these original ‘words’
and their combinations, which reach things through the attribution of
their individual names. Nothing can come into existence without
ontological names; no object can be maintained in existence if its
ontological name was withdrawn from it. This close connection
between the name and existence further clariﬁes the already
mentioned rapprochement between, on the one hand, the breath,
which blows life and existence into created objects and beings, and on
the other hand, the attribution of the names. The following passage
illustrates the existential dimension of the ontological name:
36 Cf. Chapters 1 and 2.
37 The relationship between the universal ontological language and human
languages is examined in Part Two.
Words of Power

If you wanted to separate the [ontological] ‘word’ from things,
which are the loci of manifestation of the divine ‘words’, this
would be impossible, either in actuality (bi-i-ﬁʿl), or in
imagination or intellect (na bi-wahm wa na bi-tas.awwur wa na
bi-taʿaqqul) . . . The divine Word is the pre-existent (qadīm)
attribute of God, rooted in the divine Essence (qāʾim bi-dhāt-i
ilāhī). It is present in everything. God said: ‘He encompasses
everything’ [Q. 41:54]. If, by supposition (bi-l-fard.), the divine
Word were extracted from all existing creatures (jamīʿ-yi
mawjūdāt), [the existence] of which is founded (qāʾim) on [this
Word], there would remain no existence in the things (ashyāʾ-rā
wujūd namānad) . . . If, [for example], the [ontological] ‘word’
were separated from [the stone], there would remain nothing of
this stone, [nothing] by the means of which it could be referred to
(hīch chīzī bāqī az-ān sang namī-mānad ki it.lāq-i shayʾ bar-ū
konī) . . . To conclude, nothing [really] exists except the Word
(ghayr az kalima chīzī dīgar nīst) (463b–464a).
The ontological name constitutes the quiddity of all things. It cannot
be expressed by any conventional name, and manifests itself as a sound
speciﬁc to any particular object or substance:
If someone asks what is this thing that ﬂows in a stream, the
answer is: ‘it is water’. The questioner says then: ‘I do not ask
what is the name of this thing that ﬂows in the stream, so do not
say to me it is water.’ And if he is told that it is a transparent,
glittering, life-giving substance (jawhar), fresh and clear, [the
questioner] will say: ‘These are its qualities (s.ifa), but what is this
thing that is the support of these qualities?’ [His interlocutor]
cannot give an answer. Such is the situation of the people who
discuss the matters of wisdom without having reached the
wisdom of the prophets (h. ikmat-i anbiyāʾ), peace be upon them.
They say: ‘This is quiddity (māhiyya), and the quiddity of things
cannot be known.’ . . . [The true] answer is that the name is
identical to the named (ism ʿayn-i musammāst). The answer
‘water’ is correct, and it is true that it is transparent, fresh, cool
and life-giving. But . . . when water meets a stone, they produce a
‘word’ (kalima) from the [number] of the 32 [ontological]
‘words’. [By the means of these ‘words’], they [i.e., water and
stone] tell themselves what they are, and what is their essence
(dhāt) . . . All birds in the air and leaves on the trees, and
anything [else], when they collide with each other, produce the
voice of the 32 divine ‘words’ (awāz-i 32 kalima-yi ilāhī), and
they say: ‘I am this ‘word’. If this ‘word’ were extracted [from the
The Universe

thing] and annihilated, there would remain no existence (wujūd)
[in the thing] . . . [This ‘word’ proper to any particular thing] is a
divine attribute (s.ifat-i ilāhī) manifested (tajallī) [in this thing].
How could it be extracted from it? This is absolutely impossible.
It is impossible that they [the divine ‘words’] were extracted from
the things and there still remained something from these things
. . . To [be able to] discern these ‘words’ in everything is what
makes the true monotheist (muwah. h. id) (443b–444a).
The identity between the name and the form of the named object is
made possible by the fact that the same standard of differentiation
realised in the human bodily form is applied to the rest of creation:
‘The division of all things and bodies (ashyāʾ wa ajrām) is determined
by the original nature (khilqa) of the face of Adam. In virtue of the
[principle] of unity (tawh. īd), the division of time and of the hours
(taqsīm-i zamān wa sāʿāt) is [made] in accordance with the division of
[the body] of Adam’ (84a). From the ninth heavenly sphere
encompassing the whole universe down to the tiniest atom, everything
is structured in accordance with the same 28/32 basic elements of
form, or ‘letters’, originally synthesised in the human form: ‘All things
are divided in accordance with [the numbers] 28 and 32, so that they
all became the science of the ‘words’ of the divine [Word] (ʿilm-i
kalima-yi ilāhī)’ (417b). The following passage is interesting from the
point of view of terminology:
The seven heavens and seven planets that rotate in 360 degrees,
and the 28 mansions of the moon possess the same form and
composition (īn shakl wa īn s.ūra wa īn wad.ʿ) as Adam. Various
things that are educated (marbūb) by them are [divided] by the
same line of balance as [the heavens], and obtain thus a similar
form and shape. All [that is contained] within the heavenly
spheres is also [contained] in Adam, who is His true Well-
preserved Tablet (lawh. -i mah. fūz.-i h. aqīqī) (53a).
All diversity of particular forms is produced by the combinations of
these 28/32 basic forms, or primary letters, which are the same
throughout the entire universe. This makes any existing form
potentially ‘readable’ by whoever has the knowledge of the primary
letters. While the symbol of the Throne describes the human form
essentially as the source of the Balance, the symbol of the Well-
preserved Tablet mentioned in the two passages cited above is
Words of Power

probably the central symbol in the Jāwidān-nāma referring to the
human body, originally represented by Adam, as the template or
matrix, which, while containing the complete set of the original letters,
also ensures that the form of any particular object or being is a
fragment of the ontological writing:
From [the contemplation] of this Well-preserved Tablet and

all contained in the Well-preserved Tablet of Adam, who is the

Along with the Well-preserved Tablet, other Qurʾānic symbols such as
‘explicit Imām’ in which all things are counted (Q. 36:12), the ‘Book

All existing [objects and beings] (mawjūdāt) were created in

the Face of God because they [all] face towards Adam, and
they are [all] created in accordance with his original nature
(khilqa) (128a–b).
The human form is the intermediary between the science of the divine
Word and all general and particular forms contained within the
universe. The latter are shaped in accordance with the standard
introduced by the human form with its line of Balance: ‘All [entities] of
the superior (ʿulwī) and inferior (siﬂī) [worlds] are educated
(murabbā) by the body (wujūd) of Adam’ (4b); ‘The human form
(hayʾa) is a body (jism), it is corporeal (jismānī). In its dimension of
‘science’ (az rū-yi ʿilmiyyat), it points to the [32 ontological ‘words’],

The Universe

while in its corporeal dimension (az rū-yi jismiyyat), all things [are

What has been said concerning the representation of the human
body as the divine Throne and as the Well-preserved Tablet can be
summarised as follows. The human body contains the complete set
of basic elements, which compose the shape of any possible object
or being in the created world. The human body is the matrix and
source starting from which the ontological names reach the objects,
and the universal standard in accordance with which the ‘science’ of
these names is written into their forms. There is therefore an
essential kinship or congruence between the human body and the
form or body of any existing object or being. This idea is expressed
in the Jāwidān-nāma by the statement that any thing is actually or
potentially part of the human body, represented by the body of
Adam: ‘Adam is a single body (badan). Any writing, object or being
(maktūbāt wa makhlūqāt) that you are able to imagine (tas.awwur)
is a part of the members (aʿd.āʾ wa jawārih. ) of his body . . . all things
are the single body of Adam; they are [all] identical to him’ (237a).
The Word (kalima) of the divine Presence (h. ad.rat-i ilāhī)
reaches every atom of the universe. Everything is a locus of
manifestation (maz.har) of the 32 [ontological] ‘words’. However,
it is the human being (insān) who is the real locus of
manifestation [of the complete divine Word]. Also, the science
(ʿilm) [of the Word], represented by the visible lines of the shape
and form (shakl wa s.ūra) [of the bodies], refers to the human
shape (hayʾat-i bashariyya), from which [this science] reaches all
worlds and atoms. Indeed, the matter of all bodies is the same,
and from this point of view all things are, in their innermost
reality (bi-h. aqīqa), one and the same body (jism); and [all the
ontological ‘words’] are one and the same spirit (rūh. ). One
human soul (nafs-i insān) replaces therefore all things. [There is
only] one Word (kalima), and the human being is its locus of
manifestation (190b–191a).
This idea is further developed in the following fragment. The parts of
the universe are articulated together as the members of the human
body and bound to the cosmic body of Adam by effusions:39

Words of Power

All things are the body (wujūd) of Adam, while Adam is the
single body of all things. He [is made] of the four natural
elements (chahār t.abāʾiʿ), and the speech (nut.q) contained in the
four elements manifests itself from his [Adam’s] body. All stars
and heavenly spheres are linked (muttas.il) by their effusions
(fayd.) to his body, and among all these various essences
(dhawāt), the Essence of God (dhāt-i khudā) remains concealed
to the non-initiated eye (chashm-i nāmah. ram). When the
innermost truth (h. aqīqa) of all things, [namely the fact] that
they are [all part] of Adam’s body, is known, the essence of the
[divine] Truth (h. aqq) becomes manifest, and polytheism (shirk)
is removed (60b).
The congruence between the human body and the bodies of all other
objects and beings is also a co-substantiality, since the human body,
like any other existing body, is made of earth, the principal element of
form. We have seen above that earth has the power to produce any
form existing on its surface. The human body is equivalent to the
whole surface of the earth and, therefore, potentially contains any
other particular form produced on the earth:
Things exterior to Adam are nevertheless parts of his body
(wujūd). Earth is a part of Adam and possesses the aptitude
(qābiliyya) to [produce] the whole [body] of Adam. Outside the
earth, everything is turned in the direction of Adam. [Every animal
species] possesses the same aptitude [as earth], and every
[particular] thing is a science (ʿilm) from among the 32 [‘sciences’
correspondingtothe32ontological‘letters’]ofAdam’sface(349a).
Earth is what remains from the body of Adam (baqiyyat-i
wujūd-i Adam). Earth and the four elements (chahārʿuns.ur) have
the aptitude (qābiliyya) to constitute the body of a snake (mār),
an ant (mūr), a lion (shīr), or any other animal. The animal
powers (quwwa) and qualities (s.ifa) are also visible in the human
being (insān). But, since [the human being] became the locus of
manifestation (maz.har) or the complete speech and all names
(tamāmī-yi nut.q wa asmāʾ), and received the form of God (s.ūrat-
i khudāʾī), [the human being] was ennobled and became
vicegerent (khalīfa) (25b).
There is also another aspect of the congruence between the form of the
human body and the forms of the particular objects. We have seen
that, in the Jāwidān-nāma, the human body is essentially the locus of
manifestation of the Word. In addition, human beings are endowed
The Universe

with speech, which means that they possess the knowledge of the
Word and are able to express it actively. In several fragments, Adam is
described as the ‘Speaking Word’, while the universe is the ‘Silent
Word’. Since every existing object and being is part of the human body
and, as such, a locus of manifestation of a fragment of the Word –
more exactly, of its own ontological name – every object and being
shares, to a certain extent and at least potentially, the faculty of speech
which characterises the human body. Another formulation of this
same idea is the statement that, since the human form, as the locus of
manifestation of the complete alphabet of the creation and of the
Supreme Name of God, synthesises all possible ontological names, any
particular object or being, as a locus of manifestation of one of the
names issued from the Well-preserved Tablet of the human form, is
the manifestation of a fragment of the human form. From this
perspective, every existing thing is a fragment of the human body;
everything is therefore potentially endowed with speech, and this
potentiality becomes actualised when these fragments are brought
together to re-compose a complete human body. The following
selection of passages is rather long, but I found them all expressing
different approaches to the issue under discussion here:
Everything is endowed with speech (nāt.iq) and will [possess this
quality] in the future, because all objects are the remains of the
members of Adam’s [body]. ‘God gave us speech, as He gave
everything speech’ [Q. 41:21]: [this verse] refers to [the fact] that
all things will be speaking [by virtue of] his [Adam’s] unity (bi-
wah. dāniyyat-i ū) and [within his] single body . . . Look at the
bodily form (s.ūra) of Adam, and at the structure (naz.m) of the
universe. All that you can observe [is an expression of the] unity
(tawh. īd), and Adam is the locus of manifestation of the speech
(maz.har-i nut.q). Therefore, the speech of Adam is potentially
(bi-l-quwwa) in everything, and each thing is brought into
existence [by] the speech of Adam. ‘God gave us speech, as He
gave everything speech’, because the speech is the distinctive
feature of Adam (nut.q makhs.ūs. bi-Adam ast) (25b).
Everything has [an ontological] name, which is that ‘word’
contained in it in potentiality (bi-l-quwwa). [This name]
manifests itself externally in accordance with the innermost
reality (h. aqīqa) of [any individual] thing . . . Read [these names]
in the visible Well-preserved Tablet (lawh. -i mah. fūz.-i z.āhir) [of

the human bodily form]. There is the science (ʿilm) of everything
manifested in the visible world (z.āhir) (243a).
All things are the single body of Adam. Starting from the line
of balance (khat.t.-i istiwāʾ) of Adam, discover the line of balance
of everything, and read the divine Word (kalima-yi khudāʾī), of
which Adam is [the most complete] locus of manifestation
(maz.har). By the means of attribution of [the ontological] names
(az rū-yi ismiyyat), the 32 ‘words’ reached everything, and
manifested themselves (tajallī) in everything. Everything, in
potentiality and in actuality (bi-l-ﬁʿl wa bi-l-quwwa), is the locus
of manifestation of [these ‘words’], [the most complete form of

[created] ‘in the form of the All-Merciful’ . . . Everything is in
reality he (hama ashyāʾ bi-h. aqīqat ūst). It is in this sense that he
[Adam] is the mirror of God and of everything (āyina wa mirʾāt-i
khudā wa hama ashyāʾ). He [Adam] is the Lote-tree of the
Boundary (sidrat al-muntahā) and the ‘inhabited house’ (bayt al-
maʿmūr), [i.e., the heavenly counterpart of the Kaʿba] (274b).
In the following passage, the idea that everything is potentially
endowed with speech as a part of Adam’s body is linked to
astrological and alchemical motifs. Since the body of Adam is equal to
the whole surface of the earth, not only all objects and beings existing
on the surface of the earth, but also effusions from the heavenly
spheres, stars and planets focused on the earth are collected and
integrated into the body of Adam through this surface and through
the four elements:
Every effusion (fayd.) coming from the heavens and heavenly
bodies (asmān wa ajrām-i samawāt) is dispersed (nuthār) on the
earth and becomes an element (ʿuns.ur) of Adam’s [body]. Night
and day, they [the heavens and heavenly bodies] turn around the
elements of [the] Adam’s [body] in a ritual of circumambulation
(t.awāf) and perform the gestures of the ritual prayer (dar sujūd
wa dar rukūʿ and). They are parts of his body (badan), and he is
[what they represent as a] whole in reality: ‘God created Adam in
the form of All-Merciful’40 (25b).
The speech is contained in everything, whether it is actually audible or
not. This speech is the expression of the ontological name of every

[The 32 ontological ‘words’] are rooted in the Essence of the
Real (qāʾim bi-dhāt-i h. aqqand); they have no beginning and no
end in time (azalī wa abadī and) and they are the pre-existent
attributes of the Real. They are not created. By the means of the
names (az rū-yi ismiyyat) they attain everything in the two
worlds. No entity (mukawwināt) in the two worlds is void of
them. When the tongue moves in the mouth, it produces [a

stone to [another] stone, the ‘word’ and the voices (s.awt wa
āwāz) produced [by the stone] cannot be outside these 28 and 32
divine ‘words’. This is why God said: ‘Does He not encompass

stricken against each other, they remain silent, but this speech
(nut.q) is nevertheless contained in them potentially (bi-l-
quwwa) . . . (410b–411a).
Whoever possesses the knowledge of the laws of correspondence
between the external forms of things and their invisible ontological
names can discern the fragments of the Word contained in them. Such
a person, initiated in the knowledge of the line of Balance of the
human form, can read the universal ontological writing in the forms of
things just as ordinary people can read conventional human writing:
Adam and his shape (shakl) . . . is the divine [ontological]
writing; he is the Tablet (lawh. ) and the foundation (as.l) [of the]
lines of the divine writing. Whosoever goes to Paradise has his
[Adam’s] shape (s.ūra) and is able to read the lines of divine
[writing]. Everybody and everything receives [the ability to
speak] from Adam, who is the foundation of all [of them]. Since,
by means of the line of balance (khat.t.-i istiwāʾ) all things are the
Words of Power

science of word and speech (ʿilm-i kalima wa kalām), they are all
the divine writing and the science of the divine Word. They all
face each other, and they are all speaking and hearing in the
language of spiritual states (bi-zabān-i h. āl).41 They all converse
by means of inspiration (wah. y) and signs (ishāra). For example,
[an ordinary] reader can read the writing which is before him, if
the convention (is.t.ilāh. ) of this writing is known to him. [It is as
if] this writing speaks [to the reader]. Similarly, whosoever
[knows] the ‘convention’ of divine writing (is.t.ilāh. -i kitābat-i
ilāhī) can see how all things are the science of His Word (kalima),
and how they speak by the means of signs and inspiration ‘from
behind a curtain’ [Q. 33:53] (175a–b).
The ‘words’ contained in things can be perceived in dreams. Indeed, in
the world of dreams, any object, plant or animal can speak. One
interesting development of this idea in the Jāwidān-nāma is the
statement that the capacity to see objects and beings speaking in
dreams is determined by the bodily form of the dreamer. The physical
form is the locus of manifestation of the ontological name of every
given entity, which is the combination of a certain number of original
phonemes or ‘words’. The Jāwidān-nāma states that no entity can
perceive more phonemes than are contained in its name. Therefore,
only the human being, whose body is the locus of manifestation of the
complete ontological alphabet, has the capacity to contemplate any
other form in dream, and be able to perceive its speech. According to
the Jāwidān-nāma, this kind of perception which can be experienced
in dreams is also that of the prophetic experience. Moses was spoken to
by the ﬁre and by a tree. Anyone who is initiated in the innermost
meaning of the human form and can ‘read’ the ontological writing in
sensible forms of the empirical world, can also discern the phonemes
and words in the images of dreams. Thus, the knowledge of the human
bodily form includes also the power of dream interpretation. This
power is usually exempliﬁed in the Jāwidān-nāma by the ﬁgure of
Joseph:
The human being (insān) has the science of the 32 [ontological
‘words’ of the complete Word written] on his or her face.

prisoner who narrated his dream to Joseph]: ‘I dreamed that I
was carrying on my head bread’ [Q. 12:36]. An initiate

‘words’ (384a).
The words contained in all things will be clearly audible at the end of
time, when the names will be withdrawn from the things and
manifested directly, without the mediation of the form:42
‘And they will say to their skins, “Why bore you witness against
us?” They shall say, “God gave us speech, as He gave everything
speech”’ [Q. 41:21]. Therefore, the speech (nut.q) is not an
exclusively human property. Everything will be speaking on the
Day of Resurrection, which means that the divine Word will
come forth from everything: ‘All that is in the heavens and the
earth magniﬁes God’ [Q. 62:1], ‘Nothing is, that does not proclaim
His praise, but you do not understand their extolling.’ [Q. 17:44].
The extolling of all things will be understood when the speech
will come forth from everything (463b–464a).
The congruence and commensurability between the human form and
any other form in the universe is founded on the line of Balance,
originating from the human body and ensuring the homogeneity of
the creation and its capacity to express the science of the Word: ‘All the
heavens, earth and everything [else] has the receptive aptitude
(qābiliyya) of the form (s.ūra) of Adam . . . because they are [all]
created according to the [division introduced] by the line of balance, in
accordance with the science of his word and speech (bi-ʿilmiyyat-i
kalima wa kalām-i ū)’ (339a).
Starting from the original nature (khilqa) of Mother (umm) and
from the face of Adam, the line of balance (khat.t.-i istiwāʾ)
[spreads] upon all things and the heavens, because they all
[constitute] the single body of Adam. This is why [Eve and Adam

Anything that has a line of balance – meaning every existing thing – is

balance of the form of Adam, like plants, animals, minerals and fruits
(nabātāt wa h. aywānāt wa jamādāt wa maʿādin wa fawākih)’ (104b–

of beings have been part of Adam’s body and will be eventually re-

that the line of balance of everything is a trace (athar) of [the line of

The next fragment highlights particularly the similarity and
commensurability revealed by the line of balance, between the
human form and the forms of animals, plants and minerals.
According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the symmetry of the bodies,
exempliﬁed by the crest of the cock and the hoopoe, or the two
halves of a grain of wheat, represents the line of balance. The line of
balance is the ‘Straight Path’ of God put in every existing form, as a
token of its bond with the human body and the science of the divine
Word contained in it; it is the ‘forelock’ mentioned in the Qurʾān by
which God grasps every creature:
Starting with the line of balance of Adam and Eve, observe the
divine power in the form of the line of balance of birds, animals,
minerals and all [other] creatures (makhlūqāt) . . . Look, for
example, at the line of balance of a hoopoe. Its crest is divided
into two parts. It has two eyes, two ears, two nostrils and a mouth,
similar to the lines of the human face. Read these seven and eight
lines. Every line contains four [subsidiary] lines, so that they are
28 and 32 lines. Look then at the crest (ʿurf) of a cock – ‘And the
dwellers on the Battlements [al-aʿrāf] shall call to certain men they
know by their sign’ [Q. 7:46] – and [look] at all [other] animals,
and see the path of God (s.irāt. Allāh) and the divine original
nature (khilqat Allāh): ‘There is no creature that crawls, but He
takes it by the forelock. Surely my Lord is on a straight path’
[Q. 11:56]. Since Adam is the divine synthesis (majmūʿa-yi ilāhī),
he is the Well-preserved Tablet (lawh. -i mah. fūz.) of God. By its
original nature (khilqa), the line of balance of his face manifests
the lines of the 32 and 28 [ontological] ‘words’, because he is the
The Universe

locus of manifestation (maz.har) of the 32 ‘words’. [Starting with
this line of balance], pass [to the observation of the] line of every
leaf and grain: “It is God who splits43 the grain and the date-stone”
[Q. 6:95], and recognise the divine science (ʿilm) of His Word, as
[you recognise it] on the face of Adam. Contemplate in a grain of
wheat the same line [of balance] as that [represented by] the
parting of the hair on the face of Adam, [which passes between]
two eyebrows and [two pairs] of eyelashes (296b–297a).
This symmetry is the manifestation of divine Equity (qist.) and Justice
(ʿadl), which is given to all forms of the creation without exception. But
the most perfect manifestation of Equity and Justice is the human form:
The pre-existent Essence (dhāt-i qadīm) created various [species]
of animals in order to demonstrate that the same Essence can
have various forms [of expression]. However, the equity (qist.)
and justice (ʿadl) of this [Essence] were distributed [to all the
various forms of its manifestation], so that there is no difference
[between them from the point of view of] equity and justice:
‘There is no creature that crawls, but He takes it by the forelock.
Surely my Lord is on a straight path’ [Q. 11:56]. But the whole
measure [of equity and justice] is manifested in humans (insān)
and nowhere else. This is why [the human form is] ‘the fairest
stature’ [Q. 95:4] (390a).
Even if every object or being, be it mineral, plant or animal, has the
same symmetry and balance as the human body, only the human being
can attain the knowledge of the complete divine writing. The Qurʾānic
quotation in the following passage suggests also that the humans who
did not attain this knowledge remain at the level of animals:
[Draw] the line [of balance] of any animal. [Just as a human
being] it has two ears, two nostrils, two eyes, and a mouth.
[Multiplication of these seven members by the number of four
elements produces] 28 lines, or 32 lines of the divine [ontological]
writing [if] the line of balance [is counted]. [You can] read [these
lines]. But the animal does not recognise the divine writing,
while a human being (insān) does: ‘They are but as the cattle;
nay, they are further astray from the way’ [Q. 25:44]. The fact

that human beings possess the complete science (ʿilm-i tāmm)
[of the divine Word] distinguishes them from animals (283a).
Also, the line of balance is not manifested with the same degree of
clarity at all levels of existence. It appears in minerals, and then
develops progressively through plants and animal forms. But none of
these forms of existence possesses all elements of the balance: the
perfect balance can be attained only in the human form, which
contains the complete set of 28/32 original Letters:
The human form (shakl-i insān), and most particularly the face,
possesses 32 sciences (ʿilm) . . . which are the distinctive signs
(iʿlām) of the 32 [ontological] ‘words’. Every science [is expressed
by] a particular form (hay’at) [i.e., feature of the human face] . . .
The forms (s.ūra) of all things [existing] in the universe are
composed of these [32 particular elementary forms of which the
human face is the sum]. [Some of these forms] are [already]
visible in the minerals, but the division in two symmetrical halves
[by the line of balance] (munās.ifa), which appears in the original
nature (khilqa) of the animals, attains its perfection in humans.
The division in two halves is also visible in all plants. From this
point of view, every leaf is similar to the human form. Since the
human form is the divine [ontological] writing with its 32
‘words’, you can ﬁnd every atom of any existing object or being in
the human form and face (365a–b).
This brings us to the Jāwidān-nāma’s theory of evolution and
involution of forms that we will address in the rest of this chapter. We
have already seen that, according to the Jāwidān-nāma, the forms of all
existing objects and beings are determined by their ontological names,
and are fragments of the science of the divine Word. Every name is the
combination of the original phonemes and carries a fragment of the
divine truth. The corresponding bodily form reﬂects the name and is
composed of the number of original letters proportional to the number
of phonemes in the name. The bodily form shows therefore the
epistemological value of every given form, its place on the scale of
capacity to express the science of the Word. The more basic elements
of form, or primary letters, are contained in the given form, the more
perfect is the corresponding fragment of the science. The most perfect
form is the form of the human body which contains the entire
ontological alphabet. To attain the knowledge of the human form
The Universe

means to realise the supreme knowledge of God available to the
created being, the knowledge that leads to salvation.
According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the forms of existing things and
objects can evolve or involve on this scale of knowledge. Since the
external form is determined by this ontological knowledge, as its
‘science’ or locus of manifestation, the progress in knowledge leads to
the acquisition of a more perfect external form, while the loss of
knowledge conversely results in degradation into a lower body. This
sounds very much like a theory of transmigration, formulated in the
Jāwidān-nāma essentially in terms of the transformation of forms
within the food chain: one given bodily form can be transformed into
another by becoming food of the latter:44
Among the entities [lit. ‘members’, juzw] created in accordance
with the original nature (khilqa) of Adam, some have an
invariable form (s.ūra), like stars and heavenly spheres with
[their] fractions. Others, such as a stone of date, grain of wheat or
[any] plant, are created from the four natural elements, [like] the
members of Adam’s [body]. Everything brought into existence by
[a combination of the] four natural elements is created, like
Adam, in accordance with the original nature of Adam and his
line of balance. If [one of such things] becomes the food of an
animal, or if an animal is eaten by another animal, it takes the
shape (shakl) of the animal [which ate it], and loses the balanced
shape of its own external appearance (shakl-i istiwāʾ-yi z.āhir-i
khūd), but the essence of its own line of balance cannot be
destroyed (mah. w). For example, the leaves mentioned [in the
verse]: ‘Not a leaf falls, but He knows it. Not a grain in the earth’s
shadows, [not a thing, fresh or withered, but it is in a Book
Manifest.]’ [Q. 6:59], which fall and decay, leaving thus externally
the station of the divine balance and writing (maqām-i istiwāʾ wa
kitābat-i khudāʾī), nevertheless keep this writing with them in
potentiality (bi-l-quwwa). This is why, wherever they come [into
existence, the things] cannot remain behind (takhalluf) the line
of balance of Adam. Firstly, because the locus of manifestation of
everything is [shaped] according to the line of balance. Secondly,
because the balance is His pre-existent attribute (s.ifat-i qadīm)
. . . The purpose [of contemplating how the things] abandon

Words of Power

[their] ﬁrst form (s.ūra) and acquire another form different from
their [initial] form is to clearly demonstrate to the seekers that the
quiddity (māhiyya) of these two [forms] is the same. The two
[forms] are one and the same thing. Externally, they appear as
two [different forms], while the [ontological] ‘word’ and speech
(kalima wa kalām), which lies in their foundation, is one and the
same: ‘God blots out, and He establishes whatsoever He will; and
with Him is the essence of the Book’ [Q. 13:39] (117a–b).
As have been noted above, the potential of speech inherent to any
particular object and being is realised when fragments of the Word
contained in things are brought together and eventually re-composed
into a complete human form. A plant or an animal eaten by another
animal becomes integrated into the bodily form of the latter.
Potentially, any existing entity can become food for a human being,
either directly or after undergoing a series of preliminary transform-
ations. It is then integrated into a human body and into its tissues and
substances, including sperm, which gives it a chance to be born in a
human body. The goal of the transformations in the food chain is to
realise such a re-composition, when the fragments of the Word
contained in all objects and beings are actualised as part of the human
body and speech. The achievement of this goal means enlightenment
and salvation, that is, according to the terminology of the Jāwidān-
nāma, return to the condition where the direct perception of the divine
Word is possible, and all objects are immediately seen from the
ontological perspective, as loci of manifestation of the divine words.
This condition is the condition of Paradise.
Additionally, several passages of the Jāwidān-nāma express the idea
that, since the human form contains the complete science of the divine
Word, a human being can intentionally transmit this science to any
object or being, and bring it to the perfection of his or her own body by
eating them. That is why the necessity to feed is an advantage proper to
the human condition unlike angels who do not eat and therefore do
not possess the power of transformation proper to the food chain:
If someone formulates [the following] question: ‘Satan robbed
Adam when he said “[Your Lord has only prohibited you from this
tree] lest you become angels, or lest you become immortals.”
[Q. 7:20]. But Adam knew that the angels bowed down to him,
and Satan knew that the station of Adam was beyond the station
of the angels, in accordance with [the verse]: “And when We said
The Universe

to the angels, ‘Bow yourselves to Adam’; so they bowed themselves,
save Iblis” [Q. 2:34]. And [Adam] taught angels [the names of all
things]. So why did [Satan] deceive [Adam] by saying “[lest] you
become angels?” ’ The answer is that [Satan] knew that [Adam] is
superior [to angels], in virtue of ‘tell them their names’ [Q. 2:33],
and in virtue of ‘And when We said to the angels, “Bow yourselves
to Adam”’ [Q. 2:34]. But he supposed that the [station of] angels,
free from [the necessity to eat and to drink], is better than the
station [requiring] eating and drinking (maqām-i akl wa shurb).
This is why he attempted [to deceive Adam with this argument].
However, to God, the station [requiring] eating and drinking is
superior to the opposite [condition] for the following reason.
When things acquire the forms (s.ūra) of minerals, plants and
fruits, they become food for Adam. [After being eaten], they
become his sperm (nut.fa) and reappear from the bodily form of
Adam, of which [it is said]: ‘God created Adam in the form of the
All-Merciful.’ This is how are born the prophets and Muh.ammad,
peace be upon him. This station [requiring] eating and drinking,
related to the prophets, is beyond [the station that implies the]
abandonment of eating and drinking. This is why, in the
promised Paradise, the spiritual beings (rūh. āniyān) eat and drink,
and all their food, such as fruits, is endowed with speech: ‘God
gave us speech, as He gave everything speech’ [Q. 41:21] (110a–b).
All aliments and beverages (aghdhiya wa ashriba), which
receive their education (parwarish) from the heavens and stars
(samawāt wa ajrām-i kawākib), evolve until they become food
for humans (t.uʿmat-i insān). They re-emerge then from the
human original nature (khilqa), [provided with its] beauty (h. usn
wa jamāl) . . . Every movement of any [object or being] is guided
by the desire to acquire the qualities proper to the human form
(muttas.if shawand bi-s.ūrat-i insān), which is the Throne of the
Presence of the divine Unity (ʿarsh-i h. ad.rat-i ah. adiyya) (305b).
When angels opposed the creation of man saying that he will ‘shed
blood’ (Q. 2:30), they did not know that when a human being kills an
animal and eats it, or consumes a fruit, vegetable or mineral, it is in fact
an expression of love and a great favour which brings these forms of
existence on a higher level: ‘When a human loves something, he or she
wants to eat it, in order to make [this object or being] identical to his or
her self’ (242b).
When God [spoke] to angels: ‘“I am setting in the earth a viceroy.”
They said, “What, wilt Thou set therein one who will do
corruption there, and shed blood, while we proclaim Thy praise
Words of Power

and call Thee Holy?” He said, “Assuredly I know that you know
not.”’ [Q. 2:30]. The angels did not know that there is perfection
in shedding blood, and this perfection gives to humans advantage
over the angels. [Adam] shed blood and [killed] animals . . . in
order to bring their animal forms (s.ūra) to his human form
(s.ūrat-i bashariyyat-i khwishtan). Angels do not have this
aptitude . . . No angel is able to eat plants and minerals in
order to remove their vegetal or mineral form and bring them
into the form and garment (s.ūrat wa kiswat) of the person before
the father of which all angels were obliged to bow down (350a).
‘Wilt Thou set therein one who will do corruption there, and
shed blood?’ [Q. 2:30], that is to say, someone who will spoil Thy
creation by killing and corrupting it? They [angels] did not know
that the intention of shedding blood is to bring [the killed beings]
to the divine form (s.ūrat-i khudāʾī), which is that of Adam. It is
illicit to kill someone who has already reached the form of Adam.
As to the animals, their blood is shed in order to make them re-
emerge from the divine form. ‘Assuredly I know that you know
not!’ [Q. 2:30] (263b).
According to the Jāwidān-nāma, this is the inner meaning of the
practice of ritual slaughter in the Muslim tradition. In order to be
permissible as food, the animal must be killed facing the qibla.45 Since
in the Jāwidān-nāma the qibla symbolises the face of Adam, the
slaughtering of an animal facing the qibla means that it is immolated
on its way of evolution towards Adam’s face, which is the perfect
manifestation of the complete ontological alphabet:
Any living creature lawful to eat used to be killed by the prophets
in the name of God the All-Great, [after its face was turned]
either in the direction of the Kaʿba or that of the Temple of
Jerusalem. The angels opposed [the creation of] Adam who shed
blood and ate,46 [though Adam did this in order] to bring [the
killed and eaten animals] into the human form (s.ūrat-i insānī).
But whosoever goes to Paradise goes there in human form and
shape (257a).
If minerals, plants and animals can evolve towards the human form,
the opposite is also possible: the human beings who do not attain the
full knowledge of their own bodily form are reduced to lower forms of
45 E. Francesca, ‘Slaughter’, Encyclopaedia of the Qurʾān, vol. 5, pp. 54–56.
46 Allusion to Q. 2:30.
The Universe

existence. In Chapter 12, we will see that this gap between human
knowledge and form was initially introduced by Satan, who ‘stripped’
Adam and Eve of the knowledge of their own bodily forms and thus
caused their expulsion from Paradise.
According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the Cosmic Human represented
by the original couple Adam/Eve, Time and the Universe are three
counterparts of the complete divine Word. The Cosmic Human is the
form of the Word, Time is its receptacle, and the Universe contains all
forms issued from the Word in the process of differentiation. Each of
these three essentially identical entities is the starting point of a great
cycle. From the original couple begins the transmission of the physical
shape of the human body and of the knowledge of the divine Word
contained in this form within the historical humanity living in physical
time and space. This knowledge is transmitted in the line of prophets,
the ultimate goal of which is the revelation of the complete Word. The
actualisation of the Word at the end of the prophetic cycle means the
restoration of the Cosmic Human as the sum of the historical
humankind, during the gathering of the last Hour. Since the measure
of Time and Universe is determined by the Word, the restoration of
the complete Word means also the accomplishment of the cycle of
Time and the disappearance of all visible forms of the universe,
because the ontological ‘words’, which sustained the existence of
forms, will return to their original condition within the primordial
Word. The cycles of Time and Universe seem thus determined by the
prophetic cycle, which gradually unfolds the knowledge of the Word
and eventually brings not only humankind, but all of creation to its
original condition within the divine Word. In Part Two, we will
address the Jāwidān-nāma’s theories related to the unfolding of the
Word and its return to the Origin in the concerted parallel cycles of
Prophecy, Time and Universe.
Words of Power

Part II
Prophetology: The Descent of the Word and its
Return to the Origin
The Jāwidān-nāma repeatedly emphasises the idea that God created
the world in order to be known.1 The most important means by which
the divine knowledge is conveyed to the creation is the divine
ontological language. The idea that the unfolding and manifestation of
the Word through the forms of created objects and beings provides a
path leading to the knowledge of the divine Reality is central to the
Jāwidān-nāma. We have already seen that, according to the Jāwidān-
nāma’s interpretation of Qurʾān 2:31: ‘He taught Adam the names, all
of them’, God gave the knowledge of the Word to Adam, and
simultaneously wrote this knowledge into the shape of Adam’s body,
thus making the human form the locus of manifestation of the
complete Word. As we have seen when discussing the theory of
evolution/involution in Chapter 6, the human bodily form represents
the limit of the knowledge accessible to any given form of existence.
Humans are therefore the only beings able to realise the fullness of the
divine knowledge attainable within the limits of the creation.
We have also seen in previous chapters that Adam, or the Cosmic
Man, is the central concept of the Jāwidān-nāma’s cosmogony. He
represents the standard, which introduces proportion and measure
into the creation, structuring Time and the Universe in accordance
1 This idea is formulated in a well-known tradition where God speaks in ﬁrst
person: ‘I was a hidden treasure and I wished to be known, so I created the creatures in
order to be known’ (kuntu kanzan makhﬁyyan fa-ah. babtu ʿan uʿrafa fa khalaqtu al-
khalq likay uʿrafa). For the references, see Murata, The Tao of Islam, p. 61 ff., and A.
Eschraghi, ‘ “I Was A Hidden Treasure”. Some Notes on a Commentary Ascribed to
Mullā S.adrā Shīrāzī’, in A. Akasoy and W. Raven, ed., Islamic Thought in the Middle
Ages: Studies in Text, Transmission and Translation, in Honour of Hans Daiber
(Leiden and Boston, 2008), pp. 91–99, in particular p. 92.

with the ‘line of Balance’ of the original Word. In this sense, that is to
say, in his quality of standard and mediator who conveys the divine
ontological ‘words’ to the creation, Adam is essentially the archetypal
Prophet. The historical prophetic cycle represents, therefore, the pro-
gressive revelation of the knowledge of the Word in time and in the
physical universe already structured in accordance with the Word
through the mediation of the cosmic Adam. With regard to the pro-
phetic cycle, Adam is, at the same time, the personiﬁcation of the
whole cycle and the prototype of any individual historical prophet.
After Adam, the knowledge of the Word is transmitted in the line of
prophets. It will be recalled that this knowledge is not discursive, but
ontological. Like Adam, Time and the Universe, the cycle of prophecy
is structured in accordance with the 28/32 original ‘words’. Its
unfolding is, therefore, closely related to the temporal and cosmic
cycles. Since Adam, Time and the Universe are conﬁgurations of
the complete Word, the realisation of the complete knowledge of the
Word through successive prophetic missions means simultaneous
completion of these three entities. In other words, the end of the pro-
phetic cycle necessarily coincides with the end of Time and the
Universe, and with the re-appearance of the cosmic Adam.
The interaction of divine knowledge with the world of creation
includes two closely interrelated phases. The ﬁrst phase is that of the
‘descent’ (tanzīl) of the Word into the creation and its progressive
revelation in the prophetic missions. The Word assumes at this stage
the active role, the prophets being essentially the instruments that
convey the revelation to humankind. The memory of the Word is ﬁxed
not only in the holy books revealed to the prophets, but also in the
structure of the religious laws and rituals introduced by them. In this
regard, the Jāwidān-nāma focuses principally on the precepts of the
Muslim religious law and the elements of Muslim rituals, the most
eminent place among which is given to prayer.
The Word and its 28/32 ‘words’, as well as some central concepts of
the Jāwidān-nāma, such as the ‘line of Balance’, are also symbolised by
the objects, constructions or speciﬁc capacities and deeds usually
associated with particular prophets.
The second phase, that of the ‘ascent’, is ‘return to the origin’
(taʾwīl), which reverses the roles between the Word and the creation.
At this stage, by the means of ontological hermeneutics, the prophets
Words of Power

and saints actively bring the Word from its loci of manifestation in the
visible world back to its original state within the unfathomable divine
Reality.2
The passage from tanzīl to taʾwīl also addresses the paradox of the
manifestation of the divine language by means of human language and
writing. During the process of tanzīl, this paradox remains, in a sense,
latent, the divine Word being revealed to the prophets in their own
languages without any conscious effort of ‘translation’ on their part.
But taʾwīl supposes the realisation of a conscious passage from the level
of the human language, determined in fact by the empirical reality of
the physical world and by arbitrary social agreements, to the universal
ontological language of the Word based on metaphysical truths.
Every prophetic mission combines in some proportion both phases
of tanzīl and taʾwīl, and the division between the two remains
therefore conditional. But, as the general tendency, the former process
dominates in the ﬁrst half of the prophetic cycle, and the latter in the
second. The ﬁrst half of the prophetic cycle includes, in the Jāwidān-
nāma, the prophets of the Old Testament. The most salient ﬁgure
among them is that of Moses. The second half begins with Jesus, who
inaugurates the sub-cycle of the ummīs, or ‘motherly’ prophets, whose
mission consists, particularly, in the revelation of the foundations of
the Word, related in the Jāwidān-nāma, as we have seen in the
previous chapters, with the bodily shape and facial features of Eve/
Mother. The missions of Jesus and Muh.ammad, the second ‘motherly’
prophet, complete the revelation of the foundations of the Word
without which the last stage of the prophetic cycle, that of the taʾwīl
proper, could not be realised.
The ‘motherly’ prophets are situated between the tanzīl and the
taʾwīl. Their missions bear, therefore, the distinctive marks of these
two opposite ﬂows of the divine Word. The prophetic role of Jesus is
limited to his historical mission, but he is himself the personiﬁcation of
the divine Word, which will be fully revealed in his second coming. At
this point, the Jāwidān-nāma makes extensive usage of Christian
2 At least one short fragment (fol. 103a–b) seems to suggest that, just as tanzīl is
the revelation of the progressively increasing number of the primordial ‘words’, taʾwīl
moves in the opposite direction, leading from multiplicity towards the original Unity,
from the 32 revealed ‘words’ towards the one Word.
Prophetology

apocalyptic symbolism: Jesus will open the seven seals of the Book of
Life; through his sacriﬁce he will deliver humankind from the diversity
of languages, making available the universal language of the creation.3
Muh.ammad, in his historical mission, is the ‘Seal of the Prophets’. He
closes the ‘descent’ of the Word.4 But his heavenly ascension (miʿrāj)
symbolises the whole period of taʾwīl, the return to the origin of the
Word, which will follow his historical mission.
This last period of taʾwīl is only vaguely outlined in the Jāwidān-
nāma. As we mentioned in the Introduction, Fad.l Allāh probably
claimed that his own enlightenment, consisting basically of the
revelation of the innermost meaning of the separate letters, opened the
period of taʾwīl; and in this sense the Jāwidān-nāma could be
conceived of as sacred book of taʾwīl.5
The most straightforward way to give an account of the Jāwidān-
nāma’s prophetology would be to follow the chronological list of the
prophets mentioned in this work and to describe the most
characteristic features of every prophetic ﬁgure. However, such a
presentation could be confusing. Each prophet is, in the Jāwidān-
nāma, a powerful symbol expressing a complex combination of ideas.
These combinations can overlap, and in this case we will ﬁnd different
aspects of the same idea in the fragments related to different prophets.
In addition, there is no clear correlation between the chronological
order of the prophets and the phases of tanzīl and taʾwīl mentioned
above. For these reasons, I have adopted another approach: in the
