Conclusion
The Jāwidān-nāma in the Context of Islamic Thought
The preceding study of the Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrinal contents
inevitably raises the following question: how can this doctrine be
situated in the history of Islamic religious thought? The present
conclusion is intended to discuss this question and to provide
observations which, hopefully, can be developed in future research.
As mentioned in the Introduction, the known sources do not
contain any signiﬁcant information concerning Fad.l Allāh’s afﬁlia-
tions, such as the names of his teachers, or of any other ﬁgures who
may have played a prominent role in his spiritual and intellectual
education, and in the maturation of his thought. Careful identiﬁcation
of possible references to known authors or currents, such as speciﬁc
technical terms or other borrowings in the text of the Jāwidān-nāma,
could shed more light on this issue. But such a study can hardly be
undertaken before an accurate critical edition of this work becomes
available.
In the meantime, any effort of contextualisation will remain
necessarily tentative. In the absence of direct textual evidence that
would attest links with speciﬁc trends or works, such an effort can only
be based on a comparison of the Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrines with those
of similar religious trends. However, a general, indistinctive compar-
ison with all possible similar currents risks becoming a pure (and
virtually endless) exercise of erudition, which will hardly help us to
better understand the real place of the Jāwidān-nāma in the history of
Islamic religious thought. It seemed to me more useful in this chapter
to focus on the literary genres and religious trends that had some kind
of functional afﬁnity with the Jāwidān-nāma, or which could have,
with a reasonable degree of probability, inﬂuenced the author in his
time and place.

Since the Jāwidān-nāma has some features that give it the appear-
ance of a Qurʾānic commentary, and since Qurʾānic hermeneutics
(taʾwīl) is at the core of this work, the ﬁrst section brieﬂy assesses the
Jāwidān-nāma’s relationship to this major genre of Islamic religious
literature. But, as we have seen in many fragments cited in the previous
chapters, the Jāwidān-nāma’s hermeneutics is not limited to the
Qurʾān, it is also extended to the biblical texts. Therefore, this section
will address the issue of speciﬁc use of biblical texts in the Jāwidān-
nāma and its possible precedents in the history of Islamic exegetical
literature.
From the point of view of its intellectual orientation, the doctrine of
the Jāwidān-nāma is part of the mystical and messianic current that
has existed from the beginning of Islam, but attained some
prominence in the period immediately preceding the Mongol
invasion, especially in the works of Ibn al-ʿArabī and in the Ismaili
doctrinal literature. In the Mongol and post-Mongol Iran, including
the time of Fad.l Allāh, various elements of this current can also be
found, in particular in the works of authors belonging or related to the
inﬂuential Kubrawī Suﬁtradition. The latter produced a messianic
ﬁgure very similar to Fad.l Allāh, namely Muh.ammad Nūrbakhsh (d.
869/1464).1 On the Shiʿi side, Nizārī Ismailism constitutes arguably
one of the most important channels through which the re-actualised
doctrines of early Shiʿi esotericism, re-shaped in the framework of the
messianic doctrine of qiyāma, spread in the post-Mongol mystical
circles. For these reasons, it seemed to me more productive to focus on
the above-mentioned trends in the second section of this chapter. This
section is concluded with a brief assessment of various possible
parallels to and inﬂuences on the central doctrinal themes of the
Jāwidān-nāma.
The third section contains some remarks on the contents of the
Jāwidān-nāma that could indicate Fad.l Allāh’s project of messianic
reorganisation of the Muslim community. These contents situate the
Jāwidān-nāma in line with the general tendency during the post-
Mongol era towards conciliation and uniﬁcation of various trends
within Islam and restoration of its universal ecumenical dimension,
1 On him, see S. Bashir, Messianic Hopes and Mystical Visions: the Nūrbakhshīya
between Medieval and Modern Islam (Columbia, SC, 2003).
Words of Power

which was arguably one of the most salient characteristics of the
mystical and messianic pattern of religious authority in that period. In
this perspective, the use of Christian apocalyptic texts, including the
canonical Revelation of John and the Arabic Apocalypse of Peter, is
particularly notable, and provides new evidence for the reﬂection on
the inﬂuence of these texts on the development of the Islamic
messianic discourse.
This attempt at contextualisation of the kind of thought represented
by the Jāwidān-nāma is followed by ﬁnal notes, focused on the future
directions and persepectives in the study of messianic movements in
Islam generally, and of the H. urūfīs in particular.
The Jāwidān-nāma as Qurʾānic Commentary
In the previous chapters, we have seen how deeply the Qurʾānic text
and the h. adīth material are woven into the discourse of the Jāwidān-
nāma. Muslim scriptural sources constitute the fundamental proof
texts for the Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrinal developments. It has also been
mentioned that the principle of Qurʾānic exegesis (taʾwīl) is the central
theme of the Jāwidān-nāma. This work interestingly combines some
features of the traditional Qurʾānic commentary genre with the
metaphysical theory of universal ontological hermeneutics, which
constitutes the core of Fad.l Allāh’s doctrine. Fad.l Allāh’s approach to
the Qurʾān commentary reﬂects the interaction between the Qurʾānic
revelation and Fad.l Allāh’s personal inspiration based on his mystical
experience.2 In a sense, the latter is presented as an extension of the
former: the extensive use of Qurʾānic citations and h. adīth material
frames Fad.l Allāh’s doctrinal views within the body of the Muslim
tradition. Fad.l Allāh’s concern to emphasise his adherence to the
traditionist current is also discernible behind the regular references to
Ah.mad b. H. anbal (d. 241/855), one of the few prominent ﬁgures of
Muslim religious thought explicitly mentioned in the Jāwidān-nāma.3
2 To some extent, this feature is characteristic of any mystical exegesis of the
Qurʾān. On the personal experience as hermeneutical principle, see L. Massignon,
Essai sur les origines du lexique technique de la mystique musulmane (Paris, 1922), and
P. Nwyia, Exégèse coranique et language mystique (Beirut, 1970).
3 On him, see C. Melchert, Ahmad ibn Hanbal (Oxford, 2006).
Conclusion

In several catalogues of manuscripts, the Jāwidān-nāma has been
described as a Qurʾānic commentary (tafsīr), and this description is
not entirely wrong.4 Indeed, many fragments of the Jāwidān-nāma
begin with a Qurʾānic verse, or a sequence of verses, followed by the
author’s explanations and interpretations. In some fragments, the
author’s personal input is reduced to a few words, the explanatory
function being fulﬁlled by a selection of h. adīths. The Iranian scholar
S.ādiq Kiyā, who had a thorough ﬁrst-hand knowledge of H. urūfī texts,
observed: ‘This book [i.e., the Jāwidān-nāma] is a Qurʾānic commen-
tary (tafsīr), written by Fad.l Allāh. His interpretation of the Qurʾānic
verses is original and reﬂects his vision of a particular mission that he
believed to be in charge of.’5
The originality of Fad.l Allāh’s approach to the interpretation of
scriptural sources relies most probably on his claim of direct
inspiration. This would explain why the Jāwidān-nāma contains no
explicit reference to previous Qurʾānic commentaries, which is
fundamental for classical works of this genre.6 The wealth of scriptural
material is used not to legitimise the proposed interpretation by a solid
chain of transmission linking it to the trustworthy sources, as in strict
traditionist style, but to express the intuition of Fad.l Allāh, his
individual understanding, which he presumably believed to be
inspired directly from the prophetic source. This direct inspiration
would dispense Fad.l Allāh from concern with legitimisation through
transmission and related issue of authenticity of the exegetical
traditions. His selection and interpretation of the Qurʾānic verses
and h. adīths is determined by his speciﬁc doctrinal views. In other
words, Fad.l Allāh does not merely interpret the prophetic revelation
contained in the Qurʾān and traditions deemed ‘trustworthy’
according to the criteria of h. adīth criticism, but rather uses the rich
symbolic language of the Revelation in order to convey his own

khat.t.ī-yi fārsī, 6 vols. (Tehran, 1349/1969), vol. 1, p. 1111: ‘tafsīrīst ʿirfānī-yi h. urūfī’.
5 Kiyā, Wāzha-nāma, p. 34 (my translation).

and Medieval’, in the Encyclopaedia of the Qurʾān, vol. 2, pp. 99–124.

inspiration. The latter, and not the h. adīth criticism, determines his
understanding of ‘authenticity’ of the material of tradition that he uses
in his work. This explains the amazing variety of traditions in the
Jāwidān-nāma.
Sunni and Shiʿi canonical h. adīths, apocrypha,
‘theophatic’ utterances attributed to ʿAlī b. Abī T. ālib, elements from
the ‘stories of the prophets’ and other materials, the sources of which
are sometimes difﬁcult to identify, are cited and combined most
generously, so far as they corroborate the doctrinal developments of
the author and provide him with eloquent symbolism.7 Scriptural
material still fulﬁls its legitimising function, but not exactly in the way
it is understood in the traditionist approach. The legitimacy, in the
sense of compatibility with Muh.ammad’s revelation, is based, in this
case, not on the formal criteria of authenticity, but on the fact that the
inspiration and mystical experience of Fad.l Allāh is perfectly
compatible and authentically expressed in the language of the
Islamic revelation.8
These particular characteristics bring the Jāwidān-nāma close to the
mystical conception of Qurʾānic exegesis. The latter includes the idea
that the Qurʾān can be understood progressively, on several levels,
disclosing its ever deeper meanings as the mystic progresses in his or
her effort to reproduce and to live through the prophetic experience.9
The interaction between personal experience and Qurʾānic revelation
is thus essential for mystical exegesis, as it is in the Jāwidān-nāma.10

Conclusion

Notwithstanding these common features, the speciﬁc nature of the
personal experience supposedly claimed by Fad.l Allāh somehow sets
the Jāwidān-nāma apart from the ordinary mystical Qurʾānic
commentaries. We have seen that, according to the accounts of his
followers, Fad.l Allāh received the revelation of the ultimate ontological
hermeneutics, the taʾwīl, enabling him to operate the ‘return’ of the
Qurʾānic revelation to its origin in the primordial divine Word. Unlike
any typical work of mystical exegesis, the Jāwidān-nāma does not deal
just with the interpretation of Qurʾānic verses from the point of view of
personal enlightenment and its degrees; it is also focused on the
expression of a speciﬁc doctrine of an absolute and universal taʾwīl in
the language of prophetic revelation, that is, through interpretation of
the scriptural sources.
This last feature characterises the Jāwidān-nāma as a work of taʾwīl,
understood not just as a commentary, but as a counterpart and
complement of tanzīl, of the Qurʾānic revelation regarded as the last
and most perfect realisation of the ‘descent’ of the eternal divine
Word.11 The idea that prophetic revelation, the tanzīl, or ‘descent’ of
the divine Word into a human language and its external (z.āhir)
manifestation, has to be completed by the taʾwīl, a ‘return’ ascending
back to the original source of the revelation and disclosing its
innermost (bāt.in) meaning, is one of the most fundamental tenets of
the Shiʿi worldview.12 The taʾwīl requires an inspiration close to the
prophetic, but instead of ‘descending’ in the form of an independent
prophetic book, as in the case of tanzīl, the taʾwīl operates the ultimate
hermeneutics of the previously revealed prophetic book. The power of
the taʾwīl is one of the characteristics attributed to the Shiʿi Imāms,
who beneﬁt also from a permanent link with the source of the
prophetic revelation, resulting from their particular closeness to God

meaning of the Revelation.13
There is some evidence in H. urūfī literature which suggests that the
Jāwidān-nāma was, if not originally conceived by its author, at least
perceived by his followers as a book of taʾwīl, in the sense described
above. In the Introduction, we have seen that one of the honoriﬁc
names Fad.l Allāh was referred to by his followers was s.āh. ib al-taʾwīl,
‘Master of the taʾwīl’. This is mentioned in fragment of the anonymous
note containing the plan of six chapters or ‘beginnings’ of the Jāwidān-
nāma that has been discussed in the Introduction:
The Master of the taʾwīl [i. e., Fad.l Allāh] has founded the divine
Jāwidān-nāma upon six ‘beginnings’. From the beginning to the
end, the discourse of the divine Jāwidān-nāma is divided and
contained within these six ‘beginnings’, and sealed by them. In
the same manner, the inimitable word of the Master of the tanzīl
[i. e., the Qurʾān revealed to the Prophet Muh.ammad, the ‘Seal of
the Prophets’] contains 29 suras introduced by the combinations
of the disjointed letters, and is divided into 29 parts, which are the
treasure sealed by the disjointed letters (481b).
If, as suggested by this citation, Fad.l Allāh’s followers regarded him as
a ‘Master of the taʾwīl’, this would explain also a certain degree of
sacredness that they apparently attributed to Fad.l Allāh’s writings.
However, with the possible exception of some ‘extremist’ H. urūfī
groups, it is unlikely that the Jāwidān-nāma was regarded, either by
Fad.l Allāh himself or by his followers, as the sacred text of a new
prophetic
dispensation.

Jāwidān-nāma’s interpretations of biblical material corroborate the

citations from the Qurʾān and the h. adīth is most probably intended as
a tacit argument in favour of the universal validity of Fad.l Allāh’s

component of Fad.l Allāh’s thought. In fact, the absolute and ﬁnal
disclosing of the innermost levels of the Qurʾānic revelation, addressed
not only to the Muslim community but to entire mankind, echoing the

features of the eschatological Saviour, particularly emphasised in Shiʿi

the New Testaments, and of some Christian apocryphal literature.22

That Fad.l Allāh had direct knowledge of canonical biblical texts is

refer to the Torah or the Gospel (Injīl). It is noteworthy that the
canonical biblical texts and apocrypha are mostly cited in Persian in
the Jāwidān-nāma. Persian translations of at least some biblical texts
should have been available at the time of Fad.l Allāh;23 and it is
perfectly possible that, during his travels, he established personal
contacts with Jewish and/or Christian circles where such translations
were produced. However, some citations of biblical and apocryphal
texts in Arabic found in the Jāwidān-nāma24 suggest that Fad.l Allāh
could have translated or paraphrased these texts himself from the
wealth of biblical material largely available in Arabic at his time. The
question remains why he does not cite the biblical texts consistently in
Arabic, as he does with the h. adīths and Qurʾānic citations.

theory of language and writing and mystical anthropology, have close
parallels in Jewish and Christian mysticism.25 Of course, by the time of

The Jāwidān-nāma, Suﬁsm and Esoteric Shiʿism
The Mongol and post-Mongol period was marked by a signiﬁcant
rapprochement between various Islamic currents and the emergence
of synthetic systems of thought.26 The emergence and increasing
power of organised Suﬁsm, with its veneration for the person of ʿAlī b.
Abī T. ālib and the family of the Prophet, fostered the rapprochement
between Suﬁsm and Shiʿism. This process was further accelerated by
the input of the Nizārī Ismailis who, after the destruction of their
strongholds by the Mongols, tended to blend in with Suﬁs.27 This
resulted in the emergence of forms of mysticism for which the Sunni/
Shiʿi difference seems hardly relevant.
The Jāwidān-nāma is a work produced in this context of synthesis
and eclecticism. It incorporates several intellectual and theological
currents, including Sunni and Shiʿi traditionalism and mysticism. It
Corbin, En Islam Iranien, vol. 3, p. 252 and note 72. However striking the parallels, the
concrete evidence is difﬁcult to pin down.

also includes elements of ‘occult’ sciences, such as alchemy, astrology
and, of course, the science of letters and numbers, which became the
hallmark of H. urūﬁsm. The Neoplatonic aspects of the Jāwidān-nāma’s
cosmology coexist with the normative discourse of jurisprudence
(ﬁqh). References to Ah.mad ibn H. anbal do not exclude examples of
metaphorical interpretations of the anthropomorphic vocabulary of
the Qurʾān associated with the Jahmites and Muʿtazilites. The
Jāwidān-nāma clearly formulates its position concerning such general
theological issues as the eternity of divine attributes, or the createdness
of the Qurʾān. But the Jāwidān-nāma is not just a synthesis: the free
and creative use of scriptural sources, and an original approach to the
rich intellectual and literary heritage of various currents of Muslim
theology and mysticism form a unique multilayered technical
language, which conveys the original doctrine of Fad.l Allāh based
on his personal mystical experience.
From this point of view, the Jāwidān-nāma continues the tradition
of eclecticism in Islam, in line with thinkers and groups such as al-
H. akīm al-Tirmidhī (d. after 318/936), the Ikhwān al-S.afāʾ, Shihāb al-
Dīn al-Suhrawardī (d. 587/1191) and Ibn al-ʿArabī (d. 638/1240), who
creatively integrated, synthesised and reworked any material useful for
the development of their original outlook, disregarding inter-
confessional and inter-sectarian barriers.28
Notwithstanding this essentially eclectic character of the Jāwidān-
nāma, a discussion of the proportion in which elements of various
religious trends have been combined and integrated to produce this
speciﬁc doctrine can be useful in order to better understand the place
of the Jāwidān-nāma in the intellectual landscape of its time. This can
also shed some more light at the still relatively obsure issue of the Suﬁ/
Shiʿi relationships during the Mongol and early post-Mongol periods,
and the forms of survival of esoteric Shiʿism, in particular in its Ismaili
branch, during that turbulent time. As noted at the beginning of this
Conclusion, a systematic analysis of the textual markers revealing the

The Concept of Sainthood in Early Islamic Mysticism; I. R. Netton, Muslim

Conclusion

inﬂuence of speciﬁc lines of Islamic religious thought on the doctrinal
developments of the Jāwidān-nāma is still to be attempted. The
purpose of the present section is, therefore, limited to a preliminary
discussion in anticipation of a more thorough analysis.
At the beginning of this section, I will focus on the Suﬁaspects of the
Jāwidān-nāma. The possible inﬂuence of esoteric Shiʿism, most
probably through the Nizārī Ismaili channel, will be discussed in the
second part. A short discussion of the possible Suﬁand Shiʿi inﬂuences
on the central doctrinal themes of the Jāwidān-nāma concludes this
section.
Any assessment of the Suﬁinﬂuence on a religious movement of the
8th/14th century cannot bypass the towering ﬁgure of Ibn al-ʿArabī. It
is certainly possible that Fad.l Allāh studied Ibn al-ʿArabī’s works, since
almost all central doctrinal developments of the Jāwidān-nāma have
close parallels in the comprehensive thought of the Shaykh al-Akbar.
However, the exact extent of Ibn al-ʿArabī’s inﬂuence seems difﬁcult to
assess because only few explicit traces of the typically Akbarian
technical vocabulary can be found in the Jāwidān-nāma.29 We will see
some examples of this vocabulary in the following pages. In addition,
even if the Jāwidān-nāma often echoes the themes of Ibn al-ʿArabī’s
mystical thought, it rarely adopts them directly; they are cast in the
mould of the speciﬁc doctrinal context of this work.
One of the most important doctrinal developments of Ibn al-ʿArabī
that could have had a substantial inﬂuence not only on some particular
chapters of the Jāwidān-nāma, but also on the general messianic
orientation of this work and, subsequently, on the socio-political
involvement of the H. urūfīs, is Ibn al-ʿArabī’s theory of sainthood and
its Seal (khātam al-awliyāʾ).30 Let us note that, although not found in
the Jāwidān-nāma, the terms ‘second Seal’ (khātam-i thānī), and ‘Seal

lingua franca and does not necessarily prove an immediate and speciﬁc inﬂuence. See
Chodkiewicz, Un océan sans rivage, p. 22 ff.

More particularly, Ibn al-ʿArabī’s ideas on the relationship between
the saintly and properly prophetic quality of a prophet, in the
interpretation they received in some mystical circles, could be
recognised in the statement found in fol. 232a of the Jāwidān-nāma:
Concerning prophecy (nubuwwa) and sainthood (walāya), the
seekers of truth (muh. aqqiqān) and those ‘rooted in knowledge’
(rāsikhān-i ʿilm) [Q. 3:7] uphold that the saintly quality of a
prophet (walāyat-i nabī) is superior to his prophetic quality
(nubuwwat-i nabī), in virtue [of Muh.ammad’s utterance]: ‘I have
a time with God when I am not attended either by any angel
brought near nor by a Messenger-prophet’32 (232a).
This passage refers to the thorny issue of superiority of sainthood over
prophethood (tafd.īl al-walīʿalā-l-nabī), present and much discussed in
Islamic mysticism, Sunni as well as Shiʿi, from early times.33 The focus
on the saintly and properly prophetic quality of a prophet seems close
to the formulations of Ibn al-ʿArabī.34 Among the thinkers linked with
the Kubrawī Suﬁcircles, this issue was emphasised, in particular, by
Saʿd al-Dīn al-H. ammū’ī (7th/13th century) and, probably with closer
reference to Ibn al-ʿArabī’s statements concerning the saintly and
properly prophetic sides of a prophet, by ʿAzīz-i Nasafī (d. ca. 700/
1300).35 On the Shiʿi side, Fad.l Allāh’s contemporary H. aydar Amulī
maintained the superiority of the walāya over both nubuwwa and
risāla, emphasising that this does not mean that walī is superior to the

An interesting point related to the topic of relationship between
sainthood and prophethood is the association of sainthood with the
return of the divine Word to its metaphysical Origin (taʾwīl), after its
descent into the physical world (tanzīl) has been completed by the
prophets. This idea is expressed, for example, in the already mentioned
passage from the Mis.bāh. fī-l-tas.awwuf by al-H. ammūʾī.38 In a work of
another author belonging to the Kubrawī line, Nūr al-Dīn al-Isfarāyinī
(d. 717/1317), the ‘returning’ part of the cycle is associated with the
heavenly ascension (miʿrāj) of the Prophet Muh.ammad.39 This implies
that the divine message transmitted to, or ‘descended upon’
Muh.ammad by the intermediary of the archangel Gabriel constitutes
his properly prophetic mission, while the heavenly ascension, bringing
him up to the source of the divine Word, into the region where Gabriel
cannot follow him, corresponds to the saintly dimension of
Muh.ammad’s prophethood. In Chapter 10, we have seen that exactly
the same idea emerges from the Jāwidān-nāma’s fragments. There is

It seems that Ibn al-ʿArabī’s ideas concerning the Seals of
prophethood and sainthood inspired some latently messianic devel-
opments in the period immediately preceding the formulation of Fad.l
Allāh’s doctrine. For example, the writings of ʿAzīz-i Nasafī contain
views close to a quasi prophetic or messianic claim.40 This speciﬁc line
of development and interpretation of Ibn al-ʿArabī’s doctrine could,
therefore, have contributed to the preparation of more straightforwad
manifestations of messianism as that represented by Fad.l Allāh.
We have seen that the Jāwidān-nāma maintains a certain ambiguity
as to the identity of the eschatological Saviour, the Mahdī, in an
apparent attempt to reconcile the traditional Sunni views, which
ascribe this role to Jesus, and the Shiʿi belief that the Mahdī/Qāʾim will
be a descendant of Fāt.ima in the line of the Shiʿi Imāms.41 This
ambiguity can partially be explained by the ambiguity of the Muslim
eschatological traditions themselves.42 But it can also be a result of the
juxtaposition of Ibn al-ʿArabī’s theories concerning the Seal of
Sainthood and traditional Shiʿi beliefs.43 It seems that a similar
hesitation about the identity of the Mahdī can be discerned in the
thought of some authors belonging to the Kubrawī Suﬁtradition.

works that the Mahdī will be the 12th and the last of the awliyāʾ, while

It should be noted that a combination of the canonical Sunni h. adīth

Some more speciﬁc similarities between the Suﬁdoctrines (mainly
those of Ibn al-ʿArabī, Saʿd al-Dīn al-H. ammūʾī and ʿAzīz-i Nasafī) and
the contents of the Jāwidān-nāma will be discussed further below,
where we will turn to speciﬁc doctrinal topics.
Another inﬂuence clearly visible in the Jāwidān-nāma is that of the
‘school of Persian mystical poetry’ which, at the time of Fad.l Allāh, was
most prominently represented by the works of such authors as Sanāʾī
Ghaznawī (d. 525/1131), Farīd al-Dīn ʿAt.t.ār (d. end of the 6th/12th or
beginning of the 7th/13th century), Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī (d. 672/1273),
Saʿadī Shīrāzī (d. 691/1292) and H. āﬁz. Shīrāzī (d. 792/1390 or 791/
1389).47 It will be recalled that, according to his biographers, Fad.l
Allāh’s spiritual quest began following an emotional crisis introduced
by a verse of Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī, accidentially heard from a wandering
dervish. We have further seen that the technical vocabulary of Persian
mystical poetry is used extensively in the Jāwidān-nāma. The speciﬁc

The Jāwidān-nāma could have been produced either in a Suﬁmilieu
impregnated by Shiʿi ideas, or vice versa. In fact, the evidence pointing
in the direction of esoteric Shiʿi roots of this work seems to be
predominant. At the time of Fad.l Allāh, the integration of Suﬁideas
and language was ongoing in both major branches of Iranian Shiʿism,
the Ismaili and the Twelver. The Ismaili rapprochement with Suﬁsm
was intensiﬁed in the period following the destruction of Ismaili
strongholds by the Mongols, and subsequent persecution of the
Ismaili community.50 On the Twelver side, the integration of Suﬁ
inﬂuence, signiﬁcantly fostered by the works of Ibn al-ʿArabī, was
accompanied by a return to the sources of early esoteric Shiʿism. At the
time of Fad.l Allāh, this tendency was most eminently represented by
H. aydar Amulī (d. after 787/1385), who was not only an older
contemporary of Fad.l Allāh, but also lived and worked in the same

Allāh had a connection with the Ismailis through his family.59 The
plan of organisation of the Jāwidān-nāma in six chapters or
‘beginnings’, in accordance with six days of creation,60 has parallels
in Ismaili literature.61 Most importantly, some central doctrinal lines
of the Jāwidān-nāma, in particular the speciﬁc kind of the ‘science of
letters’ used in this work, have close analogies in Ismaili thought.62
The doctrine of kalima as direct emanation of the divine Essence is a
strong argument in favour of Ismaili inﬂuence.63 The same can be said
concerning the ontological role of language; the distinction between
metaphysical knowledge and blind imitation; the earth as the most
noble element and centre of the creation; and many other topics of the
Jāwidān-nāma.64 There are also more speciﬁc details that very
probably point in the direction of Ismaili inﬂuence, such as the cyclic
manifestations of prophets by the series of seven.65 This explains why
the thesis of Ismaili inspiration of the Jāwidān-nāma, albeit in a much
more attenuated formulations than in the citations of Browne and
Ivanow above, has continued to be maintained in modern scholarship.

In substance, H. urūﬁsm is still an expression of Ismaʿilism, in the
sense that the theological terms deﬁning it on the religious plane

Some doctrinal features of the Jāwidān-nāma, and more exactly a
characteristic combination of speciﬁc features, brings it close to the
doctrine developed by the Nizārī Ismaili community of Iran. For

manifestation of metaphysical truths (h. aqāʾiq) of the original divine
Word, and subsequent ecumenical tendency based on the idea that
these truths, made available through messianic disclosure, are
addressed to the entire humankind, seem to be in line with the doctrine
developed at Alamūt immediately before the Mongol invasion; and so is
the strongly emphasised anthropocentrism of the Jāwidān-nāma.68 It

doctrine that the divine Word is the ﬁrst emanation of the otherwise

manifestation, and that any existing being and object is essentally a

the central position of earth and its relation to the realisation of

Browne doubt his ﬁrst conclusion about the purely Ismaili afﬁliation of
the H. urūfīs:
This harping on the number 7 and its multiples, together with the
prominence given to the doctrine and method of taʾwīl, or
allegorical interpretation, disposed me to regard the H. urūfīs as a
branch of the old Ismaʿīlīs, or ‘Sect of the Seven’. But I am bound
to say that a poem of Nesīmī’s . . . devoted to the praise of the
Twelve Imāms recognized by Shiʿites of the ‘Sect of the Twelve’, is
a strong argument against this view.83
A closer scrutiny of the Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrines does not allow us to
unambiguously identify the predominant source of its Shiʿi inspira-
tion. It appears that the Jāwidān-nāma drew on an ancient stock of
traditions, beliefs and doctrines of esoteric Shiʿism, common to both
the Ismaili and Twelver branches. This scriptural and doctrinal
material is creatively reworked, cast in original concepts and integrated
into Fad.l Allāh’s speciﬁc theoretical framework. In this process, traces
of particular channels – Ismaili, Twelver or others – through which
this material of esoteric Shiʿism reached Fad.l Allāh seem to be either
lost or intentionally removed. The following pages contain, by the way
of example, some preliminary notes and observations concerning Shiʿi
and/or Suﬁparallels to the Jāwidān-nāma’s approach to some central
doctrinal topics.
The Science of Letters and Taʾwīl
The 8th/14th and 9th/15th centuries witnessed an amazing expansion
of various versions of the Islamic ‘science of letters’ (ʿilm al-h. urūf), in
the Sunni and the Shiʿi intellectual circles alike.84 As mentioned in the
previous section, by the time of Fad.l Allāh, the ‘science of letters’ had

by the Fāt.imid scholar Qād.ī al-Nuʿman.89 The characteristic numbers

Another aspect of the H. urūfī science of letters strongly suggesting
an Ismaili inﬂuence is its link with the conception of taʾwīl.91 In the
Shiʿi context, taʾwīl refers to a particular kind of hermeneutics of the
prophetic books, in particular the Qurʾān. This hermeneutics is
regarded not as a purely intellectual or literary exercise but, in
accordance with the etymological meaning of the word taʾwīl, as an
operation that brings the words of the Qurʾān back to the source of the
prophetic inspiration, where their original meanings belong. The same
operation can be applied to any other Scripture, and even to any object
or being considered as a ‘word’ in the great Book of the creation. The
operation of taʾwīl, understood in this speciﬁc sense, requires a special
power or knowledge, fully possessed, in the Shiʿi perspective, only by
the Imāms. The link between this special power of taʾwīl and the
knowledge of the ontological ‘science of letters’, suggested in the Shiʿi
h. adīth literature, was most thoroughly developed in Ismaili thought.
The interpretation of the Qurʾān based on the symbolic meanings
ascribed to the letters of the alphabet and their numerical values was
regarded as one of the hallmarks of Ismaili taʾwīl. The Jāwidān-nāma
contains similar theoretical developments based on letters and
numbers, which could point in the direction of an Ismaili channel of
transmission of the stock of ideas related to the concept of the taʾwīl
common for esoteric Shiʿism in general.92 As mentioned above, the

The Human Being as Locus of Manifestation of the Divine Word
and the Doctrine of Imamate
The idea of manifestation of the knowable aspect of the divinity in the
human ﬁgure is one of the central themes of early Shiʿi esotericism.
This idea is essential for the deﬁnition of the ontological status of the
Imām, who is regarded, in his archetypal, cosmic dimension, as the
locus of manifestation of the divine attributes or, in other words, as the
representation of the revealed aspect of God, Deus Revelatus.93 A
similar conception in Suﬁmysticism was focused on the perfect
human being (al-insān al-kāmil), which occupied a central place in the
thought of Ibn al-ʿArabī.94 There are numerous doctrinal parallels
between the Jāwidān-nāma and the works of such authors, already
work is at best illustrative. As we have seen in Parts Two and Three, the Jāwidān-
nāma’s doctrine of taʾwīl cannot be reduced to numerology.

an explicit link between the perfect human being and the Imām. The
former is usually represented by the original couple Adam/Eve. The
thesis that the human being is the most perfect locus of manifestation
of the divine Word is developed mostly with reference to ‘neutral’
scriptural material, including the Qurʾān and the h. adīth used in both
Suﬁand Shiʿi circles. In addition, the Suﬁand, more speciﬁcally,
Akbarian term insān-i kāmil occurs in several fragments of the
Jāwidān-nāma.
A closer examination, however, shows several traces pointing in the
direction of Shiʿi doctrines. It should be noted that a synthesis of Ibn
al-ʿArabī’s doctrine of the perfect human and the Twelver Shiʿi
doctrine was realised in the works of H. aydar Amulī, whom Fad.l Allāh
might have met in person.96 The revelation of the divine ontological
writing contained in the human form, which makes possible the
perception of the latter as the locus of manifestation of the complete
divine Word, is realised in the Jāwidān-nāma by the ‘motherly’
(ummī) prophets and saints, and is closely related to the operation of
taʾwīl. In Chapters 10 and 13 we have seen that the Jāwidān-nāma
establishes a link between ummis and imāms, two words derived from
the same Arabic root ʾmm. These features bring the Jāwidān-nāma
close to the views developed in Nizārī Ismaili doctrines, such as
expressed in the Rawd.a-yi taslīm.
The Jāwidān-nāma’s approach to the issue of the perfect human
being and the possibility of attaining the corresponding level of
knowledge is, therefore, to be located somewhere between the properly
Suﬁand Shiʿi interpretations.
95 See Meier, ‘Die Schriften des ʿAzīz-i Nasafī’, p. 132, and his ‘Das Problem der
Natur’, pp. 149–227.
96 On H. aydar Amulī’s ideas related to the perfect human being, see C. Jambet,
Qu’est-ce que la philosophie islamique? (Paris, 2011), pp. 306–328.
Conclusion

The Myth of the Fall
The ‘myth of the fall’, including the degradation of humans from their
original rank in the cosmic hierarchy and their subsequent return
through salutary knowledge, is one of the central elements of the
Gnostic Weltanschauung.97 In Islam, the ‘myth of the fall’ is part of
several, mostly Shiʿi, cosmological theories.98 In particular, it plays a
pivotal role in early Ismaili literature.99 The Jāwidān-nāma also
contains a version of the ‘myth of the fall’, but it is developed mostly
with reference to Qurʾānic material100 and does not contain any trace
of the Neoplatonic interpretation characteristic of Ismaili works.
The Jāwidān-nāma’s version of the Fall is based on the alchemical
relationship between earth, the element related to form and know-
ledge, which is also the principal component of the human body, and
ﬁre, the element associated with Satan and ignorance. Let us recall
from Chapter 12 that the Jāwidān-nāma’s interpretation of the
Qurʾānic story of Adam and Eve’s expulsion from Paradise, caused by
the suggestions of Satan, emphasises the role of ﬁre covering the faces
and bodies of Adam and Eve, and thus veiling from them the
innermost meaning of the human bodily form and facial features.
Since the human form and face constitute the locus of manifestation of
the divine Word, they contain knowledge that in itself constitutes the
condition of Paradise. Therefore, the ﬁre that covers and veils this
knowledge leads to Hell of ignorance.
I was unable to ﬁnd close parallels to the Jāwidān-nāma’s
description of the Fall. However, the Jāwidān-nāma’s fragments
related to the salutary knowledge by means of which it is possible to
redeem the effects of the Fall and restore the original human

Ethics (New York and Edinburgh, 1914), vol. 6, pp. 231–242.
98 Different versions of the ‘myth of the fall’ and subsequent strife for redemption
are present in the texts related to the early ghulāt tradition, such as Umm al-kitāb and
Kitāb al-az.illa, in the Nus.ayrī and Druze literature. See H. Halm, Die islamische Gnosis
(Zurich and Munich, 1982), pp. 113–198 and 240–274; R. Freitag, Seelenwanderung in
der islamischen Häresie (Berlin, 1985), p. 47 ff.; and Friedman, The Nus.ayrī-ʿAlawīs,
pp. 96–101.
99 See Halm, Kosmologie und Heilslehre, pp. 110–114, and H. Corbin, Temps
cyclique et gnose ismaélienne (Paris, 1982), p. 47 ff.
100 For the relevant Qurʾānic material, see Johns, ‘Fall of Man’.

condition, display both Suﬁand Shiʿi features. The possibility of
salvation through self-knowledge and love has a Suﬁcolouration. But
we have also seen that, according to the Jāwidān-nāma, the most
fundamental condition of redemption and return to the original
condition of Paradise is the ‘return to the Mother’ and realisation of
‘motherly’ knowledge. This is achieved either through individual
effort, or under the guidance of the ‘motherly’ (ummī) prophets and
saints. This brings us again to the possible link between the Jāwidān-
nāma’s ummīs and the Shiʿi Imāms. If the Jāwidān-nāma’s conception
of the ‘motherly’ knowledge is inspired by the Shiʿi idea of initiatory
knowledge held by the Imāms, then its description of salvation can be
considered as a reformulation of the Shiʿi idea of salvation through the
teachings of the Imāms. The latter doctrine, though essential for
Shiʿism in general, was particularly emphasised in the Nizārī doctrine
of qiyāma, and should have remained inﬂuential in Iranian Ismailism
at the time of Fad.l Allāh.
Evolution and Transmigration
In Islam, the doctrines of transmigration apparently emerged ﬁrst in
the Shiʿi milieus, but various kinds of transmigration theories were
developed afterwards also in philosophical and Suﬁcircles.101 The
doctrines of transmigration, or metempsychosis, usually imply that an
entity or substance, like soul, spirit, light or other, is preserved after the
demise of the physical body and transmitted into the body of the next
life. The Jāwidān-nāma contains only few scattered traces of such a
kind of transmigration theory. The typical terminology used in the
Islamic context regarding transmigration and its particular kinds, such
as tanāsukh, intiqāl, takrīr, naskh, maskh, raskh, faskh, etc., is not
found in the Jāwidān-nāma. The developments closest to a theory of
transmigration seem to be associated in the Jāwidān-nāma with the
term idrāk, pl. idrākāt, ‘aperception, impression’. The most explicit
formulation of the idea that the idrākāt survive the death of the
physical body is found in the following fragment:
101 The most comprehensive overview of the theories of transmigration in Islam is
Freitag’s Seelenwanderung.
Conclusion

It is ﬁrmly established that aperception (idrāk) constitutes the
innermost reality (h. aqīqa) of humans. The aperception is
composite (murakkab). In the world of Recompense (ʿālam-i
jazāʾ), to any composite (entity) [corresponds] an imperishable,
indestructible and self-sufﬁcient (bi-nafs-i khūd qāʾim ast) mark
(naqsh). When [the soul? spirit? aperception?] leaves the body, it
will see the marks it acquired [during its lifetime] in this
[physical] world, and will be identiﬁed with them (ān naqsh-hā-
rā ki darīn ʿālam kasb karda ast khwāhad [dīd wa]102 ū khūd ān
khwāhad būd).
This fragment is problematic for several reasons. First, I was unable to
ﬁnd it in three of the four manuscripts of the Jāwidān-nāma available
to me.103 In the manuscript of the British Library Oc.Or. 5957, it is
placed in the folio preceding the beginning of the main text, under the
title Masʾala, with another fragment that will be cited further below.
Secondly, this fragment is written entirely in standard Persian, without
any trace of the Astarābādī dialect characteristic of many fragments of
the Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr. And ﬁnally, it apparently alludes to a well
elaborated doctrine of transmigration, which does not seem to be
developed in other fragments of the Jāwidān-nāma. These arguments
introduce some doubt as to whether the fragment cited above is an
authentic part of the Jāwidān-nāma.
But there are also some counter-arguments. In the manuscript of
the British Library, both fragments under the title Masʾala begin with
Bismi-l-lāhi-r-rah. māni-r-rahīm, as do most of the regular fragments of
the Jāwidān-nāma. Another fragment included in the Masʾala with the
fragment cited above concerns a topic discussed in many other
passages of the Jāwidān-nāma. The Masʾala is followed by a short
note, which says that the two fragments it contains were written ‘on
the back of the eternal divine book’ (īn dū nāma-yi qadīm-i jāwidānī
bar z.ahr-i kitāb-i qadīm-i khudāʾī būd). Even if the theory of
transmigration related to the idrākāt does not seem to be system-
atically developed in the main text of the Jāwidān-nāma, the term
idrāk, pl. idrākāt occurs in several fragments, sometimes in the context
close to that of the fragment cited above. Finally, Sayyid Ish.āq

nāma of Sayyid Ish.āq Astarābādī, which will be mentioned further below.
103 Cambridge Ee.1.27, Istanbul Ali Emiri Farsi 920, and Basel M.VI.72.
Words of Power

Astarābādī cites this fragment in his Mah. ram-nāma, with an explicit
reference to the Jāwidān-nāma, together with some notes:
It is well-known that human consciousness (shuʿūr) and
awareness (agāhī) persist (muqarrar) after the destruction of
the [physical] body (kharābī-yi badan). Aperceptions (idrākāt)
and actions (aʿmāl) of the humans [accumulated during their
lifetime] appear [then in the other] world [as] marks (nuqūsh), as
[it is mentioned by Fad.l Allāh], izza fad.lah, in the divine
Jāwidān-nāma . . . [here follows the text of the fragment cited
above]. Nobody among God’s servants has a detailed knowledge
concerning the quality of these aperceptions and actions, and the
corresponding shapes and marks to which they will lead every
particular person [in the Hereafter], with the exception of the
Master of ontological hermeneutics (s.āh. ib-i taʾwīl), who has a
perfect knowledge [in this ﬁeld].104
The ‘stray’ fragment from the Jāwidān-nāma and the passage from the
Mah. ram-nāma suggest a theory of transmigration, especially if it can
be supposed that the shapes (shakl, pl. ashkāl) and ‘marks’ (naqsh, pl.
nuqūsh) mentioned in these texts refer to the bodily form of the next
birth. Such an extrapolation seems to be indirectly supported by the
idea of correspondence between the external form (s.ūra) and inner
ontological reality (maʿnā, h. aqīqa), which is essential to the Jāwidān-
nāma. Since the bodily form of human beings is, in the Jāwidān-nāma,
the locus of manifestation (maz.har), or ‘science’, of the complete
divine Word, it is possible that the term ‘aperception’ (idrāk, pl.
idrākāt) refers, in the fragments cited above, to the degree of
knowledge of the external form attained during the lifetime. The
perfect knowledge of the innermost meaning of the human form
corresponds then to the ontological perception of the human form in
the Hereafter; but if this knowledge is not fully realised then, in the
‘world of Recompense’ it will be brought in balance with the cor-
responding formal aspect, and receive the ‘mark’ of a body expressing a
lesser amount of knowledge than human, that is animal, vegetal or
mineral. But let us repeat that such a development is only suggested,
and does not seem to be clearly formulated in the Jāwidān-nāma.
104 Astarābādī, Mah. ram-nāma, in Huart, Textes persans, pp. 41–42 of the
Persian text.
Conclusion

If a theory of transmigration of this kind was indeed part of Fad.l
Allāh’s doctrine, it could have been inspired by the Shiʿi gnostic
currents.105 The focus on the ‘aperceptions’, related to ﬁxed ‘marks’
and ‘shapes’ in the ‘world of Recompense’, identiﬁed in several other
fragments of the Jāwidān-nāma with the ‘world of [archetypal]
Images’ (ʿālam al-mithāl) could also point in the direction of Shihāb
al-Dīn Yah.yā Suhrawardī and his followers, though the characteristic
terminology of the Ishrāqī school is not apparent in the Jāwidān-
nāma.106 The same features bring the conception of transmigration of
the Jāwidān-nāma in line with the doctrine of metamorphosis in the
intermediary world of Images developed, in particular, under the
inﬂuence of Ishrāqī thought, by Mullā S.adrā Shīrāzī (d. 1050/1640).107
Signiﬁcantly, the Rawd.a-yi taslīm mentioned above, also contains
some passages on ‘imaginal soul’ and ‘imaginal body’ which survive
the death of the physical body.108
More explicitly formulated in the Jāwidān-nāma is a theory of
evolution and involution of forms, which has been addressed in
Chapters 4 and 6. As it stands, this theory can hardly be characterised
as a doctrine of metempsychosis or transmigration. The fundamental
idea that makes possible the tranformation of forms in the Jāwidān-
nāma is the thesis that all created forms are essentially the loci of
manifestation of metaphysical meanings or truths, which constitute
the original divine Word. The correspondence between a material
form and a metaphysical truth is ensured by the ‘line of balance’, which
runs throughout the universe and is present in every existent form,
from minerals to humans. The difference between the bodily forms of

pp. 102–110.

existents is therefore only quantitative: from minerals, through
vegetals and animals, the capacity to express the metaphysical truths
of the divine Word increases, and reaches its limit in the human bodily
form, which is the locus of manifestation of the complete Word. We
have seen that, in the Jāwidān-nāma, the cosmic human form is
identical to the outer sphere encompassing the universe; more
particularly, the body of Adam is earth, both as natural element and
as planet. Therefore, all inhabitants of the earth, including the mineral,
vegetal and animal realms, are literally parts of the human body,
because their bodily forms express a part of the metaphysical truth that
is fully represented by the human form, and because they are all
generated on earth and return to earth, which is the body of Adam. It
is in this sense that the Jāwidān-nāma states that every object and
being on earth has the aptitude to become a part of the human body. It
is interesting that a fragment expressing these ideas is included in the
same Masʾala as the fragment suggesting a more explicit doctrine of
transmigration that we cited and discussed above. Could this
combination of fragments indicate a link between the Jāwidān-
nāma’s theory of transformations and a less explicit doctrine of
transmigration? The text of this second fragment of the Masʾala which,
unlike the ﬁrst, expresses the ideas well developed in the main body of
fragments, is as follows:109
The existence (hastī) of anything [composed] of earth, water, air
and ﬁre, of heavens and stars, and of the physical world (mulk)
[in general] consists of the divine Word (kalima-yi khudāyast).
All [these entities] are created by the Word and in accordance
[with the structure] of the Word (bar-mithāl-i kalima-and). [For
this reason], in the world of dreams (khwāb), visions (wāqiʿa) and
spiritual disclosure (kashf), they are seen as speaking, hearing,
seeing and walking. [In that world], it can be seen that every atom
speaks and hears. Therefore, every atom from the circles of
existence (dawāʾir-i wujūd) has the possibility to become a
human being (insān). At the moments of inspiration (wāqiʿa), it
is possible to see that the body members of a person speak to this
person, [as if every member] were a separate human being. Since,
from the perspective of their innermost reality (az rū-yi h. aqīqa),
every existing thing is a part of Adam, and Adam [encompasses]
109 In fact, this fragment is the ﬁrst one, preceding the fragment on the idrākāt
cited above.
Conclusion

all [that exists], in the world of spiritual disclosure it is possible to
see that any particular [object or being] is the body (wujūd) of
Adam, and it is possible to see Adam [in] everything.
We have seen in Chapters 4 and 6 that this capacity to constitute a part
of the human body is realised through the food chain, when a mineral,
plant or animal is consumed by a human being. Similar developments
concerning the transformations in the food chain can be found in the
Risāla al-jāmiʿa, included in the Rasāʾil Ikhwān al-S.afāʾ, and in the
works of the Yemenite Ismailis.110 A hint on transmigration can be
seen in the fragments that specify the transformation of food into
sperm. By the intermediary of sperm, minerals, plants and animals can
acquire a human bodily form and be reborn as humans. A particularly
interesting aspect of this theory of transformation in the food chain is
its link with the sacriﬁce of animals. In Chapter 4, we have seen that,
according to the Jāwidān-nāma, animal sacriﬁce is a means by which
human beings integrate animals into human bodily form, thus giving
them access to the superior knowledge of the divine Word and,
therefore, to salvation. The link between transformations in the food
chain and progress in salutary knowledge can also be found in the
Rawd.a-yi taslīm, the primary source on Nizārī Ismaili doctrine men-
tioned several times in the preceding pages. The Rawd.a’s doctrine
concerning the different kinds of ‘submissions’ seems particularly
close to the Jāwidān-nāma’s conception of transformation and related
theme of salutary knowledge.111
Further connections made in the Jāwidān-nāma between animal
sacriﬁce and sacriﬁce of the lower self (nafs) have a Suﬁcolouration. In
addition to the work of Sayyid Ish.āq Astarābādī mentioned above, the

Words of Power

Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrine of transmigration apparently was also
developed by another of his followers, Mah.mūd Pasīkhānī, founder
of the Nuqt.awī offshoot, which was particularly active in Mughal
India.112 This is also reﬂected in the fact that the Nuqt.awīs were
referred to as the ‘adepts of transmigration’ (ahl-i tanāsukh). However,
a detailed study of Pasīkhānī’s writings is still to be done.
With the exception of the role attributed to the food chain, the
Jāwidān-nāma’s theory of evolution and involution of forms seems to
share many common features with similar views of ʿAzīz-i Nasafī.113
As in the Jāwidān-nāma, Nasafī’s ideas concerning the topic of
transformation and transmigration are based on the afﬁrmation of the
unity of existence.114 This parallelism is emphasised by the choice of
proof texts. In his reﬂection on the unity of existence, Nasafī refers to
an utterance from the Nahj al-balāgha attributed to ʿAlī b. Abī T. ālib:
‘God is with everything but not linked to anything; He is unlike
anything but not separate from anything’ (maʿa kull shayʾ lā bi-
muqārana wa ghayr kull shayʾ lā bi-muzāyala).115 In a similar context,
the Jāwidān-nāma refers to the saying of Jesus that sounds very close:
‘I am the Word, I am with everything and without everything’ (man
kalima-am wa bā hama ashyāʾ wa bī hama ashyāʾ hastam).116
Common to both Nasafī and the Jāwidān-nāma is also the idea that
the unity as a whole is not subject to evolution or involution; only parts
of the whole (cf. ‘parts of Adam’s body’ in the Jāwidān-nāma) can rise
or fall in the hierarchy of existents. Nasafī’s seven-step cosmic
hierarchy, stretching from minerals to the sphere of spheres, with
humans in the middle position, matches closely that of the Jāwidān-
nāma. We have seen that, in the Jāwidān-nāma, the cosmic human

des ʿAzīz-i Nasafī’, pp. 125–182, and summarised by Freitag, Seelenwanderung,
pp. 246–252.
114 Let us recall that the Jāwidān-nāma’s approach to the unity of existence is the
idea that the original Word with its 28/32 phonemes or ‘words’ constitutes the
ontological principle of all existents: ‘nothing [really] exists except the Word (ghayr az
kalima chīzī dīgar nīst)’ (fol. 464a).

71 (my translation).

form is identical to the sphere of spheres – the location of the Lote-tree
of the Boundary contemplated by Muh.ammad during his heavenly
ascension – and the sphere of spheres is also the furthermost limit in
Nasafī’s hierarchy.
In the absence of explicit references, the question of origins of the
Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrine remains open. In the present state of our
knowledge, and basing myself on what has been said earlier, I think
that there are two lines particularly promising for a further research on
the possible sources of the Jāwidān-nāma: the Kubrawī Suﬁtradition
(including the transmission of Ibn al-ʿArabī’s ideas) and thinkers
associated with it on the one hand, and esoteric Shiʿism, most probably
conveyed through the literature of Nizārī Ismailis, on the other. The
extent of interrelation between these two currents has still to be
elucidated,117 and the Jāwidān-nāma could be one of the forms where
they converged and mixed together.
In the meanwhile, it is probably more productive to regard the
Jāwidān-nāma as essentially an eclectic work, combining elements
taken from various sources within an original theoretical construct.
From this perspective, it is not the origins and inﬂuences, but
parallelisms in the contemporary dynamics of eclecticism that are
brought into focus. In other words, leaving aside the question of where
the different strata of doctrines could be taken from, it is more fruitful
to see if the way these doctrines and ideas are brought together pursues
a speciﬁc aim, either at a purely theoretical level or at a level of social
and political action. This brings us to the last section of this
Conclusion, where we will examine whether some features and
conceptions of the Jāwidān-nāma are in line with the general
tendencies developed in mystical and messianic circles of its time.

in his Introduction to Badakhchani, Paradise of Submission, pp. 2–3 and note 5,

Words of Power

The Messianic Project of the Jāwidān-nāma and the Use of
Christian Apocalyptic Texts
As discussed in the Introduction, Fad.l Allāh’s doctrine had some
socio-political implications related to the issue of religious authority.
One of the central doctrinal positions of the Jāwidān-nāma, the
principle of taʾwīl – a universal authoritative hermeneutics of Script-
ures based on the knowledge of the metaphysical meanings of the
letters of the alphabet – provided the messianic paradigm of religious
authority with an elaborate theoretical basis supporting the idea of
direct access to the source of prophetic revelation.118 In addition, some
developments of the Jāwidān-nāma can be regarded as a preparation
of the ground for the uniﬁcation of the Muslim community beyond
the old confessional divisions, and for interreligious dialogue open to
the integration of Jewish and Christian communities.
It should be noted that the latter tendencies are fully in line with the
Islamic description of the eschatological Saviour. Both Shiʿis and
Sunnis agree that the Saviour will restore the pristine purity of Islam
and the unity of the Muslim community. It is true that the points of
view on what constituted that pristine purity and the ways of its
restoration vary signiﬁcantly between Shiʿis and Sunnis, as well as their
views concerning the identity of the Saviour.119 The Jāwidān-nāma’s
emphasis on taʾwīl certainly brings it closer to the Shiʿi standpoint.
However, concerning the identity of the Saviour, the Jāwidān-nāma
seems to seek a conciliation between the Shiʿi and the Sunni positions.
118 Among Iranian messianic movements of the 8th/14th–9th/15th centuries, the
scholarly level of the Jāwidān-nāma’s doctrinal developments can arguably be
compared only to those of Muh.ammad Nūrbakhsh. The doctrinal basis of such
movements as the Sarbadārs or Musha‘sha‘ seems to be much less developed. On
them, see J. Aubin, ‘La ﬁn de l’état Sarbadār du Khorassan’, Journal Asiatique (1974),
pp. 95–118, and his ‘Aux origines d’un mouvement populaire medieval’; Y. Āzhand,
Qiyām-i Shīʿī-yi sarbadārān (Tehran, 1363/1984); A. Kasravī, Tārīkh-i pāns.ad sāla-yi
Khūzistān (Tehran, 1313/1934); P. Luft, ‘Mushaʿshaʿ’, EI2, vol. 7, pp. 672–675;
M. Mazzaoui, ‘Mushaʿshaʿiyān: A Fifteenth Century Shīʿī Movement in Khūzistān and
Southern Iraq’, Folia Orientalia 22 (1981–1984), pp. 139–162, and his The Origins of
the S.afawids, pp. 139–162; J. M. Smith, The History of the Sarbadar Dynasty, 1336–
1381 A.D. and its Sources (The Hague, 1970).
119 For the beliefs associated with the eschatological Saviour in various currents of
Islamic religious thought see Cook, Studies in Muslim Apocalyptic.
Conclusion

Whereas the former believe that the Saviour will belong to the line of
Shiʿi Imāms, the latter emphasise the eschatological role of Jesus in his
second coming. In Chapter 13, we have noted that the Jāwidān-nāma
cites both kinds of traditions and downplays the contradiction
between them by pointing to the ontological similarity of Jesus and an
Imām from the descendants of Fāt.ima, since both ﬁgures represent the
living Word of God. Another idea associated with the ﬁgure of
eschatological Saviour is the restoration of the universal message of
Islam, addressed to the entire humankind. The Jāwidān-nāma’s use of
biblical texts in parallel with Qurʾānic quotations is consistent with this
ecumenical dimension of the Islamic messianic expectation.
In this regard, the use of Christian apocalyptic literature in the
Jāwidān-nāma is particularly remarkable. As we have seen on several
occasions, the main source of Fad.l Allāh was apparently the Arabic
pseudo-Clementine literature, in particular the Arabic Apocalypse of
Peter referred to as the ‘Book of Peter/Simon’ (Kitāb-i Fit.rūs/Shamʿūn)
in the Jāwidān-nāma. The Arabic Apocalypse of Peter is a long text,
which existed in several recensions. Some manuscripts apparently
begin with the text known as the Cave of Treasures, followed by a
substantial continuation. There are two editions of the Arabic version
of the Cave of Treasures: by Carl Bezold, who also edited the Syriac
version and translated it into German, and by Margaret Dunlop
Gibson, who edited the Arabic version with an English translation.
The text following the Cave of Treasures has been translated by
Alphonse Mingana and published together with the Karshūnī text.120
The Jāwidān-nāma incorporated in its doctrinal discourse several
concepts from this Christian apocalyptic text, such as a speciﬁc

speaking Christian communities, and its possible role as one of the main channels

concept of Trinity (Father, Holy Spirit and Son being respectively
identiﬁed as Power without beginning, Voice and Word). It is almost
certain that the presence of the Arabic Apocalypse of Peter in the
Jāwidān-nāma is not limited to direct citations; traces of its speciﬁc
vocabulary can be also found in the fragments that do not contain
explicit references to the ‘Book of Peter’. Clearly recognisable citations
from the Arabic Apocalypse of Peter and their integration into the
Jāwidān-nāma, along with Muslim scriptural sources and canonical
biblical texts, provide important new evidence concerning the
circulation of this Christian apocalyptic text in Islamic milieus and,
more broadly, the mutual inﬂuence between the Christian and Islamic
messianic and apocalyptic traditions.121
The Arabic Apocalypse of Peter contains fragments close to the text
of the canonical biblical books. It is therefore possible that some of the
Jāwidān-nāma’s citations from the Old and New Testaments could
have been received by the intermediary of this apocrypha. However,
while examining the sections of the Arabic Apocalypse of Peter
published by Gibson and Mingana, I was unable to ﬁnd some of the
Jāwidān-nāma’s citations, explicitly referred to as the ‘Book of Peter’.
This concerns essentially the citations close to the canonical Revelation
of St John, such as the episode of the opening of the sealed Book and
the sacriﬁce of the Lamb. But the name of John is not mentioned in the
Jāwidān-nāma at all, which suggests that this episode could have been
in Fad.l Allāh’s version of the Apocalypse of Peter.122
In the light of what has been said in the previous chapters
concerning the Jāwidān-nāma’s conception of taʾwīl and the
eschatological role of Jesus during his second coming, the Jāwidān-
nāma’s use of the Christian apocalyptic texts, though unusual in the

Conclusion

Islamic context, seems perfectly logical. It is consistent with
ecumenical dimension inherent to the messianic outlook, and
represents an example of the synthesis of scriptural material and
symbolism belonging to various religious traditions in Islamic
messianic milieu. The Seven Twofold of the Qurʾān and the seven
seals of the apocalyptic Book mentioned in the Revelation of John
point, in the Jāwidān-nāma, to the same event of disclosure of the
original divine Word, to the ultimate taʾwīl that constitutes the goal of
all religions, and to the subsequent uniﬁcation of the entire
humankind beyond all linguistic and religious divisions.
The Jāwidān-nāma’s conception of ‘motherly’ (ummī) knowledge
and the ‘motherly’ prophets and saints, associated with the doctrine of
taʾwīl, is particularly important from the point of view of Shiʿi/Sunni
conciliation. This conception arguably preserves the principal features
of the Shiʿi doctrine of the Imām as possessor of esoteric initiatory
knowledge, and expresses them in a form, if not smoothly compatible
with, at least not directly contradicting the mainstream Sunni views on
prophecy
and
sainthood.
The
Jāwidān-nāma’s
conception
of
‘motherly’ saints can, therefore, be arguably regarded as an attempt
at elaborating a conﬁguration of religious authority acceptable to all
factions of the contemporary Muslim community.
The period immediately preceding Fad.l Allāh’s lifetime was marked
by a dramatic evolution of the doctrines concerning the nature of
sainthood, associated with more or less expressed messianic expecta-
tions. On the Suﬁside, Ibn al-ʿArabī revitalised the reﬂection on the
issue of ‘Seal of the Sainthood’ formulated earlier by H. akīm al-
Tirmidhī, and the relationship between legislative and non-legislative
prophecy in Islamic mysticism.123 Notwithstanding the fact that Ibn
al-ʿArabī seems to explicitly demarcate the functions of the Seal of
Muh.ammadan sainthood from those of the Seal of general sainthood
identiﬁed with Jesus in his second coming, Ibn al-ʿArabī’s conception
of the Seal of Sainthood still implies a tremendous religious authority
123 On Ibn al-ʿArabī’s conception of two Seals of sainthood, see Chodkiewicz, Le
Sceau des saints, in particular pp. 121–150.
Words of Power

that exerted a signiﬁcant inﬂuence upon the later reformist and
messianic developments.124
On the Shiʿi side, the major contribution along the same line was the
doctrine of qiyāma formulated in Alamūt. This doctrine evolved, in
the Nizārī Ismaili tradition, from a radical to a moderate messianic
worldview, the latter being reﬂected in the works such as Rawd.ā-yi
taslīm, attributed to Nas.īr al-Dīn T. ūsī. Previously, we have mentioned
the parallelisms between the ideas developed in the Rawd.ā and the
contents of the Jāwidān-nāma. More generally, the Nizārī doctrine
appears to have offered a mature theoretical framework for later
messianic
developments.
The
idea
of
disclosure
of
universal
metaphysical truths, essential to the doctrine of qiyāma, in association
with the strict observation of religious law, emphasised in its reformed
version,125 provided a powerful basis for doctrinal developments
aiming at the uniﬁcation of the Muslim community beyond sectarian
divisions, and for the re-vitalisation of the ecumenical dimension of
Islam. These tendencies strongly marked the intellectual and socio-
political atmosphere of the 8th/14th and 9th/15th centuries, and were
shared by several messianic groups of that time.
These messianic doctrines present in both Suﬁand Shiʿi currents
emphasised the high, quasi-prophetic religious authority which could
be achieved by a Suﬁsaint, who would obtain direct access to the
source of divine inspiration, or manifested in a Shiʿi Imām. Both the
Suﬁand Shiʿi forms of messianism and related conceptions of
sainthood could be a source of inspiration for the Jāwidān-nāma’s
theoretical constructions, which seem to prepare the foundations of a

Conclusion

new conﬁguration of religious authority together with an ecumenical
dimension ensured by the integration of the Jewish and Christian
scriptural sources. Such a conﬁguration had a good prospect of being
eventually adopted as ofﬁcial ideology by any of the numerous clans
competing for power in Iran and Anatolia in the 8th/14th and 9th/
15th centuries.
At this point, after the study of the textual evidence from the
Jāwidān-nāma, it will be useful to return to the set of ideas discussed in
the Introduction. We have seen that Fad.l Allāh most probably claimed
a saintly status for himself, based on his knowledge of taʾwīl, and
sought an alliance with political leaders of his time. We do not know
precisely how close Fad.l Allāh and his followers came to the realisation
of their political projects. But we do know that they were not alone.
The H. urūfīs apparently entertained difﬁcult and contradictory
relationships, including mutual inﬂuence and ﬁerce competition,
with similar contemporary currents of thought developing the ‘science
of letters’ as a path of direct access to the source of prophetic
inspiration, in particular with reference to the ideas of Ibn al-ʿArabī.
The prominent Iranian thinker S.āʾin al-Dīn Turka Is.fahānī (d. 835/
1432), and ʿAbd al-Rah.mān al-Bistāmī (d. 858/1454) from the
Ottoman capital of Bursa, very probably had ﬁrst-hand knowledge
of Fad.l Allāh’s doctrines and vehemently rejected them, while
advocating essentially similar ideas.126 Already in the Tīmūrid period,
a doctrine combining mystical and messianic ideas with the ‘science of
letters’, like Fad.l Allāh’s works, attracted the interest of the ruling
elites.127 The uniﬁcation of Iran was eventually achieved not by the
H. urūfīs, but by a movement similarly relying on mystical and

founded by Fad.l Allāh, see Corbin, En Islam Iranien, vol. 3, pp. 252–257; Āzhand,
H. urūﬁyya, pp. 80–81; Melvin-Koushki, The Quest for a Universal Science, in particular
pp. 235–247; D. Gril, ‘Esotérisme contre hérésie: ʿAbd al-Rah.mân al-Bistâmî, un

messianic conception of religious authority, the S.afawids, whose
alliance with the Turkic Qizilbash proved more successful than the
political enterprise of the H. urūfīs. The impact of Fad.l Allāh’s ideas on
the S.afawids and their presence in the Qizilbash milieus, though highly
probable, seems difﬁcult to trace in the actual state of research. The
inﬂuence of H. urūfī ideas on the ruling elites is more visible in Mughal
India, where the Nuqt.awīs, an offshoot of the H. urūﬁs, arguably played
an important role in the reforms of Emperor Akbar.128 It will be
recalled that H. urūfī ideas circulated widely among the Ottoman Suﬁ
orders, and had particularly solid roots in the inﬂuential Bektāshī
milieus, where H. urūfī works, including the Jāwidān-nāma-yi kabīr,
were preserved, studied, copied, translated and interpreted.
It can, therefore, be concluded that, although H. urūﬁsm as such did
not achieve any political success, the messianic project of the Jāwidān-
nāma was a signiﬁcant contribution to the elaboration of a new para-
digm of religious authority that contributed to the emergence and
consolidation of a new socio-political order in the eastern part of the
Islamic world. Produced in the mystical and messianic milieus as an
answer to the radical crisis of religious authority intoduced by the
Mongol invasion, this paradigm, in conjunction with other factors,
eventually led to crystallisation of the mystical and messianic ideal of
uniﬁcation of the Muslim community under the rule of a divinely
inspired leader, combining both religious and political power.129 In
various ways and in various proportions, this ideal played a signiﬁcant
role in the emergence and consolidation of three great Muslim empires:
Ottoman, S.afawid and Mughal. And the Jāwidān-nāma was arguably
one of the earliest advocates of this ideal in the post-Mongol era.

Monarchs, and Messiahs: Cultural Landscapes of Early Modern Iran (Cambridge, MA

on Akbar’s reforms, see A. Amanat, ‘Persian Nuqtawis and the Shaping of the Doct-

129 On the role played by the concept of sacred kingship in the Tīmūrid, S.afawid
and Mughal context, see Moin, The Millennial Sovereign, and on the application of
messianic and millenarist ideas by Ottoman rulers, see Fleischer, ‘The Lawgiver as
Messiah’.
Conclusion

Final Notes
As discussed in the Introduction, the primary goal of the present book
has been to provide an accurate and coherent reconstruction of the
central themes and concepts of the original H. urūfī doctrine, and to
serve as a starting point for a more systematic study of its further
evolution. It also allows us to see what is deﬁnitely not in the Jāwidān-
nāma and revise critically doctrinal positions and claims attributed to
Fad.l Allāh either by his followers or by external sources. The
familiarity with H. urūfī
technical vocabulary, the most important
terms of which are summarised in the Glossary, will, it is to be hoped,
be useful for a better understanding not only of H. urūfī doctrinal texts
but also of the symbolism used in H. urūfī poetry. Of course, the
reconstruction attempted in this book should be completed by a sound
critical edition of the Jāwidān-nāma. It can be expected that a
thorough assessment of the authenticity of other texts attributed to
Fad.l Allāh, and a subsequent comparison of his authentic works with
the contents of the Jāwidān-nāma will provide material for more or
less signiﬁcant adjustments to the present reconstruction.
The next step would be the identiﬁcation of signiﬁcant H. urūfī
doctrinal works produced by Fad.l Allāh’s followers. In the ﬁrst
generation, the works of such authors as ʿAlī al-Aʿlā, Sayyid Ish.āq
Astarābādī and Ghiyāth al-Dīn Astarābādī, seem particularly import-
ant. Ideally, the works of every individual H. urūfī author should be
studied separately, against the background of available biographical
information about his intellectual and socio-political environment.
The results of such individual studies on H. urūfī authors could be then
compared between them and with Fad.l Allāh’s original doctrine. To
this should be added important anonymous works.130 I believe that
such an approach can provide an accurate reconstruction of the
intellectual history of the H. urūfīs, avoiding the shortcomings involved
in conclusions based on random selections of H. urūfī works and
external sources.
A systematic study of H. urūfī intellectual history should be
completed by the study of the historical, bio-bibliographical and
130 For example, Sharh. -i Jāwidān, an anonymous commentary of the Jāwidān-
nāma used by K. M. al-Shaybī. See references in al-S.ila, p. 156, note 6.
Words of Power

hagiographical works of H. urūfī authors. Several of these works have
been described by A. Gölpınarlı in his Huruﬁlik metinleri kataloğu,
and fragments from some of them have been used in scholarly
literature on the H. urūﬁs.131 A thorough exploration of this category of
sources can signiﬁcantly extend our knowledge concerning Fad.l
Allāh’s intellectual and political relationships and sources of inspira-
tion, as well as the actual links between the H. urūfīs and other Islamic
movements and individual thinkers. The contribution of H. urūfī
literature on Persian and Turkic poetry and visual arts, especially
calligraphy, is another and still very little explored ﬁeld of study.
A careful identiﬁcation of Jewish and Christian canonical and
apocryphal materials used in H. urūfī texts is another interesting and
promising ﬁeld of study. The presence of citations from the Old and
New Testaments in the Jāwidān-nāma and, in particular, the use of
such texts as the Revelation of St John and the Arabic Apocalypse of
Peter provide important new evidence for the reﬂection on the mutual
inﬂuence and exchanges between Muslim, Christian and Jewish
messianic circles and literatures and, on a still deeper level, between
the material of tradition of the three great monotheist religions. As
already noted above, the Jāwidān-nāma provides examples of a
coherent, non-polemical integration of the Jewish and Christian
sources in an Islamic messianic discourse on a par with Islamic
scriptural material. This demonstrates that the messianic outlook,
integrating the idea of ecumenical unity of mankind, possessed a
signiﬁcant potential for a deeper dialogue among the intellectual and
mystical circles of the three religions.
In a broader socio-political perspective, further research of H. urūfī
history and doctrines will enable a better understanding of an
important stratum of mystical and messianic ferment, which played an
important role in the reconﬁguration of the concepts of religious and
political authority in the Muslim East in 8th/14th and 9th/15th
centuries, and had a lasting and multifaceted inﬂuence on the
subsequent evolution of Muslim societies.
131 These include such works as the Khwāb-nāma’s of ʿAlī Nafajī and of Sayyid
Isḥāq, the Mah. ram-nāma of Sayyid Ish.āq, the Kursī-nāma of ʿAlī al-Aʿlā, the Istiwāʾ-
nāma of Ghiyāth al-Dīn Astarābādī, the Bayān al-wāqiʿ of Mīr Sharīf, and several
other works.
Conclusion

Glossary of Key Technical Terms
28/32:
A reference to the dual number of the primary
ontological ‘words’ (kalima, pl. kalimāt), which
constitute together the original Word (q.v.) of
God. According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the 28/32
are present within the uniﬁed divine Essence, and
appear as separate simple sounds, or phonemes,
after the differentiation (q.v.). The 28/32
phonemes are the basis of all existing words and
sounds: no sound in the world, produced by
humans, animals or inanimate objects, can
exceed their number. The relationship between
the series of 28 and 32 can be ‘complementary’,
when they sum up to 60 (28+32=60). In this case,
60 is described as a number expressing fullness or
perfection. For example, according to the well-
known h. adīth, Adam’s body measures 60 cubits,
an hour contains 60 minutes, and the heavenly
sphere contains six times 60 degrees. The
relationship can also be ‘inclusive’, when the
series of 28 is contained in the series of 32. In
this case, it is the number 32 that expresses the
idea of fullness. For example, at the beginning of
the prophetic cycle, the full number of the 32
ontological ‘words’ was revealed to Adam. In the
process of revelation (tanzīl) (q.v.), 28 of these
‘words’ were progressively disclosed to mankind.
After the closure of revelation with the mission of
the Prophet Muh.ammad, four remaining words
will be disclosed in the hermeneutic process of
the ‘return to the origin’ (taʾwīl) (q.v.), at the end

of which the original number of the 32 ‘words’ of
the divine Word will be attained. The
identiﬁcation of the 28 with the number of letters
of the Arabic alphabet, and of the 32 with the
number of letters of the Arabo-Persian alphabet,
is certainly alluded to in the Jāwidān-nāma, but
does not seem central to the set of ideas related
to these numbers. The conclusions that Fad.l
Allāh’s intention was to emphasise the supremacy
of Persian over Arabic should, therefore, be
approached carefully. First, the Jāwidān-nāma
states that the four additional ‘words’ are
contained implicitly already in the Arabic of the
Qurʾānic revelation, and were explicitly shown to
Muh.ammad during his heavenly ascension.
Second, the number 32 is not necessarily related
to the number of letters of the Persian alphabet.
For example, in the Jewish esoteric tradition, the
Sefer Yetsirah mentions the 32 ‘ways of wisdom’,
constituted by the 22 letters of the Hebrew
alphabet and the 10 numbers. The number 33 is
also mentioned by the Ismaili thinker Abū H. ātim
al-Rāzī in his Kitāb al-zīna, with reference to a
tradition from Jaʿfar al-S.ādiq, as the total number
of letters in human languages, of which the
Arabic is the most perfect.1
Adam and Eve:
According to the Jāwidān-nāma, the human
bodily form (s.ūra) (q.v.) has been created as the
locus of manifestation (q.v.) of the complete set
of the 28/32 original ‘words’ (q.v.). It is therefore
the most perfect form in the universe, the only
form that contains the ‘science’ (q.v.) of the
complete divine Word. The human form is the
form of the supreme Name of God. According to

the Jāwidān-nāma’s interpretation of Qurʾān
2:31, after having created the body of Adam as

taught Adam the metaphysical meaning (q.v.) of
this form. While Adam’s bodily form is given
unconditionally to all his descendants, the

Twofold’), are called ‘motherly’ (ummī) (q.v.)

writing on the male bodily form has only one

lines, namely the line of balance (q.v.). These
lines are multiplied by the number of four
natural elements, which gives 28 and 32 lines,
for female and male bodily forms respectively.

additional aspect of the duality represented by
the series of the 28 and 32. If Adam is compared
to the Qurʾān, Eve is the ‘mother of the Book’
(umm al-kitāb), ‘she who opens the Book’

the fact that all inhabitants of Paradise, including

youth. The royal way of taʾwīl is the way of love,

when two lovers discern the ‘science’ of the

In this case, the union of two lovers, each of
